Designing dislocation-driven polar vortex networks in twisted perovskites

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 45 min read (8988 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~45 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Twisting two atomic layers produces a geometric moiré pattern but bonding-induced interfacial reconstruction fundamentally transforms this into an ordered dislocation network—a distinction obscured in weakly bonded van der Waals systems.
  • Dislocations are topological line defects central to materials science5,6.
  • Recent findings suggest that although two-dimensional materials provide a powerful platform for moiré engineering, they are mostly limited to compounds with non-covalent interlayer bonding, in which coupling is mediated by weakly hybridized s and p electrons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Twisting two atomic layers produces a geometric moiré pattern but bonding-induced interfacial reconstruction fundamentally transforms this into an ordered dislocation network—a distinction obscured in weakly bonded van der Waals systems. Although in-plane topological vortex nanostructures arising from twisting-induced lateral strain modulation have been linked to periodic moiré patterns in freestanding perovskite layers1,2,3 and 2D bilayers4, their coupling to the interfacial dislocation network in twisted layers remains unresolved. Here we demonstrate that twisted freestanding SrTiO3 (STO) layers undergo interfacial reconstruction into a network of screw dislocations, accompanied by the emergence of in-plane topological vortices. Unlike in previous reports, these vortices are associated with the dislocation network rather than with geometric moiré patterns. Four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4DSTEM) reveals a beam deflection texture in registry with the interfacial dislocation network. A machine learning interatomic potential, trained on first-principles calculations, together with phase-field modelling, confirms that competing strains within the dislocation network stabilize polar vortex–antivortex pairs; first-principles calculations further reveal the emergence of an electronic superlattice with a well-defined periodicity. Our results establish twist-controlled dislocation networks as a newly introduced and versatile route to designing local polar and electronic structures in oxide materials.

Dislocations are topological line defects central to materials science5,6. By relieving elastic energy through local symmetry breaking, they strongly modify mechanical, electronic and structural properties. In two-dimensional materials, ordered defect networks and moiré structures demonstrate that controlled symmetry breaking can generate emergent electronic and optical states7,8,9,10,11,12, establishing dislocations as tunable building blocks for latest functionalities.

Recent findings suggest that although two-dimensional materials provide a powerful platform for moiré engineering, they are mostly limited to compounds with non-covalent interlayer bonding, in which coupling is mediated by weakly hybridized s and p electrons. This inherently restricts the range of accessible interactions and properties. By contrast, transition metal oxides (TMOs), governed by strongly correlated d electrons, host a much richer electronic landscape absent from most conventional two-dimensional materials. Their strong coupling between charge, spin and orbital degrees of freedom result in phenomena including high-temperature superconductivity13, colossal magnetoresistance14, Mott insulating states15 and multiferroicity16.

TMOs are traditionally grown epitaxially17,18, in which lattice matching and coherent interfaces restrict viable material combinations. Quasi-atomically thin freestanding oxide membranes now provide an alternative route to synthetic heterostructures through layer-by-layer stacking3,19,20,21. By bypassing the constraints of heteroepitaxy, this approach enables interfacial configurations and material pairings that are otherwise thermodynamically or kinetically inaccessible. It also permits control of the relative in-plane orientation between stacked membranes, creating twisted interfaces and in-plane moiré patterns2,3,22.

It has been revealed that stacking two freestanding membranes with a twist angle θ produces a geometric moiré superlattice with observed periodicity λ = (a/2)/sin(θ/2), in which a is the cubic lattice constant23. In two-dimensional materials, long-period moirés at small θ relax into stacked domains separated by dislocation networks24,25 and a similar network has been observed in twisted Si (refs. 26,27,28). Because coherent interfacial regions are energetically favoured, lattice strain drives dislocation formation at small twist angles, whereas larger angles promote preferred coincidence-site-lattice (CSL) configurations29. As illustrated schematically in Fig. 1a, interfacial energy at small angles scales with dislocation density30, whereas at larger angles, discrete CSL configurations produce local energy minima. Dislocation formation is therefore expected to be favourable below about 15° (ref. 31). However, direct experimental evidence for such networks in freestanding TMO membranes, and their impact on structural, physical and electronic properties (Fig. 1b), remains lacking32.

In a recent development, a, Schematic of moiré, chirality and dislocation regimes as well as the CSLs of the twisted system (blue squares). The red diamond symbols in the figure represent the twist angles explored in this study. b, Graphical depiction of emergent properties at the interface: moiré pattern (M), chirality (C) and dislocations (D). The regime in which these effects occur is shown in a. c, From left to right: HAADF intensity line profile, cross-section STEM image of twisted θ = 20°, sample showing a clean and sharp STO/STO interface, highlighting the SrO–TiO2 termination, and EELS measurement spectra of Ti L2,3-edges at the interface and within the membrane, highlighting the homogeneity and cleanliness of the interface. The inset in the second panel of c is the simulated STEM image based on the structural model described in the text. a.u., arbitrary units. Scale bars, 1 nm.

Industry observers note that we show experimentally and theoretically that twisted freestanding STO membranes reconstruct into an ordered interfacial network of polar screw dislocations. High-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) and 4DSTEM, supported by ab initio TEM (abTEM) simulations and a density functional theory (DFT)-trained machine-learned interatomic potential (MLIP), reveal a long-range ordered dislocation pattern with polar vortex arrays in the interface plane. Each moiré plaquette forms a locally coherent interface, whereas strain is accommodated by an orthogonal square network of screw dislocations. Phase-field modelling on the basis of atomistic strain gradients shows that flexoelectric polarization localizes along the dislocation lines, with in-plane nodal chirality of polar vortex–antivortex arrays and an out-of-plane component. DFT indicates that the reconstructed interface is chiral and hosts mid-gap states absent in bulk STO, with potential implications for electronic and optoelectronic properties.

Industry observers note that freestanding bilayers of STO were created by stacking two STO membranes with twist angles of 5°, 7.5°, 10° and 20°. Figure 1c, left panel shows the HAADF intensity line profile along the [001] direction across a representative 20° twisted STO/STO interface. The interplanar distance d(001) between consecutive Sr columns is approximately 0.39 nm. Also shown in Fig. 1c is the cross-section HAADF image. These data show that the interface is clean, bonded and free of detectable contamination, with a well-defined [010] zone-axis orientation. The agreement between the cross-sectional STEM image and the corresponding simulation further indicates the absence of unintended defects or inhomogeneities (see inset). Electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) analysis further verifies the chemical uniformity and high quality of the interface. Ti L2,3 edge spectra acquired at the interface and within the membrane (Fig. 1c, right panels) exhibit nearly identical spectral features, accompanied by minimal variations in the Ti L-edge and low-loss EELS signals across the interfacial plane. Cross-sectional HAADF imaging demonstrates that the interfaces are also clean and well bonded for all measured twist angles, θ = 5°, 7.5°, 10° and 20° (Supplementary Fig. 1). See Methods and Supplementary Note 1 for growth, release and stacking, along with characterization details (Supplementary Figs. 2–4).

Recent findings suggest that we studied STO/STO homobilayers with twist angles of 5°, 7.5°, 10° and 20°, for which dislocations are expected at or below the critical twist angle of about 15°. Figure 2 presents a strategy view of a STEM image of the 5° sample (Fig. 2a) compared with a rigid structure (Fig. 2b), both showing a moiré pattern. The rigid moiré pattern is visualized by overlaying two periodic STO (100) plane grids with a 5° relative rotation, without allowing for interfacial reconstruction. The experimental HAADF-STEM image (Fig. 2a) shows a well-defined moiré pattern that closely resembles the rigid moiré structure (Fig. 2b). By contrast, Fig. 2c shows the interfacial relaxed structure obtained from the MLIP-DFT calculations (SrO–TiO2 termination; see Methods, Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Figs. 5–8 for details). The relaxed structure reveals coherent domains separated by a network of screw dislocations, highlighted by the black square. Figure 2d shows the simulated HAADF-STEM image generated from this relaxed structure (see abTEM description in Methods). These results indicate a dislocation network, absent from both the experimental image and the rigid structural model. This apparent discrepancy reflects the finite depth sensitivity of STEM imaging (Supplementary Note 3). The experimental HAADF signal is not generated solely by two bonded atomic planes comprising the interface but contains contributions from all unit cells above and below it, as illustrated schematically in Fig. 2a. The measured contrast therefore represents a depth-averaged projection of the twisted bilayer and naturally recovers an apparently rigid moiré pattern. Hence, Fig. 2a–d highlights that agreement between an experimental plan-view HAADF image and a rigid moiré model should not be interpreted as evidence for the absence of interfacial reconstruction. Rather, the depth-integrated nature of the HAADF signal can conceal the reconstructed interface altogether.

a, Strategy-view HAADF-STEM image of the 5° twisted bilayer, showing the square moiré pattern. The inset schematically illustrates the depth-averaged origin of the STEM signal. b, Rigid structure rotations of two [001]-oriented STO crystals. Sr and Ti atoms are shown in blue and cyan, respectively. c, MLIP-DFT-relaxed SrO–TiO2 interface, showing coherent domains separated by a square screw-dislocation network. d, Interface-restricted abTEM simulation based on the relaxed atomic structure, revealing contrast associated with the reconstructed interface. e, Local stacking configurations within the moiré cell, distinguishing AA, AA′, AB and BA regions. The dislocation lines form between AB and BA regions, marked by their Burgers vectors \({\hat{{\bf{b}}}}_{1},{\hat{{\bf{b}}}}_{2}\), and enclose coherent commensurate domains. f, Simulated (MLIP) in-plane shear strain component, εxy, extracted from the relaxed TiO2-terminated interfacial plane. The strain is concentrated along the dislocation lines, whereas the square domain centres remain weakly strained. g, Plan-view HAADF-STEM image of the 20° twisted bilayer, showing the projected square moiré pattern. h, Interface-restricted abTEM simulation based on the relaxed atomic structure, revealing a similar moiré pattern to the experimental HAADF. i, Calculated in-plane shear strain component, εxy, for the 20° twisted bilayer, indicating that the strain field follows the spatial distribution of the rigid moiré pattern, in contrast to the 5° rotation. The red lines mark the dislocation spacing, d = 4.5 nm. Scale bars, 2 nm.

The relation between the rigid moiré pattern and the dislocation network can be understood in terms of local stacking. Following the previous convention3,33, we label the stacking configurations as AA and AB. However, because the repeated moiré sites are not all crystallographically equivalent, BA and AA′ regions must be distinguished (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). On relaxation, the interface expands the energetically favourable commensurate AA and AA′ domains and concentrates the remaining twist-induced mismatch into screw dislocations located between AB and BA regions (Fig. 2e). The spacing between adjacent dislocation lines is denoted as d (Supplementary Note 2). In a strongly bonded oxide, this reconstruction maximizes interfacial coordination by increasing the area of coherent bonding across the interface (Extended Data Fig. 1). Away from the interface, the atoms regain full coordination and the driving force for reconstruction is removed, leading to rapid decay of the strain along the thickness direction (Supplementary Figs. 9 and 10).

Recent findings suggest that to visualize strain in the interfacial layer, we calculated the strain field using MLIP-DFT. We show that the reconstructed interface is distinct from a rigid moiré pattern, with strain governed by the square dislocation network (Fig. 2f). The in-plane shear component, εxy, exhibits sharp gradients along the square dislocation lines, whereas the centres of the square domains remain coherent and weakly strained (Fig. 2f, Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Figs. 11 and 12). This indicates that the strain is localized at the screw-dislocation cores and arises from interfacial reconstruction, differing fundamentally from strain maps inferred directly from STEM images, in which the apparent strain follows the rigid moiré periodicity1,2,3,33. To compare with earlier analyses, we also estimated strain from the HAADF focal series (Supplementary Note 4 and Supplementary Figs. 13–16). This yielded a vortex-like strain pattern, consistent with previous reports1,2,3,33 but distinct from the interface-resolved MLIP-DFT strain field, which is governed by the dislocation network.

To assess the thickness dependence of the simulated STEM contrast and its relation to experiment, we added further layers above and below the relaxed interface in the abTEM simulations. In HAADF-STEM, the added layers drive the contrast towards the experimentally observed rigid moiré pattern. The same approach was applied to low-angle annular dark-field (LAADF)-STEM simulations (Supplementary Fig. 17), a mode commonly used to image dislocations owing to its high sensitivity to small atomic displacements34. With increasing thickness, the simulated LAADF contrast becomes progressively more diffuse, partially obscuring the screw-dislocation network and closely matching the experimentally observed LAADF focal series (Supplementary Figs. 18 and 19).

For the 20° twisted bilayer, the relaxed interface no longer exhibits the pronounced screw-dislocation network observed at smaller twist angles (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 3). Accordingly, the experimental HAADF/LAADF image agrees well with the simulated HAADF/LAADF images as well as experimental shear strain, based on a relaxed moiré structure (Fig. 2g,h and Supplementary Figs. 20–23), unlike the 5° twisted bilayer (Fig. 2a,c). These results indicate a crossover from dislocation-mediated reconstruction at small twist angles to a non-dislocated interface at larger twist angles. The corresponding strain distribution follows the spatial periodicity of the rigid moiré pattern, in contrast to the 5° case (Fig. 2i).

In a recent development, to verify the existence of the square dislocation network, we examined the twisted bicrystal cross-sections along the orthogonal (100) and (110) planes. These cuts examine different directions through the same interfacial network and therefore provide an internal check of its geometry (Fig. 3a–c). The MLIP model predicts projected dislocation spacings of 4.5 nm along (100) and 3.2 nm along (110) (Extended Data Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 24). Consistent with this, both cross-sectional views show periodic dark-contrast features at the expected dislocation positions: 4.5 nm in Fig. 3d and 3.2 nm in Fig. 3e.

a, Schematic of the two STO membranes oriented in the cubic lattice coordinate system. b,c, Illustration of cross-section cuts in the (100) in red (b) and (110) in green (c) planes, respectively, highlighting the square moiré plaquette network in black. d,e, The (100) and (110) cuts in cross-sectional HAADF imaging are presented, highlighting the periodicity of dislocations. The distances between image contrast, marked by white circles, are denoted as d1 and d2, corresponding to 4.2 ± 0.3 nm and 3.0 ± 0.3 nm, respectively. f, Magnified HAADF-STEM (110) image of the interface used for EELS analysis. The dislocation core is labelled ‘D’ and the neighbouring reconstructed reference region is labelled R. g,h, EELS spectra of the O and Ti L2,3-edge fine structure acquired from the dislocation core, surrounding interface and bulk-like region, showing a change of fine structure only in the two interfacial TiO2 planes. i, Line spectra of the Ti L2,3-edge, highlighting the reduced crystal-field splitting at the dislocation core (D in magenta), which is different from the reconstructed region (R in dark grey). a.u., arbitrary units. Scale bar, 2 nm.

Pixel-intensity analysis based on several samples (Supplementary Fig. 25) yields spacings of d1 = 4.2 ± 0.3 nm in Fig. 3d and d2 = 3.0 ± 0.3 nm in Fig. 3e, in excellent agreement with the MLIP predictions. The recurring dark contrast is consistent with strain at the dislocation cores and lines, which lowers HAADF intensity through local disorder, lattice tilt and enhanced dechannelling. Such a regular dislocation array is unlikely without a sharp, strongly bonded interface35. Consistent with this, the reconstruction is confined to a few atomic planes and the dark contrast in Fig. 3d,e arises from the interface rather than imaging artefacts (Supplementary Fig. 24). The measured spacings differ by approximately √2, exactly as expected for a square lattice viewed along (100) and its diagonal (110), providing independent experimental confirmation of a square interfacial dislocation network. A Burgers circuit analysis for the θ = 5° relaxed structure provides a Burgers vector magnitude equal to the bulk STO lattice constant (|b| = 3.9 Å; Methods). A similar dislocation network was also observed for twist angles of 7.5° and 10°, with spacings in cross-section agreeing well with their expected values (Extended Data Fig. 4).

To determine whether the dislocation cores are also chemically distinct, we performed spatially resolved EELS (Methods) across the 5° twisted interface. The analysis was centred on the interfacial region marked in Fig. 3f, in which the HAADF-STEM imaging reveals a localized contrast feature at the dislocation core, labelled ‘D’, relative to the surrounding registry region, labelled ‘R’. Spectra acquired from D show clear differences from those measured in the bulk-like membrane region and from neighbouring non-dislocated interfacial areas (numbered (1)–(5) in Fig. 3f–h). Quantification of the elemental edges reveals the presence of Ti3+, indicating local oxygen deficiency at the dislocation core D as compared with R.

According to recent reports, the Ti L2,3-edge fine structure at D provides further evidence for a modified local bonding environment. The difference between the fine structure of the two core loss spectra indicates a reduction in the crystal-field splitting at the dislocation core compared with the surrounding region without a dislocation (Fig. 3i). This change is consistent with altered Ti–O coordination and partial oxygen-vacancy formation at the screw-dislocation core reported for screw dislocations in STO (ref. 36), supporting our assignment of chemically and structurally distinct dislocation cores.

To determine the functional properties of the dislocation network, we mapped the in-plane beam deflection at the twisted interface using 4DSTEM centre-of-mass (CoM) imaging and abTEM simulations along with phase-field modelling (Fig. 4a–h and Methods). In the 5° bilayer, the experimental CoM deflection map shows a repeating nanoscale texture with 4.7 ± 0.2 nm spacing, matching the reconstructed dislocation network (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 26). The strongest deflections are concentrated at the screw-dislocation crossings (dashed white circles), where the interfacial distortion is largest, with weaker contrast along the connecting dislocation lines (white rectangles). This assignment is supported by abTEM simulations: the MLIP-relaxed interface reproduces the periodic CoM contrast registry with the dislocation network (Fig. 4c), whereas a rigidly moiré twisted, unrelaxed structure does not (Fig. 4d). Thus, the measured field texture is not simply a moiré artefact but arises from atomic reconstruction at the bonded interface (Fig. 4e, Supplementary Note 5 and Supplementary Figs. 27–30). As seen in the CoM map, at the AB/BA stacking centres, the field winding number is n = +1. This is also reproduced in the abTEM simulation using the MLIP-relaxed atomic positions (Fig. 4b,c,e). At these specimen thicknesses, the CoM deflection follows from the projected atomic potential, any local field and multiple scattering within the sample37,38; we therefore read it as a structural signature of the dislocation network, with its polar character supported by the relaxed-structure displacements and phase-field results. Figure 4f shows the Ti-atom off-centring in-plane displacements in the MLIP-relaxed structure (black arrows, visualized in the SrO-terminated interface), which reveals that the twisted interface is chiral, hosting only clockwise displacement vorticity with n = +1. Hence, the screw character of the dislocations selects a single winding sense, breaking the mirror symmetry that would otherwise enforce equal populations of handedness.

Sources indicate that a, Schematic of the 4DSTEM deflection measurement on a twisted oxide bilayer hosting an interfacial screw-dislocation network. b, Experimental 4DSTEM CoM deflection map of the 5° twisted membrane (8.4 nm total thickness); hue denotes deflection direction and brightness its magnitude. Dashed circles mark AB/BA stacking; the white rectangles show the expected dislocation position. c–e, Simulated 4DSTEM CoM deflection for MLIP-relaxed structure (c, 8.4 nm, reproducing the experimental texture), the rigidly twisted, unrelaxed interface (d, 8.4 nm) and the MLIP-relaxed interface (e, 2.1 nm). f, Ti-atom off-centring calculated in the MLIP-relaxed structure, demonstrating clockwise (CW) polar vorticity (yellow) throughout, yielding a winding number of n = +1 at the AB and BA stacking locations. g, Flexoelectric |P|, from phase-field calculations, in the x–y plane, at the same scale as b–f. h, Cross-sectional |P|, showing polar confinement within about 2 nm of the interface (cut along the dashed yellow line in g). i, PDOS and valence-edge charge-density isosurfaces, showing electronic states localized along the low-angle dislocation network. Scale bars, 2 nm.

To investigate the origin of the polarization, we implemented a phase-field model using MLIP-DFT-evaluated strain gradients of the θ = 5° reconstructed interface (about 0.03 nm−1), which exceed literature reports39,40 and lie firmly in the flexoelectric regime41. Our results show that the dislocation geometry underpins the emergence of flexoelectric polarization (|P| ≈ 2 μC cm−2) that localizes along the dislocation lines, particularly the AA–AA′ boundaries (Fig. 4g, Methods, Supplementary Note 6 and Supplementary Figs. 31–35). This polarization is confined to the interface and decays within about 2 nm, revealing non-zero out-of-plane components (Pz) (Fig. 4h and Extended Data Fig. 5) indicating a decaying strength of strain gradients into registry (Supplementary Figs. 10, 31 and 32). Although the in-plane shear εxy is strongly confined to the interface, accompanying out-of-plane strain gradients couple to Pz through the cubic flexoelectric tensor. Within the flexoelectric functional used here, the model yields polarization vortices of alternating clockwise and anticlockwise handedness at the network nodes—an achiral texture that preserves topological charge neutrality (Fig. 4g and Supplementary Figs. 33 and 34). In the 20° bilayer, the polarization also reveals alternating clockwise/anticlockwise vortices with handedness reversal across the interface (Supplementary Fig. 33), indicating that twist-induced polar textures persist beyond the dislocation-rich regime—in agreement with other works42.

According to recent reports, electronic structure calculations on the relaxed MLIP-DFT structure show that, for a low-angle interface, occupied states within 0.3 eV of the valence-band maximum (Ev) localize near the highly strained screw-dislocation lines (Fig. 4i, Methods, Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Fig. 36). A partial density of states (PDOS) analysis indicates that these states lie above the bulk-like valence bands of less strained regions, whereas decomposition into node and edge-line contributions confirms their concentration at the dislocation network (Extended Data Fig. 6). Thus, the ordered screw-dislocation network may support emergent electronic behaviour as well as upcoming electromechanical properties. Consistent with this prediction, spatially resolved EELS across the network reveals electronic reconstruction localized to the dislocations (Fig. 3f–i). The electronic structure and polar topology, including possible extrinsic effects from oxygen vacancies, remain key targets for future work.

We present a defect-by-design approach: tuning interlayer commensurability drives self-assembly of targeted defect structures. At low twist angle, the interface reconstructs into a square, ordered polar dislocation network whose periodicity is set by the twist angle, providing a direct tunable structure parameter. Unlike in previous reports, the observed vortex–antivortex arrays at the interface are linked to the morphology of the dislocation network, not to a geometric moiré pattern. Interfacial termination (for example, SrO–SrO versus TiO2–TiO2) is also decisive, as different terminations stabilize distinct local bonding and thus distinct interfacial responses.

The interface reconstruction produces large strain gradients that drive strong flexoelectric polarization, which localizes along dislocation edge lines and extends several nanometres out of plane, imprinting the electromechanical response of the interface into adjacent layers. 4DSTEM CoM measurements reveal a non-trivial in-plane internal deflection texture at the dislocation cores, consistent with finite polar order in nominally paraelectric STO. The charge density at dislocation lines and nodes differs markedly from the bulk, highlighting the reconstructed interface as a platform for emergent electronic phenomena.

Recent findings suggest that these results show that reconstructed interfacial defects crucially determine polar chirality and electronic states in twisted membranes. More broadly, they suggest a bottom-up route to functional layered materials and devices, in which nanoscale control of twist angle and termination programs dislocation networks and the coupled strain, polarization, topology and emergent electronic properties they host.

Recent findings suggest that the STO films, each approximately 10 nm thick, were grown on a treated TiO2-terminated STO (001)-oriented substrate with a sacrificial layer of 10-nm-thick Sr3Al2O6 (SAO) using reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED)-assisted pulsed laser deposition (Coherent KrF ultraviolet laser with wavelength 248 nm). The SAO layer was grown at a temperature of 750 °C with a laser fluence of 1.7 J cm−2 and O2 partial pressure of 9 × 10−6 mbar. The STO film was grown on SAO at 700 °C with a laser fluence of 1.3 J cm−2 and O2 partial pressure of 4.6 × 10−4 mbar. Both STO and SAO are grown using a pulse repetition rate of 2 Hz with a chamber base pressure of 1 × 10−8 mbar. To fabricate the membranes, a cellulose acetate butyrate (CAB) support is spin-coated onto the STO/SAO/STO templates. The samples were then immersed in deionized water, which initiated the dissolution of the underlying SAO layer. Once the SAO layer was completely dissolved, the STO membranes, supported by the CAB film, spontaneously detached from the substrate. The membranes were transferred under ambient conditions using a semi-automatic rotation stage, preserving clean interfaces while allowing precise control of the twist angle using a stage manipulator. The stage controller provides 0.01° step resolution and ±0.1° twist accuracy, enabling samples with θ = 5°, 7.5°, 10° and 20°. The twisted STO stacks are annealed externally in a tube furnace at 700 °C for 2 h in a H2/N2 mixed gas (forming gas 5% H2) atmosphere with a heating/cooling rate of 2.5 °C min−1 to ensure interfacial bonding. The membrane stacks are then placed on ultrathin SiNx-based TEM grids and analysed by high-resolution STEM. For cross-sectional imaging, focused ion beam (FIB) milling was used to prepare cuts along the [100] and [110] directions of the bottom membrane from the part of the TEM grid outside the window in which both layers are present. The lamellas were prepared using a dual-beam FIB instrument after the surface of the bilayer film was coated with a 20-nm layer of carbon in a Leica EM ACE600. See Supplementary Note 1 for more characterization details.

Industry observers note that STEM imaging studies were performed at room temperature using the Thermo Fisher Themis Z 60-300 microscope operated at an acceleration voltage of 300 kV, which is an aberration-corrected microscope equipped with an S-CORR aberration corrector for the probe-forming lens and a high-brightness field-emission electron source (X-FEG). Proposal view samples and cross-sectional lamellas were studied. For HAADF imaging (Figs. 2a,g and 3d,e and Supplementary Figs. 13 and 14), a probe size of approximately 0.6 Å with a convergence angle of 30 mrad and a HAADF collection semiangle of 64–200 mrad were used. For the LAADF mode, the collection angle was 32–64 mrad using the DF4 detector. The focus was carefully varied in 2-nm increments for focus-dependent measurements and the pixel size was around 6 pm. All acquired images were drift-corrected using image series and rigid alignment43,44. The cross-sectional images were acquired at 300 kV at a 20-mrad convergence angle and a 60–120-mrad collection angle. EELS, presented in Fig. 1c, was acquired on a Titan 60-300 microscope at 120 kV using monochromated STEM-EELS with a convergence angle of 19 mrad, a collection angle of 65 mrad and a pixel size of 0.1 Å, with a dispersion of 25 meV per channel in dual EELS mode. The zero-loss peak was subtracted using a premeasured zero-loss peak in vacuum to give the low-loss EELS signal. The core loss EELS spectrum of the Ti L-edge is treated using background subtraction and binning.

4DSTEM measurements were performed on a Thermo Fisher Scientific Titan 80-300 double-corrected electron microscope at 300 kV in nanobeam STEM mode with a 2-mrad convergence angle, resulting in a probe size of approximately 0.6 nm. Scans of 128 × 128 probe positions were performed with a scan step size of approximately 0.3 nm and a 500 μs dwell time, resulting in a scan acquisition time of just over 8 s, during which sample drift and beam damage were negligible. Diffraction patterns were recorded on a Quantum Detectors MerlinEM Quad direct electron detector with 512 × 512 pixels, mounted on a Gatan Quantum energy filter. A slit of 2 eV for zero-loss filtering of the diffraction patterns was used. From each diffraction pattern, the deflection of the direct beam owing to the local electric field is measured. The nanobeam conditions were chosen to average the atomic electric fields within a unit cell and to increase sensitivity to the interface-induced electric field. Data processing was performed using custom-built software that spatially maps the CoM shift of the direct beam. CoM shift maps relative to the CoM of the position-averaged diffraction pattern were computed considering a collection range of approximately 3 mrad, in which only the central beam and no Bragg spots were measured. The relative rotation between real and reciprocal space was calibrated using the divergence of atomic-scale fields in atomic-resolution 4DSTEM datasets45 from the same set-up. The signal-to-noise of the CoM deflection maps is improved by performing a cross-correlation-based template-matching procedure to extract an averaged deflection map.

Sources indicate that monochromated STEM-EELS measurements presented in Fig. 3f–i were performed in the Nion UltraSTEM100 MC-Hermes, a monochromated Cs-corrected dedicated scanning transmission electron microscope. The microscope is equipped with a Nion IRIS high-resolution spectrometer with a Dectris ELA hybrid pixel detector for EELS. The microscope operated at 60 kV, with a 30 mrad convergence angle and the electron optics adjusted to yield an approximately 1 Å electron probe size. The energy resolution for the core loss measurements was about 80 meV, determined by the position of the monochromator slit. The collection angle for EELS was 44 mrad and the spectrometer dispersion was set to 0.1 eV per channel. The sample (5° twisted bilayer) used for this measurement was prepared by FIB lift-out, as a cross-section lamella extracted from the TEM grid and taken at an angle of 2.5° from the [110] zone axis of the bottom membrane.

In a recent development, the spectrum images were acquired as multipass spectra, each containing at least ten consecutive image frames, with the electron beam raster scanned rapidly over the regions of interest to minimize electron-beam irradiation. The acquisition dwell time was 3 ms per pixel. These multipass spectrum images were reconstructed using rigid/non-rigid alignment, as implemented in the SmartAlign plugin for the Gatan Digital Micrograph44.

According to recent reports, the simulated TEM images were obtained using the abTEM package version 1.0.5 (ref. 46). For initiative-view HAADF/LAADF and cross-section HAADF simulations, the electron beam energy was set to 300 keV, with a probe semi-convergence angle of 30 mrad. For simulating the images at the interfaces, a flexible annular detector spanning 30–64 mrad was used. A spherical aberration coefficient of Cs = 0.159 μm was applied to the probe. The probe scan sampling was 0.24 Å and the electrostatic potential was sampled at 0.03 Å per pixel. The simulated potentials were constructed from interface structures obtained from MLIP-DFT relaxed structures, which were combined with rigid SrTiO3 layers to give a total sample thickness of 20 nm. The structure was centred along the beam direction with 4 Å of vacuum added above and below. The multislice atomic potentials were calculated using the Lobato parameterization, a slice thickness of 2 Å and the infinite projection integral method. The simulated TEM calculations were performed on a single moiré supercell with periodic boundary conditions, allowing the images to be tiled in post-processing to generate a larger field of view. For cross-section images, the interface was cut out of the larger structure and repeated to achieve a total thickness of approximately 20 nm in the beam direction. The total thickness for the cross-section is assumed to be approximately 54 nm in the beam direction. In the cross-section simulations, periodic boundary conditions were applied only in the lateral directions, not along the beam direction, enabling tiling of the images in-plane. Both the plan-view and cross-section images include an interpolation with a Fourier-space padding of 0.2 pixels Å−1, followed by Gaussian blurring with a standard deviation of 0.5 Å, to better match the experimental contrast. Poisson noise was added using an electron dose of 4.2 × 106 e− Å−1, consistent with the experimental imaging conditions. A flexible annular detector spanning 0–200 mrad with a 1-mrad step size was used to generate the LAADF and HAADF detector ranges of 32–120 and 60–200, respectively.

According to recent reports, for 4DSTEM simulations, the electrostatic potential was calculated using the Lobato parameterization, with a sampling of 0.05 Å and a slice thickness of 1 Å, in the infinite-projection approximation. A vacuum region of 2 Å was included above and below the specimen along the beam direction (z). Electron propagation was simulated using the multislice method at 300 keV. The incident probe was defined by a semi-convergence angle of 2 mrad, a spherical aberration coefficient of 0.159 μm and a probe sampling of 0.5 Å. For each structure studied (Supplementary Note 5), the interface position was determined as the midpoint between the entrance and exit surfaces of the specimen. The probe defocus was set equal to the interface depth, so the probe was focused at the interface plane. The probe scanned the entire simulation cell using fractional scan coordinates that spanned the unit cell. At each probe position, diffraction patterns were recorded with a pixelated detector, with a maximum collection angle of 3 mrad, yielding a complete 4DSTEM dataset. CoM images were calculated directly from the simulated diffraction datasets. Virtual bright-field images were generated by integrating the diffraction intensity over 0–2 mrad. The CoM maps in Fig. 4c–e were generated using Gaussian averaging to mimic the experimental resolution of 2.7 Å per pixel.

Sources indicate that the DFT relaxations, which were used as data for the MLIP training, were performed at selected twist angles θ with small and computationally tractable moiré supercells from the method of refs. 42,47 (Supplemental Fig. 5) using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation (VASP) software48 with the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE)49. The local density approximation was used with the Hubbard +U correction of +5.3 eV applied to the Ti d orbitals50 within the projector-augmented wave formalism using a plane-wave cut-off of 500 eV. The forces on each atom in the training set were relaxed to less than 0.03 eV Å−1. An automated batch active learning framework for iterative uncertainty-guided data collection and model retraining (CURATOR)51 is used to generate a comprehensive dataset. An ensemble of three PaiNN graph neural network models52 were used, over four active learning iterations, for the uncertainty quantification necessary for the sampling in CURATOR. To maximize model accuracy, the MACE equivariant graph neural network architecture53 is trained on the generated dataset, yielding an accurate MLIP with a mean absolute error of 0.52 meV per atom (Supplementary Fig. 6). For the results presented, we relaxed the atomic structure while scanning the relative in-plane translation at each θ to identify the lowest-energy alignment. We refined the final structures by averaging atomic positions from molecular dynamics simulations at T = 300 K (after discarding the first 10 ps for equilibration out of 50 ps total trajectory), starting from the most stable translation (Supplementary Fig. 8). The in-plane strain tensor components at the interface are estimated from the equilibrated atomic positions using a local reference frame defined by nearest-neighbour averaging, which removes the rigid-body rotational contribution owing to the twist. The electronic structure calculations shown in Fig. 4i and Extended Data Fig. 6 are obtained with Fritz Haber Institute ab initio materials simulations (FHI-aims)54 for the relaxed MLIP-DFT atomic positions, using a linear combination of atomic orbitals in the light basis setting. Scalar relativistic corrections are included in the ZORA atomic expansion and a Hubbard correction of +U = 4.3 eV is applied to the Ti d orbitals (ensuring numerical consistency between the two DFT codes used; Supplementary Fig. 36). The atomic structures shown in this work are visualized with VESTA55. The magnitudes and directions of the Burgers vectors presented in Fig. 2e are verified using OVITO’s internal dislocation extraction analysis56. See Supplementary Note 2 for expanded and self-contained details on this approach.

Industry observers note that the 3D phase-field modelling used in this work follows the approach outlined in ref. 57, which accounts for both electrostrictive and flexoelectric coupling in cubic perovskites. The total free energy density includes bulk, gradient and elastic contributions as well as the coupling to the electric field. The polarization, elastic displacement and electrostatic potential are solved self-consistently at each time step through the time-dependent Landau–Ginzburg–Devonshire equation, mechanical equilibrium and the Poisson equation, respectively. The fourth-order Landau parameterization for STO is taken from ref. 58 and measurements of the flexoelectric coupling strength are found in ref. 41. The in-plane linear elastic strains, (εxx, εyy, εxy), owing to the interface reconstruction as estimated by the MLIP-DFT model, are fit to a truncated 2D Fourier series (N = 6) and used as an eigenstrain input for the phase-field simulation of the bilayer stack (total thickness 20 nm). These inhomogeneous strain fields are first reconstructed, ensuring strain compatibility. Periodicity is enforced on all system variables (elastic displacements and polarization vector components, as well as the electrostatic potential) in the xy coordinates. A decomposition method59 is used to ensure xy-periodic strain tensor components. The top and bottom surfaces are held fixed elastically, with the twist boundary (internal to the computational domain) allowed to be free to deform owing to the imposed strain. The orientation of the material tensors of the model (for example, elastic stiffness, electrostrictive and flexoelectric tensors) is rotated ±θ/2 about the global z for each layer in the stack.

Sources indicate that the initial condition on each polarization component is assumed to be random and small (<10−4 C m−2). The time-dependent evolution equation evolved until the change in total energy between adjacent time steps is less than 10−6 aJ. The systems of equations are solved within the finite element method, using a discretization of approximately 0.1 nm per element. The calculations are performed in Ferret60, an open-source module for studying ferroelectric nanostructures, in the Multiphysics Object Oriented Simulation Environment (MOOSE)61. ParaView 6.0.0 (ref. 62) is used to visualize some of the results. We refer the reader to the expanded and self-contained details of the continuum modelling approach in Supplementary Note 6.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Saikat Mandal | 19 Nov 2026 15:30, Last updated: 19 Nov 2026 20:33.

Kilmarnock and Aberdeen face off in an early relegation six-pointer in the Scottish Premiership on Saturday at BBSP Stadium Rugby Park.

Killie are rock bottom in the Scottish Premiership table with nine points from 13 matches, while Aberdeen are just two points and one place above them.

Kilmarnock have shown glimpses of a promising side under Neil McCann, but their reckless defending is proving to be a major stumbling block.

They have managed just two wins in 13 league matches, losing eight of those encounters, and are enduring a particularly difficult spell, having suffered three defeats in their last four outings.

Killie have scored 13 goals this season, showing that they possess the attacking threat to trouble opponents, but their defensive frailties are turning into a recurring nightmare.

McCann's side have conceded 29 goals so far, more than any other team in the division, and unless they address that problem, climbing the table will become an increasingly difficult task.

The East Ayrshire club have won just once in their last seven matches, while their home form has been particularly poor, with only five points collected from six games and 15 goals conceded.

Earlier this week, Aberdeen appointed Mario Frick as their new head coach following the dismissal of Stephen Robinson.

There is an acute sense of instability at the club, with the former Liechtenstein striker becoming their fourth manager in 2026, following Robinson, Peter Leven and Jimmy Thelin.

Frick guided Vaduz to promotion in 2020 before helping Luzern avoid relegation in 2021, and he will need to work similar magic at Aberdeen as the club look to navigate their current crisis.

The Dons have lost four consecutive matches across all competitions and managed just one victory in their last six Scottish Premiership outings.

Aberdeen have collected only four points on the road this season, but they have lost just once to Kilmarnock in their last six meetings across all competitions.

Aberdeen Scottish Premiership form:.

Aberdeen form (all competitions):.

McCann does not have any major injury concerns, with goalkeeper Maksymilian Stryjek his only absentee.

The 30-year-old is presently sidelined with a knee injury but is expected to return by the start of next month.

It will take time for Frick to get a better understanding of his squad, but his immediate priority will be to motivate the players and prevent another defeat in this crucial encounter.

The Dons, meanwhile, are without Lewis Mayo (foot), Chris Cadden (hamstring), Kristers Towers (knee), Emmanuel Gyamfi (thigh) and Mats Knoester (tendon), although all five are expected to return by the middle of next month.

Kilmarnock possible starting lineup:.

Mantl; Brandon, McCarthy, Stranger, Schjonning-Larsen; Tshibola, Lowery; Kiltie, John-Jules, Owen; Hugill.

Aberdeen possible starting lineup:.

Muller; Guinness-Walker, Happe, Milne, Devlin; Afeez, Lyons; Yogane, Ronan, Mahou; Nisbet.

A upcoming manager often brings fresh energy to a team, and that could provide Aberdeen with the much-needed impetus to avoid a fifth consecutive defeat. The Dons are unbeaten in their last three meetings with Killie, and we back them to preserve that record in this crucial encounter.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Jonathan O'Shea | 19 Nov 2026 15:34, Last updated: 19 Nov 2026 15:40.
  • Surprise Serie A leaders Lazio will welcome Lecce to Stadio Olimpico on Saturday afternoon, aiming to extend their advantage at the top.
  • Yet to taste defeat in the league, the Biancocelesti sit one point above reigning champions Inter Milan, while their visitors are hovering above the drop zone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Jonathan O'Shea | 19 Nov 2026 15:34, Last updated: 19 Nov 2026 15:40.

Surprise Serie A leaders Lazio will welcome Lecce to Stadio Olimpico on Saturday afternoon, aiming to extend their advantage at the top.

Yet to taste defeat in the league, the Biancocelesti sit one point above reigning champions Inter Milan, while their visitors are hovering above the drop zone.

Lazio left for the international break as top dogs in Serie A - which few would have predicted when they were dumped out of the Coppa Italia in August - and fans may even be dreaming of a first Scudetto for 27 years.

Under the guidance of Gennaro Gattuso, the Bianconcelesti have amassed 29 points from 11 top-flight games, setting a latest club record.

Remarkably, that tally is 14 more than they had at this stage last term, and it leaves them one clear of second-placed Inter and two above city rivals Roma.

Gattuso’s side had to fight hard for a draw against Napoli last time out, having started strongly through Davide Frattesi's latest goal before conceding, then hanging on to avoid their first league defeat of the season.

While that ended a streak of six consecutive wins, Lazio will now aim to start a similar run ahead of next month’s Derby della Capitale, in which top spot could even be at stake.

First up is a visit from Lecce, to whom they have lost just twice in 19 Serie A home fixtures while averaging above two goals per game.

One of those defeats cost Lazio European qualification, as Lecce surprisingly prevailed on the final day of the 2024-25 season, but the Salentini only took one point from two meetings last term while failing to score.

For several months now, goals have been hard to come by, and Lecce are among Serie A’s lowest scorers once again.

A distinct lack of threat was apparent as Eusebio Di Francesco’s side lost three of their last four games before the break, only finding the net three times along the way.

After narrowly avoiding relegation last season, the Giallorossi surely face another survival fight in the coming months, having slipped to within three points of the drop zone.

Nonetheless, a recent 1-1 draw at Torino gives them something to build on, and - dating back to last term - Lecce have lost just three of their last nine away games.

With only the league to consider, Gattuso has made relatively few changes so far, and it should be a familiar Lazio XI that takes to the field this weekend.

However, the absence of Nuno Tavares and captain Mattia Zaccagni could see Alfonso Pedraza and Tijjani Noslin filling in on the left flank - often deployed up front, the latter has eight Serie A goal involvements this term.

Josip Sutalo is also injured, but fit-again pair Albert Gudmundsson and Nicolo Rovella are likely to start on the bench.

Italy midfielder Frattesi and Denmark winger Gustav Isaksen both scored in the UEFA Nations League, and they each have four league goals to their name this season.

In a recent development, by contrast, Lecce have struggled to find regular scorers. Only midfielder Lassana Coulibaly and centre-back Tiago Gabriel have found the net more than once, with forwards such as Willem Geubbels, Nikola Stulic and Paco Esteban all failing to fire.

In the treatment room, Joel Monteiro has yet to recover from a calf injury, while Santiago Pierotti and Ivan Ilic are not due back until next year.

Lazio possible starting lineup:.

Mandas; Floriani Mussolini, Leite, Provstgaard, Pedraza; Frattesi, Belahyane, Taylor; Isaksen, Pinamonti, Noslin.

Lecce possible starting lineup:.

Falcone; Veiga, Gabriel, Gaspar, Gallo; Coulibaly, Ngom, Maleh; N'Dri, Geubbels, Fatah.

Though a fan boycott slightly negates Lazio's home advantage, they can comfortably claim a 10th league victory of the season.

Lecce's last success dates back to mid-October - against rock-bottom Udinese - and their wait for a win will go on.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Adeyeye Oluwapelumi | 19 Nov 2026 15:48.
  • Vitor Matos takes charge of his first game at Strasbourg on Saturday when Brest visit the Stade de la Meinau, with the hosts looking to revive their season after a disappointing run of form prior to the international break.
  • The Alsace hosts sit 13th in the Ligue 1 table with 10 points from as many matches, just two clear of the relegation zone and five behind this weekend's opponents, who are themselves two points adrift of sixth-placed Nice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Adeyeye Oluwapelumi | 19 Nov 2026 15:48.

Vitor Matos takes charge of his first game at Strasbourg on Saturday when Brest visit the Stade de la Meinau, with the hosts looking to revive their season after a disappointing run of form prior to the international break.

The Alsace hosts sit 13th in the Ligue 1 table with 10 points from as many matches, just two clear of the relegation zone and five behind this weekend's opponents, who are themselves two points adrift of sixth-placed Nice.

Strasbourg head into Saturday's encounter having lost five of their last six league matches, with their only victory during that spell coming in an emphatic 5-1 home triumph over Auxerre on November 1.

While that result provided a brief respite following defeats to Paris FC, Nice and Paris Saint-Germain, Le Racing were unable to build on that success before the international break, going down 3-1 away to Toulouse on November 6.

That setback left Strasbourg with six defeats from their opening 10 league fixtures, scoring 18 times, while conceding 22 at the other end leaves the Alasce side with the second-worst defensive record among teams outside the bottom three, with at least three goals shipped in four separate matches.

Defensive frailties have been particularly evident on the road, where the Alsatian side have lost five of six league outings and conceded 16 goals, with a 6-2 victory over Troyes in early September accounting for their only away win during that spell.

However, Strasbourg have been considerably more competitive at the Stade de la Meinau, where they have picked up seven points from four games (W2, D1, L1) this term, and home advantage could prove valuable as the club looks to make a fresh start.

Saturday's fixture also marks the beginning of Matos's tenure following the club's decision to part manufacturer with Hugo Oliveira on Wednesday, with the former becoming Le Racing’s fourth head coach in less than a year after the departures of Liam Rosenior and Gary O'Neil.

Brest will be looking to maintain their momentum after signing off before the international break with consecutive 2-0 victories over Lorient and Lyon, recording back-to-back league wins for the first time this season and since three straight triumphs between late February and March.

Julien Lachuer's side have now won four of their opening 10 Ligue 1 fixtures (D3, L3) and have shown a reasonable balance at both ends of the pitch, conceding 12 goals while their tally of 18 scored is bettered only by Rennes (21) among teams outside the top six.

The Pirates have also been relatively consistent away from home, picking up eight points from five league trips through two wins, two draws and one defeat, with Auxerre responsible for their only setback on the road.

Furthermore, Brest have enjoyed considerable success on recent visits to Strasbourg, winning three of the last four encounters and drawing the other, while keeping clean sheets in three of those matches.

However, the visitors will be mindful of their most recent encounter, which ended in a 2-1 defeat when both sides met in Brest in May.

Strasbourg are waiting to assess Filip Jorgensen after the goalkeeper withdrew from Denmark duty with a minor injury, while Giovanni Reyna remains doubtful after missing international commitments following a thigh problem against Toulouse.

Joaquin Panichelli continues to recover from a torn anterior cruciate ligament and Fabio Balde is also doubtful after missing the last three club fixtures with a muscle injury.

Andy Robertson admitted Scotland don’t have time to get things right under Sebastien Pocognoli after the team were humbled by Switzerland on the night of the skipper’s record 103rd cap.

John McGinn warned this week it could take the Scots up to 18 months to fully grasp the Belgian’s tactical looks.

But serious questions are now being asked of Pocognoli after his team were swept aside in a miserable 4-0 defeat to a much-changed Swiss side.

The result, combined with Slovenia’s 3-0 win over North Macedonia, ended Scotland’s already scant hopes of a Nations League promotion play-off spot and condemned them to pot three in next month’s Euro 2028 draw.

Robertson was hoping for a night to remember as he overtook Kenny Dalglish as the country’s most capped player but was clearly furious as the Scots crumbled in St Gallen.

Asked if it was going to take time for things to click under Pocognoli, he told the BBC: ‘I don’t think you’ve got time in international football, you have to do it.

Scotland skipper Andy Robertson laments a night to forget on the occasion of his 103rd cap.

It has been revealed that ‘These supporters who travel everywhere, are they going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden, who are going to be critical and rightly so? No.

‘We don’t have time, the players do not have time, we have got to step up.

‘We have a long break now to March, which is not a good thing, and it is going to be a tough one to swallow.

Industry observers note that ‘We really need to step up again. In international football, you do not have time.’.

After an unconvincing start to his reign, Pocognoli needed a statement victory to convince sceptical fans that he is the right man for the job.

Despite a promising start, the rot set in after Lewis Ferguson’s 22nd minute own-goal.

The Swiss, missing a host of key players, went further ahead with goals from Winsley Boteli, Alvyn Sanches and Zeki Amdouni.

Almost 12 months on from the famous night when Steve Clarke’s side beat Denmark to reach the World Cup, the Tartan Army will be looking towards the European qualifiers with trepidation.

Robertson is tackled by Switzerland's Zachary Athekame on a night of few positives.

Robertson stated: ‘First half, I thought we were in the game. We lost a stupid goal but I thought we had chances and it could have been 2-1 at half-time.

‘By the time you get to 50 minutes and you are 3-0 down, that can’t happen in international football.

‘We were playing a good team but I felt we were in the game, it is a really tough night for us.’.

Pocognoli also felt the final scoreline was harsh and rued his side’s inability to make the most of the opportunities they created.

‘The score is heavy with the 4-0, but I don’t think it’s a reflection of the game, if I’m really honest and objective,’ remarked Pocognoli.

According to recent reports, ‘I think we had some very good moments, we started like we wanted, aggressive away from home. I think we played a good first half, we created chances, we were dominant in some moments and we faced Switzerland with different shapes and adapted well from the first minute.

Sebastien Pocognoli will now face some searching questions over his suitability for the job.

Sources indicate that ‘I think we conceded the goal from maybe one of the first chances they had. We also created chances but we were not clinical in that moment in the box.

Sources indicate that ‘In the second half, yeah, we started poorly from the first minute, a poor corner we gave away. Then you feel that, OK, we will get punished.

‘But I think when we made the substitutions, they made an impact, and we should have scored two goals in that period.

‘At the end, it’s a bad feeling, the score, but I think that the players try to do their best and create moments that we want to see.’.

  • Sources indicate that lionel Messi’s haunted expression told you more than a three-page retirement statement, artfully displayed alongside a golden pen, ever could.
  • Where four years earlier he had adorned the greatest World Cup final with two goals, he found no artistry to salvage this abomination of an encore, drifting into anonymity while his team-mates triggered a bare-knuckle brawl.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

Sources indicate that lionel Messi’s haunted expression told you more than a three-page retirement statement, artfully displayed alongside a golden pen, ever could. Sobbing and desolate under a cloudless Latest Jersey sky, he understood that his last game for Argentina had also been among his worst.

Where four years earlier he had adorned the greatest World Cup final with two goals, he found no artistry to salvage this abomination of an encore, drifting into anonymity while his team-mates triggered a bare-knuckle brawl. No wonder he stood apart while Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina did their worst, preferring to absorb one more chorus of adoration from the blue-and-white disciples before forsaking the stage for good.

You could make the case that Messi, as captain of an unholy rabble that had sought only to kick lumps out of Spain, should have taken a moral lead by hauling his team-mates into line, rather than reducing himself to their level by agitating to have Marc Cucurella sent off.

Recent findings suggest that and yet for 20 years, the little sorcerer stayed aloof from his nation’s most lurid antics on the pitch, establishing himself as a strangely beatific presence on whom the highest ideals could be projected. Anybody who has heard Messi’s name being chanted by 50,000 fervent Argentines would have felt it. He was as close as 21st-century sport has come to a secular deity, the object of such veneration that Pope Francis felt compelled to remind Catholics that it was sacrilegious to keep calling him God.

Today, with one agonised announcement, that glorious delirium is over, and already Argentina seems not to know what to do with itself. Pablo Giralt, a sports anchor in Buenos Aires, was unable even to speak when he heard the news live on air, while shattered young fans described how they had called their parents in tears.

Everybody had known the moment was approaching, given the finality of his exit from the final and the subsequent death of his father, Jorge, but it still triggered an unbearable sense of loss.

Recent findings suggest that messi was the force who galvanised a nation, propelling his side from the unfathomable low of defeat to Saudi Arabia at the 2022 World Cup to holding the trophy aloft 26 days later. Who could ever hope to emulate him, to detonate such joy that the team’s homecoming bus parade in the capital had to be abandoned for a helicopter ride because of the millions on the streets?

Industry observers note that “Thank you, God, for making me Argentine,” Messi wrote in his earnest sign-off, his strength of allegiance unfailing to the end. As a veteran of 207 international matches, with his last at La Bombonera distinguished by an ecstatic ovation, he understood both the passions he unleashed among his people and the extent to which his own story became that of an entire country.

In a recent development, you struggled to imagine what life was like in the eye of this madness, with his every move stalked. For the wonder of Messi was that the cult went beyond borders, that the joy he inspired across six World Cups made him beloved to billions. An abiding memory of the 2022 final is of the walk back to the metro station in Doha, where thousands of Nepalese and Bangladeshi supporters, all part of the vast migrant workforce that had built the stadiums, united in “Messi, Messi” refrains even at 1am.

Messi was majestic at that tournament, so imperious in filleting Croatia in the semi-finals that Argentina’s TV reporters abandoned even the pretence of objectivity. “Truly, you made your mark in everyone’s life, and that to me is beyond winning any World Cup,” gushed Sofia Martinez of Television Publica. And when he won it all, the mark only deepened. To occupy any press box at the World Cup where Argentina were involved this summer was to see South American colleagues in “Messi 10” jerseys, helplessly in thrall to his greatness.

As a 39-year-old, he confounded every expectation, scoring a hat-trick against Algeria and breaking Miroslav Klose’s World Cup goals record. Even when engineering those implausible fightbacks against Egypt and England, he held a volatile team together with a minimum of fuss.

Lionel Messi: #FIFAWorldCup edition 🇦🇷🌟 pic.twitter.com/E2xOh3Iose.

Sources indicate that to study Messi at his last World Cup was to see a man spared the obligation to do anything off the ball. For large periods of each game, the most minutely scrutinised athlete on the planet would do little besides wander around, only to ignite when it mattered most. You saw it in the fateful semi-final with England, where, at 1-0 down, he sloped off to the right touchline as if absent-mindedly gardening. Except he was plotting his opponents’ downfall, working out the precise spots from which to unleash two sumptuous crosses and shatter English hearts.

That alchemy would elude him in the final, where Argentina’s bid for immortality brought only instant notoriety, not to mention £236,000 in fines for misconduct. Was Messi’s image hurt by his connection to the chaos? Not in the long run. Nobody likes to cling to the fact that Pelé’s swansong for Brazil was a drawn friendly with Yugoslavia, or that Diego Maradona bowed out of World Cup football by failing a drug test for ephedrine. What endure are the indelible masterpieces those players bequeathed en route.

Sources indicate that it will be the same for Messi, a genius defined less by his ending than by the electrifying adrenalin rush he produced along the way, spanning three finals, 21 goals, and countless flourishes to take the breath away. “Thank you” was all he had left to say. And yet the gratitude, ultimately, is all ours.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Saudi Arabia PIF led takeover came with PSR headroom from the Mike Ashley years and looser rules on owner-linked sponsorship.

Around £450m went on transfers in the Amanda Staveley era, but it was spent steadily, not decisively, and commercial income never grew fast enough to fund the next step.

By June 2024 Yankuba Minteh and Elliot Anderson had to go for a combined £60m-plus just to stay inside PSR.

It has been revealed that the structure never worked. Amanda Staveley was bought out in July 2024. Dan Ashworth left for Manchester United.

Paul Mitchell lasted under a year, branded the transfer operation “not fit for purpose” and ended up in a turf war with Eddie Howe which was largely irrelevant as every financial decision was made by Saudi Arabia PIF. Mitchell might have identified the problem but he had no answers.

Darren Eales and Dan Ashworth struggled to get past PIF’s processes. Good football people kept failing inside this framework. At some point you have to blame the framework.

I agree Eddie Howe came back much too early and fatigued mentally and physically. But he still delivered the Champions League football.

Industry observers note that last seasons 12th with 17 league defeats was a bitter pill swallow and faced with the upcoming strategy and sale of his best players he walked away in July. He certainly was not at his best and was working with a divided squad where both Gordon and Tonali indicated to the club they were leaving before Christmas.

The central glitch is our senior players simply had much higher earning potential at the six clubs who do not face the same SCR restrictions. Alexander Isak was reportedly assured of an improved deal by Amanda Staveley and Mehrdad Ghodoussi in March 2024. Paul Mitchell shelved it and Eddie Howe publicly cited PSR as the reason. Isak downed tools. Every dressing room and every agent drew the same conclusion: PSR then, SCR now, this club can’t pay you what you’re worth. So Gordon, Tonali and Bruno followed him out, with Trippier also gone.

Blaming Eddie Howe for transfers is a simplistic and nuanced view. None of the players signed in summer 2025 were his first choice, the embarrassing prolonged struggle to get transfers over the line are a clear manifestation of that. Nick Woltemade and Yoane Wissa were signed two weeks after the season started in desperation. That after the board took direct control of the Alexander Isak situation and prevented Eddie Howe from communicating with the player.

Beware the convenient narrative. It was Amanda Staveley’s naivety, then Paul Mitchell’s manner, then Alexander Isak’s greed, then Eddie Howe’s stubbornness. Now it is Matthias Jaissle’s tactics or Ross Wilson’s signings. A new scapegoat every season is very useful to the people who never change. When the same problems outlast every individual blamed for them, the individuals were never the problem.

Under Ross Wilson the new model has seen eight of the summer’s signings being 24 or younger, including 18-year-old Sean Steur from Ajax for about £20m. Dortmund is the stated template. Roughly £249m of players went out. The CEO’s line is that anyone under contract leaves “on our terms.”.

The problem is they still leave. Call it what it is: develop to sell. Under SCR, trading profit inflates the revenue side of the ratio, so I understand the logic.

Newcastle United are mid-table under Matthias Jaissle with the youngest squad in years. The question for Saudi Arabia PIF: is this a staging post at Newcastle United, or the destination?

Sources indicate that early suggestions are that he’s struggling with an issue with his hip or his thigh, so some more information is required there. Ultimately, though, the Rossoneri are wanting information on whether he’ll be facing some time on the sidelines.

#15155. Evidence for p-wave magnetism in electronic band structure of metallic EuSi
