It has been revealed that although individual variation in protein amino acid sequences can exist between individuals, we find, among the regions of the proteins covered in our ancient data, only a single position with sequence variation among the worldwide distributed modern humans included in our database search (Table 1). In general, among extant hominids, out of the 43 amino acid positions variable among and between great ape individuals included, and in cases in which we have coverage for at least one of the four hominins studied here, only five positions contain sequence heterogeneity between the included individuals where at least four or more individuals of a single genus share variation (one position in H. sapiens, three in the genus Pan and one in the genus Pongo; Table 1). Notably, the four teeth carrying the derived AMBN A253G substitution shared with the previously reported H. erectus specimens from Zhoukoudian, Sunjiadon and Hexian differ from those six specimens, as the Naxian and Baxian hominins do not carry the derived AMBN M273V substitution (Table 1, Fig. 4 and Extended Data Fig. 3). Thus, the observation of the AMBN Gly253 substitution combined with the observation at AMBN Met273 in four hominin teeth, of at least three individuals, if the two M1s from Naxian cave represent the same individual, from two late Middle Pleistocene sites suggests that the hominin population to which they collectively belonged has not previously been sampled using molecular methods, either genetic or proteomic.

To further explore the phylogenetic placement of the Naxian and Baxian specimens, we conducted a Bayesian phylogenetic analysis. Note that, owing to the sparseness of dental enamel proteomic data, such analyses in palaeoproteomics generally have to assume that there has been no recent gene flow between the individuals and populations included in the analysis. We find that the four Naxian and Baxian individuals with the AMBN A253G substitution cluster together in a clade outside the branch of previously reported Denisovans, Neanderthals and modern humans (Fig. 4 and Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5). The topology of the clade formed by Denisovans, Neanderthals and modern humans matches the expected configuration in the main analysis, albeit with low internal node support (Fig. 4). The topology of these three hominin populations changes once additional modern human and great ape individuals are added to the phylogenetic analysis (Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5). The expected topology of this clade is challenging to obtain when using proteomic data from dental enamel proteins, as reported previously29,39,40, and it is evidenced by the low support value of this clade in our analyses (Fig. 4 and Extended Data Figs. 4–6). Nevertheless, the values supporting the nodes for the remaining branches, including the one placing the Naxian and Baxian specimens as an outgroup to the other hominins, are high in all analyses (>0.995). The Naxian and Baxian individuals are placed in a clade together with six previously reported H. erectus specimens. Those six specimens are placed together with strong support and separate from the four Naxian and Baxian individuals carrying the AMBN A253G substitution (Fig. 4). This strengthens the notion that these four Naxian and Baxian cave specimens represent a H. erectus hominin population that has not been sampled molecularly before. Furthermore, the phylogenetic analysis suggests that, although based on sparse data, this hominin population might have diverged before the divergence of the common ancestor of modern humans, Neanderthals and Denisovans. These phylogenetic observations are in accordance with the morphological analysis of these specimens, strengthening the case that these specimens belong to a previously unsampled lineage of H. erectus.

By contrast, proteomic analysis of PA1796 from Baxian cave reveals that this specimen does not contain the derived AMBN A253G amino acid substitution (Extended Data Fig. 6b). It has no uniquely derived substitutions compared to the other four teeth, nor does it share uniquely derived amino acid substitutions with the Denisovan, Neanderthal or modern human individuals present in our reference panel (Table 1). Phylogenetic analysis of this specimen places it outside of the H. erectus clade, with varying topologies with low support in relation to its placement in relation to archaic hominins (Denisovans and Neanderthals) or the clade including Neanderthals, Denisovans and modern humans (Fig. 4 and Extended Data Fig. 6a). The protein sequences reconstructed for this tooth are therefore different from the other four specimens studied proteomically, mirroring the morphological analysis that also indicates this specimen represents a taxon other than H. erectus. Only a single Denisovan genomic reference is at the moment available, the D3 specimen from Denisova cave, Russia, implying that our understanding of protein sequence polymorphisms for Denisovans is by definition limited. Future morphological and genomic or proteomic research on hominin teeth from the region could provide additional frameworks to allow more precise taxonomic classification of PA1796 into a non-erectus group, representing either southern Asian representatives of Denisovans (H. longi) or potentially another population or species.

Recent findings suggest that eight of the late Middle Pleistocene Homo teeth from the Naxian and Baxian caves exhibit metric and morphological features that lie within the range of East and Southeast Asian H. erectus and that differ from those of Denisovans (H. longi), Neanderthals (H. neanderthalensis), or Pleistocene and Holocene modern humans (H. sapiens). The palaeoproteomic evidence provides further confirmation that four of these teeth indeed fall outside of the known genetic and proteomic sequence variation of H. neanderthalensis, H. longi and H. sapiens, but are consistent with a H. erectus-derived substitution recently described for Chinese specimens dating to around 0.4 Ma (ref. 13). The recovered proteomic evidence is therefore compatible with the morphological data. Dated to between 324 and 184 ka (ref. 12), these H. erectus teeth substantially extend the known temporal range of H. erectus fossils on the Asian mainland, bringing the extent of the mainland H. erectus fossil record closer to the latest known Javanese H. erectus, dated to 117–108 ka (ref. 8). The recovery of a unique proteomic signature of mainland H. erectus from the Middle Pleistocene of East Asia furthermore suggests that specimens attributed to this species could harbour several hominin populations13, and make it possible to molecularly test whether other H. erectus fossils from the region that could potentially date to the late Middle Pleistocene, such as those from Changyang cave (Hubei province, China)11,22 and Chaoxian cave (Anhui Province, China)23, also represent specimens belonging to the same mainland H. erectus hominin population, or whether they have a proteomic signature more similar to earlier H. erectus13.

It has been revealed that the discovery of the Naxian and Baxian H. erectus specimens in the late Middle Pleistocene of southern East Asia enriches the hominin occupation scenario in the region. A Denisovan mandible has been described from the Penghu channel off the coast of Taiwan, dating to either 190–130 or 70–10 ka (refs. 7,48). In Laos, based on morphological analysis, a Denisovan molar has been described from Tam Ngu Hao 2, dating to between 163 and 131 ka (ref. 6). Genetic evidence on the timing of Denisovan introgression into the genomes of living humans also suggests that Denisovans were present in East and/or Southeast Asia well into the Late Pleistocene1,49. Moreover, several craniodental remains, such as Harbin, Penghu 1 and Xiahe 1, were identified molecularly as H. longi (Denisovans)7,9,17,19, and several other late Middle Pleistocene specimens probably belong to this population as well (for example, Xujiayao and Hualongdong), including also some non-erectus fossils from southern Asia (for example, Maba, Narmada, TNH2-1)6,50. It therefore seems plausible that the H. erectus population represented by the fossils from Naxian and Baxian cave on the mainland existed in relatively close proximity to Denisovan hominins.

Industry observers note that even though the geometric morphometric analysis of the EDJ suggest that the PA1796 M2 retains plesiomorphic aspects (mostly due to the short EDJ height), the specimen also differs from the morphology of the comparative H. erectus sample (Supplementary Note 2). The lack of a comparative sample for Denisovans (H. longi) represents a substantial bias in our ability to morphologically identify them. The non-metric morphology of PA1796 differs markedly from that of Chinese H. erectus by the lack of wrinkling on the EDJ, the absence of accessory fossae, the relatively large talon and the lingually shifted hypocone25,26 (Supplementary Notes 1 and 2). Moreover, the palaeoproteomic analysis of PA1796 indicates a different signal compared to the other Baxian and Naxian specimens, as well as to the six H. erectus teeth from Zhoukoudian, Hexian and Sunjiadong13 (Fig. 4), strongly suggesting the presence of a hominin population other than H. erectus in Baxian cave. However, among the protein sequences available to us now, the PA1796 specimen does not exhibit the known proteomic variation associated with Denisovans, although it should be acknowledged that only a single Denisovan reference genome is currently available. PA1796 could therefore either represent a still-unrecognized H. erectus group that would differ in molecular and morphological aspects from the currently known H. erectus specimens, a hypothesis that we consider unlikely (Supplementary Note 2) but cannot outright reject, or belong to a non-erectus group, possibly related to H. longi. Future morphological and proteomic research on hominin teeth from the region, as well as the availability of a growing number of Denisovan genomes and proteomes, could therefore provide additional frameworks to allow a more precise classification of the PA1796 specimen.

Recent findings suggest that the H. erectus specimens from Baxian and Naxian caves extend the geographical and temporal extent of mainland Asian H. erectus well into the late Middle Pleistocene. Occupying rainforest environments12, these H. erectus populations probably co-existed in close spatial and temporal proximity to southern Asian Denisovans. Mainland Southeast Asia therefore appears as a key region to study the evolution, genetics and archaeologically visible behaviours of multiple sympatric hominin species.

Recent findings suggest that the Baxian and Naxian hominin specimens were scanned using X-ray microtomography using the 225 kV micro-computed tomography scanner at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology (IVPP, Beijing, China) according to the following parameters: 140 kV voltage, 120 µA, 0.5 angular increment one step and 360° of rotation. The final volumes were reconstructed with isotropic voxel sizes of 15.7–32.0 µm. A semi-automatic threshold-based segmentation was carried out in Avizo v.7.1 (FEI Visualization Sciences Group) and a volumetric reconstruction was then generated for each specimen. A full morphological description of each tooth can be found in Supplementary Note 1.

Dental surface models were imported in Geomagic Design v. X 64 (3D Systems, Rock Hill) to separate the crown from the tooth roots. The crown and roots were digitally isolated at the cervix using the cervix-best-fit plane as a reference51. Five variables were then measured or calculated: (1) Ve, the volume of the enamel cap (mm3); (2) SEDJ, the surface area of the EDJ (mm2); (3) Vcdp, the volume of the crown dentine and pulp (mm3); (4) 3DAET, 3D average enamel thickness (Ve/SEDJ; mm)52; (5) 3DRED, the ratio of 3D average enamel thickness to 3D average dentine thickness (Ve1/3/Vcdp1/3 × 10)53.

Industry observers note that diffeomorphic surface matching was applied to analyse the EDJ shape of the least worn teeth from Baxian and Naxian caves (methodological details are provided in Supplementary Note 2). This landmark-free, mesh-based approach was previously demonstrated to efficiently distinguish the EDJ of various hominin species6,22,27. Owing to occlusal wear, the apex of the dentine horns of some of the specimens had to be reconstructed before the analysis (Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Figs. 18 and 21). We first confirmed that the EDJ of the Baxian and Naxian specimens differed from that of Pongo and belonged to Homo (which was also confirmed independently by palaeoproteomics). We then compared the Baxian and Naxian EDJs to those of H. erectus s.l., H. neanderthalensis, H. longi and H. sapiens. The H. erectus sample includes dental remains from African and Asia that are regarded by some as belonging to H. ergaster and H. erectus s.s. (Supplementary Table 3). We indicated the labels of the H. erectus specimens in Fig. 2 to show the distribution of the African and Asian material in the morphospace. Canonical variate analyses were conducted and the Baxian and Naxian specimens, as well as the Denisovan molar from Tam Ngu Hao 2 (ref. 6), were projected a posteriori into the canonical variate analysis morphospace. Typicality probabilities were computed for the Naxian and Baxian teeth to provide a quantitative estimation of their most likely taxonomic attribution.

Industry observers note that for Naxian cave, fauna and hominin specimens were sampled using a handheld drill with a diamond-tipped drill bit, resulting in between 10 mg and 97 mg of powder for the faunal samples and up to 6 mg of hominin dental enamel. For Baxian cave, dentine was obtained using a handheld drill (36.5 and 43.2 mg of powder), while the dental enamel was sampled using an acid etch. All sampling and extraction steps were conducted in ancient molecular laboratories regularly used for ancient DNA and/or ancient protein analysis, including standard procedures to prevent contamination from occurring in the sampling and extraction environments, including wearing full body suits, hairnets, multiple layers of nitrile gloves, footies and positive air pressure.

Dental enamel extracts for Naxian cave were generated using 5% HCl, following previously published protocols31,54. Likewise, dental enamel extracts from the acid etching of the Baxian cave specimens followed previously published protocols54. The dentine samples of fauna from Naxian cave were extracted using a variant on previously published EDTA-based protocols55. For Baxian cave, the hominin dentine extractions followed a HCl-based protocol commonly used for ZooMS analysis, but with modifications to separate protein fragments by size9,56. Full protein extraction protocols are provided in Supplementary Note 3.

Faunal extracts from Naxian cave were separated on the EASY-nLC 1200 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) system coupled to a Exploris 480 Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Hominin dental enamel extracts from Naxian cave were analysed on the Vanquish Neo UPLC (Thermo Fisher Scientific) system coupled to a Exploris 480 Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Dentine extracts from Baxian cave were first analysed on the Bruker Autoflex MaX MALDI-ToF MS instrument. Subsequent to the detection of collagen peptides, both the dentine and the dental enamel extracts from Baxian cave were analysed on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to an Easy n-LC 1200 HPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) over a 120 min gradient. Blank extractions were included in all cases to monitor the existence of exogenous contaminants during the procedure.

Raw data files were searched separately by tissue type and cave site, using PEAKS, pFind and MaxQuant in parallel. Initial searches in PEAKS revealed the possibility of a unique substitution in AMBN, while PEAKS and pFind informed on the composition of post-translational modifications (PTMs) that should be taken into account. After initial searches, final searches using an updated protein sequence database and updated PTM information for dental enamel and the full human proteome for dentine were performed (further details are provided in Supplementary Note 3).

Sources indicate that protein deamidation was calculated according to a previous study for MaxQuant data57. Other PTM ratio analyses were conducted by peptide-spectrum match spectral counts or peptide counts, unless indicated differently (applying to MaxQuant, pFind and/or PEAKS). Unipept analysis was carried out using all peptide matches against endogenous, dental-enamel-specific proteins58. As described above, a project-specific database was used for data analysis that includes protein sequence variation beyond that available within UniProt. As a result, Unipept analysis will not be able to match all peptides to the same taxonomic level as the one present in the protein sequence database used. Sequence reconstruction was performed for pFind, PEAKS and MaxQuant data jointly, resulting in a single protein sequence reconstruction for each specimen. Specifically, sequences from different search engines were overlaid for each specimen to generate a single protein consensus sequence. Amino acid positions where PEAKS, pFind and MaxQuant disagreed with each other were not called, and reversed to ‘X’. Positions possibly phylogenetically informative were manually inspected, fragment ion series were checked and E values were assessed. Where necessary, positions potentially introducing invalid sequences were subsequently removed from the protein sequence reconstructions. The consensus sequences were subsequently aligned to a subset of the PaleoProPhyler database of hominid dental enamel sequences, which included four individuals from each of the genera Pongo, Gorilla and Pan, as well as three Neanderthals41,42,43, one Denisovan44 and three present-day H. sapiens from the sub-Saharan Yoruba population. We also added the dental enamel protein sequences for Homo antecessor29 and Penghu 1 (ref. 7) (a Denisovan individual) and carried out Bayesian phylogenetic analysis of the Naxian–Baxian individuals using a combination of different proteins for each tree. The combinations are indicated in each figure (Extended Data Figs. 4–6 and Supplementary Figs. 33–43). The available H. erectus protein sequences from a single specimen (D4163) from Dmanisi, Georgia, were not included in the phylogenetic analysis carried out here because the phylogenetic position of the specimen could not be resolved in the original study29.

These fossils and their CT data are freely available to access for any researchers. Max Dowman broke another record as the 16-year-old became the youngest-ever goalscorer for England's Under-21 side on Monday night.

The Arsenal teenager has already broken a plethora of records at club level, and is now taking that to the international stage too, breaking a record set by senior team star Jude Bellingham, who scored aged 17 years and 67 days in 2020.

Dowman was called into the U21 squad for the first time this international break, and made his debut off the bench in the 1-0 defeat by Portugal on Friday.

On Monday, meanwhile, he was given a start by manager Lee Carsley, and rewarded his manager's faith with an 89th-minute winner to break the record and earn his side a 3-2 win.

It's a record he can add to his already-extensive collection, which includes being the youngest Champions League player, the youngest Premier League goalscorer, and the youngest Premier League winner.

Manager Lee Carsley said after the game: 'He played really well - he was one of four or five outstanding performances. Mikey Moore, Max, Ethan (Nwaneri), they were very good.

Max Dowman became England Under-21s' youngest-ever goal scorer when he scored against France on Monday.

Industry observers note that 'We see how good on the ball he is but he was outstanding off the ball. You have to keep reminding yourself about his age. There's a lot of expectation around him and he seems to handle that so well.

'It's vital we keep supporting him and he develops at his own pace. It's so important he enjoys his football.

'Obviously all the players in the squad are under pressure from their clubs and the expectation that surrounds them, so as much as we can we have to make that as easy as we can.'.

Despite bursting onto the scene last season, Dowman has just 19 minutes to his name in the top flight this campaign as Arsenal look to defend their title.

He has played a number of games for the Gunners' U21 side, while he was sent off against League Two side Fleetwood Town in the Carabao Cup.

Arteta scolded his player at the time, but said: 'I haven't seen the reaction to my reaction. Whether that's positive or negative. You need to understand the context, the relationship I have with him and what we discussed before we went out.

'If you see the reaction from my mother and father with me sometimes, you'd say "you don't like that reaction", but for me it was the best reaction ever as it enabled me to be who I am.

The Arsenal teenager, 16, broke the record held by Jude Bellingham with his late winner.

'But you want to see the best and most beautiful reaction. You want to see the reaction of his team-mates when they have to play with 10 men.

Industry observers note that 'What do you expect? That's the level and that's the reaction. Whether it's right or wrong, that's the reaction. And the reaction when I don't win, I'm f****d off, major time.

'This is the environment and the reality. We are not in Disneyland, we are in the Premier League. We look after him so much but we are also demanding as he needs to earn the right to play otherwise what are the rest of the boys going to tell me?'.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Milan Futuro decided to go in a newly introduced direction this summer by appointing Sergio Navarro, but is it working so far?

Milan launched the Futuro project ahead of the 2024-25 season. with the aim of creating a pathway for academy players to break into the first team. The project was designed to bridge the physical and technical gap between the Primavera and senior football.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Things didn’t go well in year one, as Daniele Bonera didn’t see out the season as the head coach. He recently stated he didn’t think the squad was ready for the level, and ultimately Massimo Oddo was unable to save the team from relegation to Serie D, the fourth tier of Italian football.

With promotion back to Serie C the objective, this summer the Rossoneri turned to Sergio Navarro, a coach with good pedigree in Spain. The Futuro now appear to have a clearer structure, a defined playing identity and the right guidance, as Rohit Rajeev has outlined.

It has been revealed that under Barquero, Milan Futuro operate in a 4-2-3-1 formation. Asanji leads the line, with Ossola playing as the number 10 and Vos and Guernier occupying the wide positions.

Plazotta and Pandolfi form the double pivot, while Cisse and Pagliei partner at centre-back, with Perera and Colombo completing the back four.

Milan Futuro favour a possession-oriented approach, circulating the ball patiently at a measured tempo while waiting for gaps to emerge in the opposition’s defensive structure. They also use passing triangles effectively to create short passing options and play through the opposition’s high press.

In possession, Milan Futuro adopt a 3-1-6 structure, with Barquero showing little hesitation in committing players forward to create numerical overloads in the opposition half.

Sources indicate that asanji positions himself just behind the opposition’s defensive line, keeping the centre-backs occupied and preventing them from stepping forward freely. Meanwhile, Pandolfi and Plazotta maintain parallel positions in the double pivot, providing a stable base for the attacking structure.

In the opposition half, Milan Futuro keep the distances between players very short, allowing them to combine through quick, one-touch passes.

This also helps them create ball-sided overloads, with two or three players surrounding the Milan player in possession to provide close passing options. Once they enter the opposition half, the tempo increases as Milan look to become more direct and progress towards goal.

In a recent development, similar to Amorim’s approach at Sporting, Milan Futuro form vertical corridors with three players positioned one behind another. This structure facilitates quick passing combinations while also creating movement to manipulate the opposition.

When Milan players drop to form these corridors or create overloads, they often drag defenders with them, opening spaces elsewhere to exploit.

Milan Futuro look to press the opposition high up the pitch, adopting a 4-4-2 shape with a man-oriented pressing scheme. This allows them to put pressure on the opposition’s build-up and restrict the time and space available to play out from the back.

Industry observers note that milan Futuro also set up pressing traps by deliberately leaving the opposition’s wide player unmarked. The pass towards the wide player acts as the pressing trigger, prompting Milan’s players to jump out of their positions and aggressively close down the receiver, while cutting off the available passing options.

Milan Futuro maintain an extremely narrow defensive shape, prioritising the protection of central spaces and forcing the opposition towards the flanks.

Once the opposition attempts to progress through the wide areas, the press shifts across to create numerical overloads around the ball, while Guernier and Colombo provide cover and prevent the opposition from switching play to the opposite flank.

Perhaps the most crucial aspect of Barquero’s approach is his willingness to build the system around his players’ strengths and allow them the freedom to express themselves.

Rather than focusing solely on tactical adaptability, he appears equally committed to their individual development and helping them grow as footballers. Here are a few examples.

According to recent reports, one of Milan Futuro’s methods of chance creation is to play direct passes into Asanji. His ability to position himself between the ball and the opposition defender, using his physicality to shield possession and hold up play, is crucial to this approach.

Rather than asking him to adapt to the role of a more technically oriented, ball-playing striker, Barquero has built a mechanism that makes the most of his existing strengths.

Perhaps the clearest demonstration of Barquero’s coaching ability is his utilisation of Vos and Guernier. Guernier is a natural winger/forward, while Vos is more accustomed to playing as an attacking midfielder.

Within the 3-1-6 structure, Vos often inverts from the left flank into an inside-left role, allowing Perera to provide the width.

According to recent reports, at times, he is also given the freedom to interchange positions with Plazotta, allowing him to drop into midfield or advance further up the pitch. This positional freedom helps him develop his midfield qualities and realise his potential.

Guernier, meanwhile, tends to maintain his width, stretching the opposition’s defensive line and creating space for Vos and the other attackers to exploit.

Barquero also gives Guernier the freedom to take on his direct opponent, even when he is outnumbered, allowing him to use his dribbling ability without being restricted by the team’s structure.

Ossola, who is particularly effective at receiving between the lines and turning with the ball, is allowed to operate higher up the pitch, closer to the opposition’s defensive line.

Idrissi, on the other hand, prefers to receive possession deeper, where he can dictate play with his passing range or carry the ball forward through dribbling.

FC Utrecht and Cambuur will both be looking to return to winning ways when they meet at Stadion Galgenwaard on Saturday.

This weekend marks the first league meeting between the sides since May 2023, with their last two encounters both coming in friendly matches.

Back in the top flight after a three-year absence, Cambuur needed time to find their feet, losing each of their opening four matches before responding with an eight-game unbeaten run in all competitions - winning five and drawing three.

Nonetheless, overcoming reigning champions PSV Eindhoven was always going to be a tall order for Johan Plat’s side, who found themselves 3-0 down inside the opening 19 minutes and ultimately fell 5-2 at Kooi Stadion on November 8.

While survival is expected to remain the Yellow-Blues’ primary objective, their recent purple patch suggests a push for continental football may not be entirely out of reach. Matches like this weekend’s will go a long way toward gauging their readiness for such ambitions.

Industry observers note that plat was beaten by his opposite number in their only previous meeting earlier this year. The 39-year-old now seeks to exact revenge and extend his side’s away unbeaten run to five matches, the last three of which have ended in victory.

Just under half of Cambuur’s 25 goals have come before half-time, and facing a team that has been outscored 15-4 in that period this season offers the visitors a significant opportunity to seize control of proceedings in the opening 45 minutes.

After winning three of four matches following the September international break, Utrecht appeared to have turned a corner. However, back-to-back defeats against Telstar and, most recently, NEC suggest the ghosts of their struggles have not been fully exorcised.

Anthony Correia’s side have collected seven fewer points than at this stage last season - the biggest drop-off among all ever-present teams over that period - and early-season hopes of a continental finish have been significantly tempered.

Sources indicate that with just a third of the campaign played, Utrecht at the moment sit 14th in the standings, only two points clear of the drop zone. A defeat this weekend could see them fall into the bottom three and potentially as low as 19th, depending on other results.

In a recent development, de Domstedelingen’s next three matches are against newly-promoted sides in the league and a second-division opponent in the cup. They will be eager to string together a positive run and relieve some of the pressure on Correia before their first December Eredivisie fixture against Ajax.

Only Saturday’s opponents have scored more goals than Utrecht’s 21 among bottom-half sides, but the Cupfighters have struggled defensively, conceding 34 goals to leave them with the division’s second-leakiest defence behind bottom club Willem II.

With five goals in nine league matches, Artem Stepanov has already matched his tally from last season, but the 19-year-old has failed to score in each of his last five outings.

Jamal Amofa is unlikely to feature again this season after suffering an ACL injury in October, making him one of three Dutch absentees for Cambuur alongside Daan Visser and Damian Westerhof.

West Ham United’s Championship promotion hopes may have received an unexpected boost following confirmation that Swansea City manager Vítor Matos has left the Welsh club to take charge of French side Strasbourg.

Recent findings suggest that the Portuguese coach had established Swansea as genuine promotion contenders, with the Swans sitting sixth in the Championship. His departure comes at an awkward time for a club attempting to maintain its challenge near the top of the table.

Strasbourg officially appointed Matos on Wednesday evening, replacing Hugo Oliveira. And whilst there’s no guarantee Swansea will suffer without him, I certainly regard this as good news for West Ham.

Matos was an extremely capable manager who had Swansea punching well above their weight.

According to recent reports, when he arrived in November 2025, Swansea were languishing in 20th position. He eventually guided them to an 11th-place finish before establishing them amongst the promotion contenders this season.

Interestingly, Claret & Hugh reported last month that Matos could be targeted by Crystal Palace, highlighting how losing their manager could benefit West Ham’s promotion ambitions.

  • But while Duncan is undoubtedly a talented young goalkeeper, West Ham must ask a simple question: why spend time, money and resources pursuing another developing keeper when they already have one of the country’s most highly-rated young goalkeepers sitting in their own academy?
  • It has been revealed that finlay Herrick joined the club at the age of six and has progressed through every level of the academy system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent reports linking West Ham with Bristol City goalkeeper Joe Duncan are understandable. The 20-year-old has enjoyed an impressive loan spell at Southend United, earned a surprise senior Wales call-up and is attracting attention from a number of clubs.

But while Duncan is undoubtedly a talented young goalkeeper, West Ham must ask a simple question: why spend time, money and resources pursuing another developing keeper when they already have one of the country’s most highly-rated young goalkeepers sitting in their own academy?

It has been revealed that finlay Herrick joined the club at the age of six and has progressed through every level of the academy system. He was part of the famous side that won the FA Youth Cup and U18 Premier League South double in 2022/23, signed a long-term contract in 2024 and has represented England from U16 through to U20 level. Herrick, now aged 20, has already made three senior appearances for West Ham.

The standout moment came in the FA Cup quarter-final against Leeds United when he replaced Alphonse Areola in the 120th minute and immediately saved a penalty in the shootout. Although the Hammers ultimately lost, Herrick demonstrated the composure and personality required to perform under intense pressure.

He also acquitted himself well in the EFL second-round 4-1 win at Southampton back in August.

In a recent development, in his last game, three saves, including a vital one-on-one against Fulham, were not enough as we were edged out of the EFL Cup 3-2 by our London rivals. However, our young custodian blamed himself for the third goal, saying he needed to be harsh on himself and should have done better to prevent it.

Regarding Duncan, he has come through Bristol City’s academy and gained valuable experience on loan at Tiverton Town and Farnborough before stepping up to National League football with Southend United. His performances have been good enough to earn a Wales senior squad call-up from Craig Bellamy despite never making a first-team appearance for Bristol City.

Southend manager Kieron Dyer and Bellamy have both spoken positively about his development, while West Ham are reportedly among several clubs monitoring his situation.

One of the biggest criticisms supporters have of modern football is that clubs often look elsewhere rather than trusting their own youth products. You only have to look at former academy prospect Nathan Trott, who was regularly loaned out to other clubs and has now swiftly established himself as the main keeper for Cardiff City.

According to recent reports, behind Herrick are a number of other keepers coming through the ranks, with high expectations of Lanre Awesu, who at just 18 years old has featured for the U21 side on a number of occasions. Standing at 6ft 5in, he has been highly praised by David Martin, along with fellow keeper Finley Hooper.

Herrick has already spent 14 years at the club. He has excelled at youth level, earned England recognition, performed well on loan and shown promise when given an opportunity with the senior side.

At some point, development becomes about opportunity.

If a goalkeeper with Herrick’s pedigree cannot move up the pecking order, then what is the purpose of the academy pathway? What message does that give to Herrick, Awesu and Hooper?

With Hermansen failing to convince and Areola proving increasingly unreliable due to injuries, the moment for Herrick could arrive far quicker than anyone anticipated.

In my opinion, the Hammers should show faith in their own. The smartest signing West Ham can make may already be wearing number 49 at Rush Green!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Adeyeye Oluwapelumi | 19 Nov 2026 16:39.

Looking to end a five-game winless run in Ligue 1, Monaco welcome Auxerre to the Stade Louis-II on Saturday evening, hoping to get their season back on track against one of the division’s most porous defences.

The hosts sit seventh in the French top flight with 16 points from their opening 10 matches, one point adrift of sixth-placed Nice and six clear of the 14th-placed visitors, who are just two points above the relegation zone.

Having made an impressive start to life under Filipe Luis, Monaco have struggled to sustain their early-season momentum, and they have not tasted victory in the league since beating Lens at the Stade Louis-II in September.

Les Monegasques won four of their opening five Ligue 1 matches, including a statement 2-1 victory away to Paris Saint-Germain, to sit top of the table on 13 points, but their campaign has since taken a worrying turn.

A home draw with Toulouse started the rot, and a 1-0 defeat at Lorient followed, as Monaco have now gone five league matches without a win (D3, L2), most recently conceding a late equaliser in a 1-1 draw at Le Mans.

Tightening up at the back will be key to any revival, with Les Rouge et Blanc having failed to keep a clean sheet in each of their last eight Ligue 1 outings, even if their overall tally of 11 goals conceded remains respectable.

Seven of their 13 league goals have come in just four matches at the Stade Louis-II, where Monaco have scored more than once in three games and won two, although they have had to settle for a share of the spoils in their last two top-flight outings on home soil.

For all their domestic struggles, the Pricipality club have been flawless in the Conference League, winning each of their three league-phase fixtures so far, and victory on Saturday would provide a timely lift ahead of next Thursday’s trip to Hearts.

Auxerre, meanwhile, have won just three of their opening 10 league matches (D1, L6) and have not tasted victory since a 3-1 success at bottom-placed Le Havre on October 18.

Will Still’s side enjoyed a revival between September 12 and October 18, winning three of four league outings after losing their opening trio of fixtures, but they now appear to be slipping back into the form that blighted the start of their campaign.

Following a 1-1 draw with Le Mans on matchday eight, Les Ajaistes have suffered back-to-back defeats, crashing 5-1 at Strasbourg and then going down 1-0 at home to Paris FC prior to the international break.

That loss was the first time this season that Auxerre had failed to find the net, and it also took their tally of goals conceded to a league-high 24, a problem head coach Still will be desperate to address.

Those defensive frailties have been especially evident on the road, where Les Ajaistes have lost four of their five league fixtures and shipped 18 goals, with the win at basement side Le Havre the only away game in which they have not conceded at least three this term.

History offers little encouragement for the visitors either, as they have failed to beat Monaco in their last 12 meetings in all competitions (D3, L9), although the most recent encounter between both sides at the Stade Louis-II did yield a 2-2 draw in April.

By Joshua Cole | 19 Nov 2026 16:47.

Amed SK will be looking to maintain their perfect home record in the Turkish Super Lig when they welcome Caykur Rizespor to Diyarbakir Stadium on Saturday afternoon.

The hosts sit third in the table with 23 points from 11 matches, while the visitors are 11th on 14 points, nine behind their opponents, although the visitors will arrive with renewed confidence after ending their winless run before the international break.

Amed had enjoyed an impressive run of results before their league outing against Galatasaray, remaining unbeaten in eight consecutive games (W6, D2) and winning three successive matches against Konyaspor, Samsunspor and Eyupspor.

Besnik Hasi's side beat Konyaspor 1-0 at home, secured a 2-1 victory away to Samsunspor and then produced an emphatic 5-1 win over Eyupspor, but that positive run was eventually brought to an end by Galatasaray.

Amed were far from overawed in Istanbul, scoring three goals in a thrilling 4-3 defeat, their second loss in 11 league matches, which has left them third with seven wins, two draws and two defeats from their opening 11 fixtures.

The hosts have been carried by their attack, scoring 28 goals during that period to become one of the most productive sides in the division, with only Fenerbahce (29) finding the net more times.

Their home form has been particularly impressive, as they have won all six of their league matches at Diyarbakir Stadium, scoring 19 goals and conceding just four, a run they will be confident of extending against a Rizespor side that has struggled for consistency.

This will be the first league meeting between these sides, although they have faced each other twice in the Turkish Cup, with both teams recording a home victory.

Rizespor, meanwhile, have endured a difficult spell, losing three consecutive league matches against Fenerbahce, Corum and Trabzonspor before drawing 0-0 away to Kocaelispor, following an earlier 2-2 stalemate with Goztepe.

However, Recep Ucar's side finally returned to winning ways before the international break, beating Erzurumspor 2-1 at home, with the victory ending a five-match winless run in the league and providing a much-needed boost ahead of their trip to Diyarbakir.

Their away form has been considerably stronger than their results at home, with three wins, two draws and one defeat from six road matches, although they are now winless in their last three away outings (D2, L1).

The Black Sea Sparrowhawks failed to score in an away game for the first time this season in the goalless draw at Kocaelispor, while the last time they failed to find the net in consecutive away matches was towards the end of the previous campaign, during a six-match winless run on the road.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

West Ham United v Preston North End EFL Championship London Stadium Saturday 21 November 2026, 3pm GMT.

Scott Parker’s first home match as West Ham United head coach is massively key. Preston North End are bottom of the Championship and, while Saturday’s fixture is not mathematically must-win, realistically it feels very close to it.

West Ham have collected one point from Parker’s opening two games and must start closing the gap to the automatic-promotion places. After two uninterrupted weeks with much of his squad, this is the first proper opportunity to judge whether the latest head coach has begun improving the organisation and intensity of the team.

Sources indicate that there is also the troubling matter of West Ham’s home form. I worried before relegation that the vast gaps between the London Stadium crowd and the pitch might turn it into a disadvantage rather than an advantage, and we now desperately need to begin winning there consistently.

According to recent reports, the London Stadium has not remotely resembled a fortress this season. Opponents have arrived believing they can frustrate West Ham, exploit the anxiety around the ground and capitalise when the players become nervous.

As one former Championship striker recently observed, visiting teams have been enjoying the London Stadium experience. That situation has to change if West Ham are serious about challenging for automatic promotion.

Parker needs his players to begin quickly and give the crowd something to respond to. The longer this remains goalless, the more Preston will believe their long-ball approach and deep defensive shape can earn them something.

Scott Parker will need to make the London Stadium feel like home.

Sources indicate that west Ham will dominate possession, so the challenge will be using it properly. Passing sideways in front of an organised defence will achieve very little; we need quicker movement, runners beyond the striker and enough tempo to pull Preston out of position.

In a recent development, I expect West Ham to be considerably tighter defensively following Parker’s first extended spell on the training pitch. However, the international break has not been quite as useful as it initially appeared because several notable players were away representing their countries.

Konstantinos Mavropanos was among those absent, while Max Kilman is suspended after reaching the disciplinary threshold at Blackburn. Parker has therefore been unable to work throughout the fortnight with the central-defensive partnership he will need on Saturday.

Sources indicate that I suspect Morato will move into his natural centre-back position alongside Mavropanos. That is probably the safe and predictable selection, although I would prefer to see Airidas Golambeckis given the opportunity.

The teenager has generally impressed when called upon and deserves serious consideration. As our examination of Parker’s defensive conundrum against Preston highlighted, the decision appears to be between Morato’s experience and Golambeckis’ encouraging performances.

Joël Veltman should start at right-back, while Ezra Mayers deserves to retain his place on the left. Kyle Walker-Peters continues to be assessed, but Parker has two natural and capable full-back options without needing to rush him back.

The biggest selection question surrounds the goalkeeper. I am finding Parker’s team difficult to predict primarily because I do not know whether he will retain Mads Hermansen or turn to Alphonse Areola.

Hermansen has produced an inconsistent sequence of performances. He excelled for Denmark against Portugal before making another clanger during the defeat by Norway, which will not have made Parker’s decision any easier.

There has been considerable pressure for West Ham to make a change in goal, but Areola’s own fitness has reportedly been an matter. Until Parker confirms otherwise, my best guess is that Hermansen will retain his place.

I suspect Parker will stick with Hermansen.

In a recent development, this is an ideal fixture in which to rebuild the goalkeeper’s confidence, but Preston’s likely use of long balls and set pieces means he must command his penalty area properly. Another nervous display would only intensify the debate but my own choice would be to select Finn Herrick.

I expect Parker to continue with the 4-2-3-1 formation. Arne Engels and Soungoutou Magassa should form the central-midfield partnership, with Divine Mukasa operating further forward.

Industry observers note that magassa gives West Ham a recognised holding midfielder and should help protect a changed defence. That will allow Engels to move the ball forward and support Mukasa rather than both central midfielders occupying similar positions.

It has been revealed that preston’s victory over Southampton was built around an aggressive pressing approach, something Parker will have worked on during the break. I previously argued that West Ham must learn to play through Preston’s press, and this midfield should contain enough composure and energy to do it.

In a recent development, jarrod Bowen will naturally start on the right, with Edvin Austbø on the left. In my opinion, Austbø has moved ahead of Manor Solomon in the pecking order and deserves a proper run in the team.

Recent findings suggest that joël Piroe should lead the attack. Parker needs to give West Ham’s most proven Championship goalscorer an extended opportunity rather than continually rotating strikers who have struggled to find any rhythm.

Sources indicate that I expect five players who were away on international duty—Hermansen, Mavropanos, Mukasa, Austbø and Piroe—to start. The key defensive change should see Morato move inside to replace the suspended Kilman.

Sources indicate that preston earned their first victory under Graham Alexander by beating Southampton before the international break, so they should arrive with renewed confidence. However, both of their Championship wins this season have come at home.

In a recent development, their away record is dreadful. Preston are winless on the road, having drawn once and lost six of their seven away league matches, including some heavy defeats.

I expect them to use plenty of long balls, remain compact and try to frustrate West Ham. Even so, the Hammers have far better players and will enjoy the lion’s share of possession.

Quite frankly, it is time they showed the difference in quality. If West Ham cannot beat the Championship’s bottom club at home after Parker has been given two weeks to prepare, serious questions will remain about our promotion credentials.

Preston may make the opening stages awkward, but West Ham should eventually have far too much attacking quality. Parker’s team need to play with intensity, move the ball promptly and turn possession into genuine chances rather than merely dominating the statistics.

I expect a much more organised performance following the international break. Preston’s direct approach may still produce a goal, particularly with West Ham fielding a changed central defence, but this should be the afternoon Parker claims his first victory.

Prediction: West Ham United 4-1 Preston North End.

By LEWIS BROWNING, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 17:56 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 19:19 EST, 16 November 2026.

Liverpool midfielder Florian Wirtz scored a stunning brace for Germany as Jurgen Klopp's side thumped the Netherlands in the Nations League.

The 23-year-old has had a tough time of it at Anfield since his £116million move to the club last summer, but has never really struggled on the international stage.

And he continued that trend on Monday evening with two goals for his side to help them top their Nations League group.

His first was the pick of the bunch. Wirtz moved along the forward line as a Dutch side without Virgil van Dijk struggled to contain him. He picked up the ball around 25 yards out, cut inside onto his weaker left foot, and curled a pearling effort into the far corner off the post.

That goal, which came on the hour mark, put his side 2-0 up after Freiburg's Derry Scherhant had scored the opener, and Wirtz wasn't done there.

Centre back Nico Schlotterbeck made it 3-0 before the Liverpool man picked up his second of the night after drifting into the penalty box unmarked and finishing high after good work from Brajan Gruda.

Cette version de Wirtz avec le maillot de la Mannschaft c’est celle qu’on aimerait voir chaque semaine en PL. Quel missile pour faire le break ! Meilleur buteur allemand sur cette édition de l’UNL. 🇩🇪🔥 pic.twitter.com/m0DqaOungS.

Florian Wirtz scored a brace for Germany as they thumped the Netherlands 5-0 in Nations League action.

Liverpool midfielder Wirtz received a big hug from a smiling Jurgen Klopp at full time.

Gruda himself, who is on loan at RB Leipzig from Brighton, wrapped up the five-star win on a night that arguably saw Klopp announce himself as Germany boss.

After full-time, the ex-Liverpool manager gave Wirtz a huge hug as the duo beamed with significant smiles on their faces.

While it was a night to remember for Germany, a Netherlands team that included the likes of Micky van de Ven, Jurrien Timber and Wirtz's Liverpool team-mate Cody Gakpo were left exasperated.

Van Dijk had pulled out of the squad with a knock after playing with a knock in recent weeks.

His side will still, though, compete in the Nations League quarter-finals after finishing second in the group, finishing ahead of Greece on goal difference.

As for Wirtz, he will hope his performance will help continue what has been an uphill climb so far this season.

He also found the net for Germany in their first match of the international break – a 3-1 win over Serbia – and picked up a goal and assist in Liverpool's 3-1 win over Crystal Palace before the international break.

In total, he has two goals and five assists in 15 games for Liverpool this season – though the Reds will hope those numbers increase as the season goes on.

His second goal came as he drifted into the penalty area and finished high into the net.

Last month, meanwhile, Reds manager Andoni Iraola insisted he has full faith in his midfielder.

In a recent development, 'I think he has had a little bit of everything this season,' he said. 'He has had good games, probably the other day was not his best game, especially offensively. We trust Florian.

It has been revealed that 'Florian is a very good player. He was coming from good performances in the international break, I think. I think it is a matter of everyone to find his moment.'.

Klopp hailed him 'exceptional', meanwhile, during the last international break.

📅 05 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that sometimes inspiration can come from the unlikeliest of sources.
  • It turned out Gasly and Russell had been playing online chess until about 15 minutes before qualifying.
  • “Since the [drivers’] briefing last night, I figured out that he [Russell] is obsessed with chess, and so am I,” Gasly explained later in his press conference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sometimes inspiration can come from the unlikeliest of sources. After claiming the first pole of his Formula One career, an absolutely stunning effort in his 192nd attempt – edging out Mercedes’ George Russell right at the death – Alpine’s Pierre Gasly revealed that a harmless jibe from his performance coach Ben Thorpe just before the session started had riled him up.

It turned out Gasly and Russell had been playing online chess until about 15 minutes before qualifying.

“Since the [drivers’] briefing last night, I figured out that he [Russell] is obsessed with chess, and so am I,” Gasly explained later in his press conference. “There are a few of us in the paddock who are. So we have exchanged our IDs on Chess.com and we have had a little game going on.

Recent findings suggest that “I won yesterday, and another one that carried on into today,” the Frenchman added. “I was feeling confident and I was picking [taking] piece after piece. Then Ben told me: ‘You are getting George here but he is going to get you in a few minutes!’. And I thought ‘F--- off!’.”.

What a way to break your duck. And what a day on which to do it. On Friday, Gasly lost his only podium of the season when the International Court of Appeal reinstated two five-second penalties he received in Monaco, dropping him from third to seventh in that race. The ruling produced fireworks when Flavio Briatore, Alpine’s executive adviser, then accused one of the judges on the ICA panel of being biased towards McLaren, one of two teams who had brought the appeal.

Another 24 hours later, the fireworks were for all the right reasons. And there was no appealing the result; the start of Russell’s final lap in Q3 was slightly compromised by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, but the Englishman could have no real complaints, losing out by 0.060secs in the end, prompting wild celebrations in the Alpine garage.

To say the result was a surprise would be an understatement. This was the Enstone team’s first pole in 17 years, since Fernando Alonso took P1 Renault at the 2009 Hungarian Grand Prix.

It has been revealed that the warning signs were there. Alpine had been quick all weekend. But the Tifosi packing Monza’s grandstands fully expected it to be a battle between Mercedes and their beloved Ferrari for pole.

Recent findings suggest that the Scuderia’s performance was underwhelming. Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were only ninth and 10th quickest in Q2, the latter squeaking into Q3 by one thousandth of a second from Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto. “F--- me,” Hamilton remarked after dodging that bullet.

Industry observers note that and although they improved a bit in Q3, Hamilton managing to claim P5, just behind Leclerc in P4, they never threatened the front row. In fact, they later got lucky as McLaren’s Oscar Piastri, who took P3, was later hit with a three-place grid drop post-qualifying for impeding Liam Lawson, meaning both Ferrari drivers rose one place.

Industry observers note that it could prove significant. Hamilton, like Russell, knows this weekend represents a golden opportunity to close the gap to Kimi Antonelli in the title race. The two Britons are tied second in the championship heading into the weekend, 59 points behind the Italian. But Antonelli, who sacrificed his qualifying to help Russell, must start from the back of the grid on Sunday due to exceeding the permitted number of engines in a season.

It has been revealed that it promises to be a fascinating race, with Antonelli fighting his way through the pack and Russell and Hamilton trying to make hay while they can. Russell sounded confident. “I think they [Alpine] have got a car that’s got some good straight-line speed, which will be nice for them in the race. But, yeah, confident I’ve got the pace to go for the win.”.

According to recent reports, could he be underestimating Gasly again? The Frenchman, who lives locally in Milan and speaks fluent Italian, has won here before. He claimed the only victory of his F1 career at Monza for AlphaTauri in 2020.

Sources indicate that “Anything is possible tomorrow,” insisted Steve Nielsen, Alpine’s managing director. “We didn’t expect to be in pole position, we are. Tomorrow, good starts, good strategy, good pit stops – who knows? Let’s try to win it.”.

According to recent reports, gasly himself said he had no idea what he was capable of. “My plan is to stay first as long as I can. How long is that going to be? I have no idea. My focus is going to be on my driving and making no mistakes and making the best out of what I have.” Perhaps that will be enough for another checkmate.

Antonelli acknowledged that his engine-parts grid penalty meant he had no reason not to assist his teamate Russell by offering towing assistance.

In a recent development, he seemed a little peeved at times on the radio, but he did his job. With Russell likely to need to return the favour for him later this season, there is no point causing bother.

He told Sky Sports: “It’s what I have to do. The team asked me and of course I did what I had to do, I tried to help as much as possible. It’s a bit weird going in two, even the lap I did alone was a bit of a weird feeling. Overall with the penalty today I had to be a good teammate and I had to help as much as I could. I think I did a good job with that and happy it worked out.”.

Sources indicate that here’s Oscar Piastri, asked if a pole had been possible: “I don’t think so, no. I think the first lap felt good and I tried to see if anyone wanted to go in front out of the pit lane but no one did and I knew it was always going to be difficult and misjudged the braking a little bit and locked up. That was the session but good to have a decent result, it has been a while. I’ll take it.”.

Industry observers note that alpine managing director Steve Nielsen remarked to Sky Sports that they were aiming high: “Pierre is a class act, as you say, if you give him the machine, he will deliver. We failed to do that a few times last year. We haven’t always given him the most competitive machinery this year, but when we have he has delivered. Particularly earlier in the season so to see the team bounce back, to see him deliver on the track he knows well, he lives locally, he lives in Milan. It was wonderful.

Sources indicate that “We mustn’t forget Franco either, he’s done a great job today. I really feel we have given them a good car, and who knows? Anything is possible tomorrow.”.

Here’s what he said immediately after the session: “Massive congrats to Pierre because that’s an incredible performance. We were actually playing a game of chess about 15 minutes before qualifying and he beat me there and I thought ‘well I think I’ll beat you in qualifying’ and here we are - he’s ahead of me again! I was disappointed not to get pole. It was a bit messy with Verstappen opening the lap. But Pierre and Alpine have been super fast, even from Q1. Happy to see them get a good result.”.

Gasly’s advantage, it appears, seems to be over Russell’s car understeering and lacking grip in turbulent air.

P1 ☝️#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/U0hebWsjWY.

He indicates: “It was amazing, thank you everyone. It was an incredible qualy. I felt very good in the car. I was trying to chip away in evert session. I’m so happy, it’s been nine years trying to get a pole. First win [was] in Monza, to get pole is very special.”.

He then pays credit to his team and the fans in Italian, and I am leaning on my Latin to get the gist of it.

“I was disappointed not to get the pole,” admits Russell who said he had been playing chess with Gasly before the game and the Frenchman won that, with Russell confident he was going to beat him in qualifying.

In a recent development, alpine been in the news all weekend. Fair to say that pole lap from Gasly is better PR for the team than Flavio Briatore’s bizarre outburst in the FIA press conference yesterday. Well done that man.

His tone is evidently disappointed. In truth, given Hamilton is fifth, he is in a strong position to have the best of the weekend.

Gasly, yes, was fastest, but Russell has been the most consistent.

Sources indicate that piastri could be in trouble, too, for impeding earlier in the day’s sesion. Ferrari, in fourth and fifth, do not look entirely competitive.

Russell is second, Piastri third, Leclerc fourth, Hamilton fifth, Verstappen sixth, Antonelli seventh, Colapinto eighth, Norris ninth and Lindblad 10th.

He starts his flying lap, and locks up at turn 1 and exceeds track limits. That means Norris will be unable to get a tow from him too.

After being the quickest at FP2 and FP3, he is top of the pack once more with a bit over five minutes left.

Antonelli has done him a favour there, but Russell may need to return the favour in similar circumstances down the line.

Hamilton is now down in ninth, and struggling, about 0.8s off the pace.

Piastri may be in for some bother.

Q2 awaits, with Gasly fastest - aiming for what would be his first pole.

Alonso, meanwhile, has wirthdrawn from the session. Things going wrong for the veteran, who must have no other hobbies.

Industry observers note that pierre Gasly takes his Alpine for a spin. He is now fastest, with Verstappen second, and Colapinto bookending the Dutchman.

Antonelli and then Russell next, with the stricken Antonelli likely to give his colleague a tow.

The Red Bull man is 0.216s clear of Hamilton, with Piastri just behind.

No surprising stragglers just yet, but 11 minutes to go of this section.

We’ve 16 minutes left, and some cars are finally coming out to do battle.

Sources indicate that 18 minutes ahead before the final two rounds. Nobody is doing anything. As they say in football: tactically fascinating.

According to recent reports, monza paddock is absolutely sweltering. 33.8C out here. I just passed Fabio Capello on my way back to the media centre. He was speaking to Sky Sports Italia so I wasn’t able to give him my thoughts on where he went wrong at the 2010 World Cup.

Decent ding dong between Hamilton and Verstappen in practice earlier. Hopefully Hamilton is fired up for this. With Antonelli taking his grid drop at his home race, there’s a substantial opportunity for both Hamilton and Russell to close the gap this weekend.

Here’s our interview with Alex Albon about a grim weekend at Monza.

In a recent development, “Alex Albon remembers the 2022 Italian Grand Prix well. He had been looking forward to it. ‘We had a car which was good down the straights that year so I was quite excited to be going to Monza,” the Williams driver recalls, a little wistfully.

‘We did FP1 and FP2 and sure enough we were quick so I was like: ‘This is going to be a good weekend.’.

Industry observers note that “Albon could not have been more wrong. He remembers waking at around 1am that night and being unable to get back to sleep.

Industry observers note that “What happened next was the stuff of nightmares. Albon called the doctor, was diagnosed with appendicitis, sent to San Gerardo Hospital in Monza for surgery, only to suffer an unexpected complication during the procedure, which resulted in acute respiratory failure.”.

He shares the joint record with Michael Schumacher for most wins at Monza.

Schumacher, a Ferrari legend, ended his career with five. Hamilton has the same.

Sport loves an emotional link to records, so be prepared for this to become a massive moment.

Five wins apiece for Michael and Lewis 🖐#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/j10lMygYft.

The Italian team are bringing an upgrade engine to Monza for the weekend.

Hamilton would desperately love to go out at the top after what is a remarkable return to decent form after some years of desperate struggle.

With Antonelli possibly out of the running this weekend, this is the chance to change the - *spits in self-scorn* - narrative.

Russell might have incurred a penalty if he had done this in qualifying.

“Just looking at the deltas there, I was losing something like 0.6secs to George on the straights, which is something we need to look into,” Hamilton stated yesterday, before explaining his conundrum for qualifying, suggesting he may go out after Leclerc.

“The tow is everything here so [I’m] likely to be looking for the tow.”.

Because Antonelli exceeded the limit of parts used for his engine, he is taking a grid penalty at Monza.

Few would entirely rule out a storming ride for him on Sunday to end up top of the pack, but is is clearly a huge task for him to score points of any kind with that disadvantage.

They are now likely both past their peaks, but Hamilton and Verstappen recalled their battles of 2021 when they clashed in practice earlier.

Verstappen was already hacked off with Hamilton for seemingly obstructing his path earlier in the session, and they almost came together in the dying moments of the session.

Hamilton needed to take the escape road at the first chicane, where the pair made contact in 2021, as Verstappen looked to slip around his occasional rival. The two of them scarcely avoided another contact.

On the radios, Verstappen claimed, “He caused that,” while Hamilton reported to Ferrari that he was, “Blocked by Max.” Perhaps there will be more aggro later.

The full list of times from earlier today.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of and qualifying for the Monza Grand Prix.

Before the weekend’s racing, George Russell was, at least publicly, less than bullish about his chances in Italy.

He did, though, believe he would deliver a better showing than he had in recent weeks.

“I don’t know if we can say we’re favourites this weekend, but we probably have a greater opportunity than we’ve had in the last two races where it’s been less about the power unit and more about the chassis,” he said.

In a recent development, “It’s so close right now, that last tenth in qualifying can be the difference of a couple of positions, which can change the podium. Right now, I don’t know who is going to be the team to beat.”.

Industry observers note that russell was almost a minute off winner Lando Norris of McLaren in Hungary, finishing seventh in his Mercedes. Two weeks ago, in the Netherlands, he took the last spot on the podium, with Norris winning again.

However, in the second practice session on Friday and FP3 today, Russell was quickest. He led his former colleague, Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, who was second fastest.

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen hinted at a rare good weekend as he was third fastest, about a third of a second behind Russell.

Russell, of course, needs a win soon, or he is in danger of seeing the championship run away from him entirely, as Kimi Antonelli already leads him by 59 points in the world title chase.

Perhaps psychologically just as pressing is that erstwhile teammate Hamilton is tied with Russell on 183 points, in third because he has one victory compared to Russell’s two. Slipping down the rankings could knock his confidence.

Russell has not secured pole for the last four races, so a strong showing in qualifying might be the boost he needs ahead of Sunday’s race, while Norris is looking for a pole position hat-trick.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Joshua Cole | 19 Nov 2026 16:48, Last updated: 19 Nov 2026 16:53.

Kocaelispor will be looking to extend their unbeaten run when they welcome Fenerbahce to Turka Arac Muayene Kocaeli Stadium on Saturday evening in the Turkish Super Lig.

Both teams are tied on 19 points from their opening 11 matches, with the hosts seventh in the table, one place below the visitors in sixth, although the Yellow Canaries have scored considerably more goals this season and therefore boast a significantly better goal difference.

Kocaelispor have responded positively to consecutive defeats against Besiktas and Goztepe, going unbeaten in their last three league matches.

Their latest outing produced a 2-0 victory away to Eyupspor, following a goalless draw at home to Caykur Rizespor and a 2-1 victory over Alanyaspor, while they also recorded a 3-0 win over Mazidagi in the Turkish Cup during that run.

Selcuk Inan's side have built their season around a solid defensive foundation, with the hosts having conceded nine goals, a tally bettered only by Trabzonspor (8), giving them the second-best defence in the league, although the Gulf have scored the fewest goals among teams in the top half of the table (13).

Their home form has also been encouraging, with three victories, one draw and one defeat from five league matches at Kocaeli Stadium, where they have scored six goals and conceded just two, although they have failed to win either of their last two home fixtures (D1, L1).

However, Kocaelispor have struggled in this fixture over the years, failing to win any of their last 14 meetings with Fenerbahce, losing nine and drawing five, while they have also lost their last three home encounters.

Fenerbahce, meanwhile, arrive in Kocaeli after producing an emphatic response to their recent domestic setbacks, beating Corum 5-0 away from home in their last outing to return to winning ways.

The Yellow Canaries had previously suffered consecutive league defeats against Goztepe and Galatasaray, both by 2-1 scorelines, with the latter result particularly damaging as they fell further behind in the title race and prompted Ismail Kartal's resignation.

Emre Belozoglu subsequently took charge and has made an impressive start, recording a 3-2 victory over Liverpool in the Champions League before overseeing the emphatic win against Corum.

Fenerbahce's attack has been particularly productive this season, scoring 29 goals in 11 league matches to give them the most prolific frontline in the division, while their 10 goals conceded also represent the third-best defensive record, although they remain nine points off the top.

Kocaelispor are expected to be without Bruno Petkovic, who is dealing with a muscle injury, while Tanguy Zoukrou and Massadio Haidara are also doubtful with respective hamstring and tendon problems.

Aleksandar Jovanovic is another absentee, while Show is sidelined with an adductor injury, leaving Inan with decisions to make in midfield and defence.

Fenerbahce will be without Archie Brown, who is suspended, while Nathan Ake, Marco Asensio and Jayden Oosterwolde remain sidelined through injury.

Amara Diouf is also unavailable with a muscle problem, leaving Belozoglu without several options as he looks to maintain the momentum generated by the victory over Corum.

Kocaelispor possible starting lineup:.

Oztasdelen; Yildiz, Dijksteel, Ortakaya, Rivas; Bingol, Kutlu, Susoho; Agyei, Aye, Baku.

Fenerbahce possible starting lineup:.

Ederson; Semedo, Skriniar, Oppong, Mercan; Guendouzi, Yuksek; Greenwood, Kahveci, Aydin; Lukaku.

Kocaelispor have been considerably more reliable at home than away, conceding just twice in five league matches at their own stadium, but Fenerbahce's attacking record makes them difficult to overlook.

The hosts should be capable of making the contest competitive, particularly if they maintain their defensive discipline and exploit spaces on the counter-attack, but we expect the visitors' quality in the final third to ultimately prove decisive.

AC Milan have the financial capability to go out and sign their top targets in January, according to Gianluca Di Marzio.

It has been revealed that several reports and even the words of owner Gerry Cardinale have made it very clear that Milan plan to be busy in the winter mercato. The main target seems to be a forward to complete the attack, as well as a centre-back to help out the defensive department too.

Industry observers note that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Among the names linked have been Real Madrid’s Endrick, Club Brugge’s Nicolo Tresoldi and Sporting CP’s Goncalo Inacio. It’s one thing having the list of names, but it is another having the money and the possibility of doing a deal mid-season with the selling club.

During last night’s segment on Sky, Gianluca Di Marzio (via MilanNews) was asked whether Milan can realistically pursue names like Endrick and Tresoldi, who are likely to cost over €50m each.

Industry observers note that “That they has the strength to do these kinds of deals, yes. They demonstrated it over the summer, so I don’t think there’s a financial issue,” he began.

“Whether they manage to sign one of the two… Endrick, as far as we know, José Mourinho hasn’t changed his mind and therefore doesn’t intend to part with him in January. But Endrick is a Cardinale obsession, just as he was a Roma obsession during the summer.

“We’ll have to see if Mourinho changes his mind in the month and a half before the transfer window opens. He hasn’t changed his mind at the moment, so I see the situation as complicated at the moment.

“Just as it’s complicated for Brugge to sell Tresoldi. Brugge are a club that doesn’t need to sell and always sells at least one key player in the summer, precisely to try to get to the end of the season with its players.

According to recent reports, “Milan are looking for a striker, looking for a back-up for Ramos. The figures I’ve read, 60-70 million, are very, very high figures to try to convince Brugge to sell him. It’s a deal that – given the player’s objective value – I think is around 50 million. In my opinion.

In a recent development, “But Brugge are unlikely to sell him in January. Above all, Milan is looking for a striker to be a back-up for Ramos; it’s not like Ramos and Tresoldi will play together. In the sense that Milan has always played with a centre-forward.

Sources indicate that “Above all, they need to provide this center forward with plenty of playable balls rather than buy another. Because if Ramos doesn’t receive balls in the penalty area, he struggles to score, and Tresoldi struggles to score either.

“They need a striker to get Camarda playing. I think Camarda will go and play and therefore an investment will be needed in a player who can be a suitable deputy for Ramos.”.
