⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Unai Emery is building Aston Villa 2.0 and this was a night when his fresh kids on the block produced clear signs of lift-off for the next chapter.
  • Emery always springs into life on European nights and his reconstructed team secured their first win and goals of the season to leave Villa’s 1,700 fans singing in the rain.
  • Ten summer signings have arrived during a summer of upheaval, which included plenty of high-profile departures after the club’s Europa League triumph in May.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unai Emery is building Aston Villa 2.0 and this was a night when his fresh kids on the block produced clear signs of lift-off for the next chapter.

Emery always springs into life on European nights and his reconstructed team secured their first win and goals of the season to leave Villa’s 1,700 fans singing in the rain.

Ten summer signings have arrived during a summer of upheaval, which included plenty of high-profile departures after the club’s Europa League triumph in May.

Yet this was an evening that will have further energised Emery on his return to the Champions League.

Nicolas Jackson, Zion Suzuki and João Gomes embody this latest Villa team and all stood out here in Bruges.

Record £65m signing Jackson’s fine individual goal proved to be the winner to settle a chaotic, absorbing contest with the Belgian Pro League champions.

Jackson adds a third for Aston Villa after Sommer comes rushing out of his box! 😱📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/HZ1x3BkfK0.

Suzuki, the £30m replacement for Emiliano Martínez, has clear presence in goal and he is Villa’s version of former Manchester City goalkeeper Ederson with his wide array of passing.

Gomes was also industrious in midfield to recover from what was a nightmarish debut at Brighton, where he was sent off after 40 minutes.

Despite all the changes to this team, talismanic captain John McGinn remains essential to Villa. He became their all-time leading goalscorer in major European competitions with his 12th goal and led by example again, as he has done so many times.

Sources indicate that mcGinn strikes to put Villa ahead in Bruges! 💥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/FJnuxSwYwo.

There were also hints of a strong defensive partnership developing between Pau Torres and Victor Lindelof, following the sale of Ezri Konsa to Arsenal last month.

“Fantastic, fantastic,” purred Emery at one point in the second half from the technical area, and Villa’s season now appears up and running.

Emery noted: “This was another step forward and I am so happy and thankful for this. The old players need to keep our standards high and show everyone this is the only way we can achieve the process and reach our targets.

In a recent development, “It’s very important to start the Champions League with three points and hopefully this will give us confidence for the league. We are improving and we must work hard – it is the only way.”.

Although Emery has established a reputation as the Europa League king, winning that trophy five times, this competition has proved more difficult to master.

His best run was reaching the semi-finals in the 2021-22 season, when his Villarreal side lost to Liverpool.

It remains a tournament in which he is desperate to make an impression, with Villa returning to Champions League duty here for the first time since their thrilling encounter with Paris St-Germain in April 2025.

Only five of that starting XI from the second leg of the quarter-final remain and one of them, midfielder Amadou Onana, is out until next year after sustaining a serious knee injury at the World Cup with Belgium.

With European heavyweights Barcelona, PSG and Borussia Dortmund to come in the league phase, this always felt like a game Villa probably needed to win.

They had only managed one shot on target so far this season before arriving in this historic city, but scored three goals before half-time.

Sources indicate that their opener came against the run of play in the 11th minute, with McGinn casually finding the corner after a lung-bursting run from Torres. McGinn has overtaken former Villa striker Ollie Watkins at the top of the club’s continental goalscoring charts.

Brugge briefly wobbled but were level eight minutes later when Hugo Vetlesen swept home from 10 yards, capitalising on space in the penalty box.

Vetlesen draws Club Brugge level against Aston Villa! ⚡📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/4ZYwPcMHim.

Villa were back in front less than 160 seconds later, with Gomes teeing up Emiliano Buendía for an easy finish. Gomes was released in the box by a clever backheel from Jackson.

It has been revealed that buendia restores Villa's lead just minutes after Club Brugge's equaliser, and Unai Emery is LOVING it! 🙌📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/h2WGkwkTI1.

Two minutes before half-time Yann Sommer, Club Brugge’s new goalkeeper, then had a severe rush of blood to the head by racing from his goal to almost the halfway line in an attempt to intercept Torres’s long pass.

Sources indicate that jackson edged the ball past him and held off a defender to calmly slot into the empty net. He underlined in many moments why Emery has pursued him for so long, after the pair established a strong rapport at Villarreal.

Villa appeared relatively comfortable in the second half until Aaron Wan-Bissaka was judged to have handled a cross from Joaquin Seys, after referee Sandro Schärer was advised by VAR to review the incident on his TV monitor.

It was a simple decision and Nicolò Tresoldi put away the penalty to stir life back into the home supporters.

Club Brugge are back in it from the penalty spot after Wan-Bissaka's handball! 👀📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/pEanRJvimu.

Recent findings suggest that villa defended resolutely as time began to tick away with Suzuki providing authority in goal. The first Japanese goalkeeper to play in the Champions League also produced a number of routine saves in a nervy finish.

This was a promising night for a new Villa era.

Full-time scenes in Bruges as Aston Villa get their Champions League campaign off to a winning start! 👏📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/nYwtiQ6Xs7.

Villa are defending with six at the back as midfield and defence merge into one. There are seconds remaining as Suzuki punts the ball up field and there is the final whistle! Villa make a winning start to the 2026-27 Champions League.

Another cross from the right is met, this time, by Tresoldi, but his header has no bite and Suzuki gathers.

Industry observers note that torres heads another Siquet cross behind for a corner. Brugge load the box but none of their players are able to get a meaningful touch on the ball before Diakhon slips just as he looks to get a shot away from the left of the box.

Slightly less mature play from Gomes, though. He bundles Vermant over and earns a needless yellow card.

Really mature play by Hemmings. Looking to break away, he simply puts his body between man and ball, inviting the challenge and winning a foul.

Villa are working hard in their compact mid-block and Brugge are struggling to find a way through.

Leko sends on Vermant and Diakhon for Potts and Virgili.

Barkley is one lucky boy. Attempting to play out under pressure, the midfielder gives the ball straight to Virgili, who cannot sort out his feet before offloading to Tresoldi far too late. A massive let-off for Villa.

According to recent reports, gomes goes close after driving through Brugge’s midfield. He really should, though, have played in a free McGinn at the back post. Moments later Bogarde fires another shot goalwards but Sommer gets to it.

Abraham replaces goalscorer Jackson.

Recent findings suggest that villa have wrestled control away from their opponents. McGinn’s teasing cross evades everyone and Alysson’s cross takes a deflection which goes behind for a corner which is not up to much.

Lee hauls down Hemmings which gives Villa the opportunity to slow the game down. McGinn flights a delivery in from the left but Brugge clear their lines.

The ball comes out to Alysson who jinks in from the right, tiptoeing through a crowd, desperate to get a shot away on his left foot, but Seys does well to track his man and smother the effort.

Vanakan and Velesen and replaced by Tsawa and Lemarechal.

It has been revealed that yet another dangerous Siquet cross rains in from the right and here it is taken off Tresoldi’s toes by the tip of Lindelof’s boot. The defender did brilliantly to clear his lines at full stretch.

Hemmings burst towards the by-line and his cross trickles across the face of goal. Alysson is waiting at the far post but Seys does well to shield the ball and win a free-kick.

Recent findings suggest that villa’s best chance at putting this game to bed will come on the counter. And here McGinn plays in Jackson whose one-vs-one effort is stopped by Sommer.

It has been revealed that virgili from the left, Siquet from the right. Threats are coming from both wings and Villa need to get their foot on the ball if they are to take the sting out of Brugge’s attack.

Instead they allow Vetlesen a yard of space and his long-range sighter stings the hands of Suzuki who turns behind for a corner.

Emery switches out Buendia, Kamara and Wan-Bissaka for Alysson, Barkley and Bogarde before the corner is taken, and Suzuki stops the eventual delivery on the line after the ball spun off the post!

In a recent development, another Virgili cross threatens to carve Villa open but they just about clear their lines. Then it is Siquet who delivers, this time from the right, but his cross just evades Tresoldi and Mechele at the far post. The home fans are invested in this, they believe their side can grab an equaliser...

Villa have got their tails between their legs here. From a position of strength, they have allowed the momentum to swing in the hosts’ favour and it has been largely self-inflicted.

Maatsen has a chance to break free but cannot build a head of steam before he is stymied.

It has been revealed that club Brugge 2 Aston Villa 3 (Tresoldi pen) Suzuki dives to his right early and Tresoldi slides the ball into the opposite side of the net. Just the one goal in it now!

Club Brugge are back in it from the penalty spot after Wan-Bissaka's handball! 👀📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/pEanRJvimu.

Brugge have averted their attention to their right hand side, Siquet and Forbs attacking in tandem. A dangerous cross from Forbs is met by Tresoldi but he cannot get the requisite contact on it. Seys collects the ball on the far side and fires a delivery into Wan-Bissaka and out for a corner. Replays show that it comes off the defenders hand ...and referee Scharer is sent to the screen. He wastes no time at the monitor and awards a spot kick!

Villa do appear pretty comfortable here, despite some frequent pressure from Club Brugge.

Pau Torres has been outstanding so far at the back for Unai Emery’s team.

This is also a night where Emery’s ‘new’ Villa are coming of age, with Nicolas Jackson, Zion Suzuki and Joao Gomes also impressive.

McGinn, sensing Virgili’s growing influence on the half, takes matters into his own hands and leaves one on the Spanish winger, Siquet’s free-kick from deep is aimed at Tresoldi but Suzuki is wise to it and sweeps up.

Brugge are just reminding Villa that they are still there. Virgili is at the heart of things again, combining with Vetlesen who works the ball out to Forbs whose cross is well held by Suzuki.

Villa then spring forward, Hemmings breaching the Brugge box, but Buendia’s eventual effort does not make it through a thicket of legs.

It has been revealed that brugge are building with a three-man backline, sending Siquet forward high and wide. They’ve had much of the ball in the opening stages of this half, which is probably part of Villa’s plan. Emery’s side have settled into an out-of-possession 4-4-2.

Industry observers note that vanakan is booked for simulation after going hitting the deck off a challenge from Gomes. There is a knowing smile on the Belgian midfielder’s face which suggests the referee’s convictions were correct.

According to recent reports, we are back under way... Siquet replaces Sabbe at the interval.

Nicolas Jackson is off the mark for Aston Villa. He beat Yann Sommer to the ball, held off a defender and was left with the simplest of finishes to round off a fine first half for Villa. pic.twitter.com/gWx6kUTlOX.

Unai Emery has the upcoming kids on the block but this Aston Villa team are hangin’ tough.

This has been a pretty chaotic first-half on the return of the Champions League but Emery will be satisfied with what he has seen so far. It’s very much a case of step by step for his reshaped team, but they should see this game out now.

Sources indicate that it’s been a shocking night for Club Brugge’s new goalkeeper Yann Sommer. He’s just had a serious rush of blood to the head and was punished by Nicolas Jackson, who had an easy task to score Villa’s third goal. Sommer has probably ended his team’s hopes of a result here.

He changes his mind mid-throw and attempts to re-catch the ball but ends up wandering outside of his allotted space. The resulting free-kick crashes straight into the wall.

He offloads the ball to McGinn on the right of the area and the Scotsman steadies himself before curling the ball into the far post, beyond Sommer.

It is that duo again, Virgili and Seys. They have responded to Wan-Bissaka’s advanced position and are trying to pin him back. Virgili cuts in on to his right foot and forces a save from Suzuki to get the home fans going.

Aston Villa are still establishing their identity with a new team but it has already become clear how much they will rely on goalkeeper Zion Suzuki,.

The £30m signing from Parma possesses a wide passing range and much of Villa’s build-up play starts with the Japan international.

He is Villa’s very own version of Manchester City’s former pass master Ederson.

Much has been made of Suzuki’s distribution and he has already teased a couple of lovely flighted balls up-field. Villa’s defenders are more than happy to lure Brugge’s first line of pressure forward but have not yet been able to find an incisive line-breaking pass.

Seyes and Virgili combine down the left in Brugge’s best attack so far, but Torres is able to head behind for a corner, which is not up to much.

Wan-Bissaka has taken up a very aggressive position down Villa’s right and he earns a free-kick in a promising position. McGinn spins in a delivery which is only partially cleared but Maatsen’s effort from the edge of the box is smothered.

There is a minute’s silence for those affected by the floods in Nepal which is impeccably observed.

The players then retreat to their halves and Jackson gets us going!

Aston Villa 2.0 is clearly a work in progress after so many high-profile exits and 10 fresh signings.

Unai Emery has warned that it will take time for his fresh team to click, but this is an opportunity to spark the season into life.

Behind the scenes, Villa are feeling very comfortable about so much upheaval and it is the presence of Emery in the technical area which provides them with so much optimism.

For a deeper dive into why patience will be needed, read more here.

Recent findings suggest that brugge have conceded just two goals in five league games this season, but their Pro League opponents have threatened against the Belgian champions’ right side, especially in attacking transitions. Kyriani Sabbe is the more adventurous of Brugge’s two full-backs and the space he vacates will be inviting to George Hemmings and Ian Maatsen.

Here are a couple of examples of Brugge’s vulnerability down their right:.

Industry observers note that don-Angelo Konadu, Lommel’s centre-forward, drifts out to the left and takes on Lee Han-beom whose centre-back partner Brandon Mechele has committed too far forward. As such, the space between Lee and covering left-back Joaquin Seys is too massive and Freddie Potts attempts to recover from midfield. Konadu earns himself a yard with a feint inside and his shot is well-saved by Yann Sommer.

Sources indicate that in Brugge’s 2-1 defeat by Gent a week earlier, Leonardo Lopes punches in a pass into the left half-space for Monodu Sonko to latch on to and from there the inside forward draws a save from Sommer. Josué Vergara’s follow-up strikes the crossbar.

The Spaniard added a fifth Europa League title to his CV last season while also guiding Villa to a strong fourth-place finish in the Premier League. Emery was today declared as one of five nominees for France Football’s Men’s Coach of the Year award – one of the Ballon d’Or accolades.

Christos Tzolis enjoyed an outstanding season with Brugge in 2025-26, contributing 51 goal involvements in 52 matches. His haul earned him a £34m move to Arsenal, where he has continued in much the same vein, laying on three assists in four matches.

While Tzolis wears the No 17 at Arsenal, his former No 8 shirt at Brugge has been inherited by Englishman Freddie Potts, who made the move from West Ham to Belgium last month. Potts has made a strong start to the season, serving as Brugge’s midfield sentry and starting all five of the club’s matches thus far.

One player to keep an eye on for Club Brugge is midfielder Freddie Potts.

He was signed from West Ham last month for a significant fee and lifted the Europa Conference League trophy when David Moyes was in charge.

Also in the Brugge team is Carlos Forbs, the former Manchester City trainee who had a poor loan spell at Wolves a couple of seasons back.

Mings is on the bench today. Matty Cash is out with a muscle concern so there is a first start for summer signing Aaron Wan-Bissaka.

It has been revealed that addressing the media in Monday’s pre-match press conference, Unai Emery was asked about the challenges of taking Aston Villa into another season in Europe with a significantly changed squad. He said: “To continue in this level, changing some players, key players, but those key players we changed this year as well before the last year we were changing – not like this year, because this year was more players than normal, but we are replacing them.

“We have the players with experience like here with Emiliano [Buendía] and they deserve to continue here trying take now more responsibility and try to give the players we have … Of course we have now latest players with a lot of experience like Goretska for example, and we have some young players, they are coming from [big] clubs like Garnacho, Mbaye or Jackson. We must try to adapt them in our structure tactically and arrive [at that point] as fast as possible … We need time, I don’t know if we need time or not, it’s not for me something I’m thinking about, I am thinking about competing. To compete [in] each match.

“We started the Premier League, the first competition, as our objective at the end of the season, because through it we can achieve our objectives this year, and we’re progressing. Still not enough, because we are not getting good results. But [the match against Brugge] is a new test.”.

The experienced Yann Sommer starts between the sticks, with in-form striker Nicolò Tresoldi leading the line. English midfielder Freddie Potts is one of Ivan Leko’s two pivots.

Aston Villa are back in the Champions League and in familiar territory with an unfamiliar team.

This will be their third match at the Jan BreydelStadion in less than two years but much has changed with the players that last competed here for Unai Emery.

Two of the goalscorers in the club’s last outing in Bruges were Leon Bailey and Marco Asensio, who are no longer at the club.

Of course, they are not the only players that have left and this is a upcoming-look Emery team hoping for lift-off this season.

Villa are the Europa League winners but this could be a tricky evening against the Belgian Pro League champions.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of Aston Villa’s Champions League opener against Club Brugge. Unai Emery’s side voyage across the Channel to face the Belgian champions having triumphed in last season’s Europa League and finished fourth in the Premier League. The Villa mothership has since sailed into choppy waters, though, with a raft of significant-name sales preceding a run of two defeats and a draw in the league. An opening-weekend thrashing by Brighton and Hove Albion proved quite the storm for Emery’s fresh-look crew.

It has been revealed that morgan Rogers alighted for Chelsea in a deal worth £117m, a record fee for an English player, and goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez followed soon after, while Youri Tielemans moved to Manchester United. Ezri Konsa and Ollie Watkins completed the exodus of leading men with late-August moves to Arsenal and Al-Hilal respectively. To remedy the outgoings, Villa twice broke their transfer record this summer, pipping Newcastle United to the signing of Johan Manzambi (£59.5m) before landing Nicolas Jackson (£65m, including add-ons), and added Taylor Harwood-Bellis and Ibrahim Mbaye on deadline day. Whether they can hit the ground running remains to be seen, but Emery has a task on his hands aligning his fresh recruits before the scrutiny intensifies.

Although Villa swept aside Brugge 6-1 across two legs in the Champions League quarter-finals two seasons ago, here Blauw-Zwart (Blue-Black) represent a stern test having made the Jan Breydel Stadium a fortress in last year’s tournament. Their only home defeat in the league phase came against Arsenal, with a 3-3 draw against Barcelona backed up by 4-1 and 3-0 victories over Monaco and Marseille respectively. Belgium’s second-most decorated club have won seven of the last 11 league titles and know how to win matches. In Yann Sommer, Ivan Leko has one of world football’s most experienced goalkeepers, who kept the most clean sheets in the 2024-25 edition of the Champions League (seven). Captain Hans Vanakan, Brandon Mechele and Joaquin Seys were part of Rudi Garcia’s Belgium World Cup squad, and German striker Nicolò Tresoldi already has four goals in six matches this term. English midfielder Freddie Potts could also feature, having settled in nicely in West Flanders having moved from West Ham United during the summer.

The earlier 5.45pm kick-off time, means Villa, Brugge, LASK and AEK Athens have the opportunity to top the 36-team league …at least for a couple of hours.

Host–microbe interactions in engineered immunocompetent human gut tissues

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a primary port of pathogen entry, the intestinal mucosa has developed a sophisticated set of defences to ward off infections.
  • In a recent development, the human intestine coordinates nutrient absorption with immune surveillance of luminal commensal and pathogenic microorganisms2.
  • This context-dependent crosstalk is executed through a multi-barrier system comprising a patterned epithelium, a protective mucus layer and specialized tissue-resident immune cells5.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a primary port of pathogen entry, the intestinal mucosa has developed a sophisticated set of defences to ward off infections. Investigating the human-specific intestinal barrier responses to pathogens is limited by the lack of models integrating the necessary architectural complexity with an autologous immune compartment1. Here we developed engineered barrier models of the human small intestine and colon combining a multilineage epithelium, mucus layer, accessible microbial compartment and autologous tissue-resident immune cells. These tissues recapitulate morphological and functional properties that are region specific and compare with those of the native organ. We use the model to characterize the human epithelial response to Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhimurium at the single-cell level, uncovering the distinct gene regulatory networks that underpin luminal versus intracellular pathogen presence. Invaded epithelial cells initiate an IL-18 signalling axis that triggers cytotoxic T cell activation, resulting in epithelial shedding and barrier disruption. Overall, this work allows for the modular integration of epithelial, microbial and immune compartments, providing a versatile system for studying human intestinal physiology and pathologies.

In a recent development, the human intestine coordinates nutrient absorption with immune surveillance of luminal commensal and pathogenic microorganisms2. Controlled host–microbe interactions shape diverse aspects of human biology, including epithelial maturation and systemic immunity while maintaining a protective barrier against infection3. Conversely, dysregulated interactions contribute to pathologies such as inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer4.

This context-dependent crosstalk is executed through a multi-barrier system comprising a patterned epithelium, a protective mucus layer and specialized tissue-resident immune cells5. Integration of these three components is required to meaningfully capture intestine–microbe interactions in a human-relevant setting1.

Recent findings suggest that intestinal stem cell (ISC)-derived organoids provide key inroads into human epithelial biology6. However, intestinal organoids face limitations recapitulating intestinal physiology, owing to an inaccessible lumen, culture heterogeneity, lack of biomimetic morphology and absence of non-epithelial lineages7,8. Although bioengineered 3D extracellular matrix (ECM) scaffolds have helped to overcome some of these challenges by establishing crypt–villus architecture and apical–basal access9, physiological integration of epithelial, tissue-resident immune and microbial compartments remains a major challenge1,10.

Here we established engineered immunocompetent human intestinal models composed of autologous tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells and small intestinal or colonic ISC-derived epithelia amenable to luminal manipulation. Multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) characterization of these barriers reveal region-specific spatial niches, mucus layer formation and immune–epithelium interactions. Applying this system to Salmonella Typhimurium (S.Tm), we provide a single-cell multiomic view of the epithelial responses to luminal and intracellular infection. Finally, we modelled the pathogen–epithelial–immune axis, demonstrating that TRM cells respond to S.Tm invasion by cytokine release and concomitant epithelial damage, which may facilitate pathogen clearance and infection resolution.

To model the human intestinal epithelium, we developed a fluidic device and microstamping technology to impart crypt-mimicking topography on an embedded ECM-like hydrogel (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Human intestinal organoids were seeded into the top reservoir of the device, where they formed a tight, polarized barrier comprising crypt units sustained by basal nutrition (Fig. 1a–d and Extended Data Fig. 1b–e).

Sources indicate that to characterize the morphology, cellular composition and patterning of the epithelium, we developed a 3D-printed ‘histomold’ for simultaneous embedding and perpendicular sectioning of up to 50 engineered epithelia (Extended Data Fig. 1f). Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and mIF staining indicated histological and cell-type patterning similarity to donor-matched primary tissue (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Figs. 1g and 2a–c). In addition, a duodenal dual reporter line stably labelling chromatin (H2BC4–mTurquoise2) and LGR5+ stem cells (LGR5–IRES-NLS-mScarlet3) confirmed LGR5 ISC localization to the crypt bottom (Fig. 1f). By day 10, the thick epithelium contained proliferative SOX9+ and Ki67+ cells primarily confined to the crypt, whereas mature enterocytes (APOA4+ in the duodenum, and FABP6+ in the ileum) and colonocytes (CA1+) were enriched within inter-crypt regions (Fig. 1g and Extended Data Fig. 3a–f), with αDEF5+ Paneth cells detected in some small intestinal crypts (Extended Data Fig. 3g). EdU pulse-chase labelling revealed that cycling cells, initially localized in the crypt base, progressively migrated towards the apical surface over 4 days, similar to homeostatic turnover in vivo11 (Extended Data Fig. 3h and Supplementary Video 1). These data confirm that imposing in vivo-inspired geometries on human intestinal organoids drives reproducible cell-type regionalization and migration akin to the intestinal crypt–villus axis9.

Industry observers note that multiplexed scRNA-seq demonstrated region-specific stem, absorptive and secretory lineages across seven donors at day 10 (Fig. 1h–j, Extended Data Fig. 4a,b and Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). Cell-type composition was similar to primary tissue counterparts and proportions were consistent across donors, highlighting the fidelity and robustness of the system (Fig. 1k and Extended Data Fig. 4c). Gene Ontology analysis of enterocyte and colonocyte marker genes revealed enrichment of distinct physiological programs concordant with the primary intestinal regions12,13 (Extended Data Fig. 4d and Supplementary Tables 3 and 4). Proximal small intestinal enterocytes demonstrated higher expression of genes involving lipid, xenobiotic and iron metabolism (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 4d). Pseudotemporal ordering of the duodenal stem-to-enterocyte trajectory confirmed enterocyte maturation levels, approaching the AQP10+ expression observed at the villus tip in vivo14 (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Distal small intestinal enterocytes expressed bile acid and vitamin B12 transport genes, whereas colonocytes were enriched in cell–cell interactions and ion transport13,15 (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 4d). We confirmed differential protein expression of the transporters SLC5A1, SLC10A2 and SLC26A2 between the regions (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 4f). Among secretory lineages, enteroendocrine cells and goblet cells were differentially abundant, with substantial heterogeneity in enteroendocrine cells (CHGA+) including EC (TPH1+), MX (GHRL+ and MLN+), D (SST+), K (GIP+), I (CCK+) and L (GCG+ and PYY+) subpopulations that match tissue distribution16 (Extended Data Figs. 2 and 4g–j).

Collectively, these data show that the engineered epithelium retains region-specific cell composition, spatial organization and gene expression, providing inroads to explore nutrient, xenobiotic and host–microbe processes in a human context.

The mucus, a layered network of mucins, cellular material, antimicrobials and structural factors, provides an interactive barrier between the microbiome and intestinal epithelium. Characterizing the properties and functional role of the mucus at the host–microbe interface remains largely under-explored in vitro. To facilitate rapid accumulation of mucus, we reduced the apical volume over the course of approximately 4 days, which resulted in a fibrous mucus network covering the epithelium (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 5a,b). Shed cells were present throughout the mucus layer, where they contribute to viscosity17 and can exert an antimicrobial role18 (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c). Longitudinal sections revealed an irregular mucus profile, with higher colonic thickness and crypt plumes similar to observations in primary tissue19 (Fig. 2c–e and Extended Data Fig. 5d–g). AlcianBlue–Periodic Acid–Schiff (PAS) co-staining showed regional differences in secretion and glycosylation, with higher ratios of acidic, negatively charged groups towards colon (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 5h,i). These patterns were comparable with the primary tissue and may be influenced by relative levels of fucose, sialic acid and sulfate groups20. Proteomic analysis of the colonic luminal content identified the core mucus layer proteins21 (MUC2, FCGBP, TFF3, AGR2, CLCA1, ZG16 and MUC5B) as major constituents, alongside additional mucins, antimicrobials and lectin-binding proteins (Fig. 2g, Extended Data Fig. 5j and Supplementary Table 5). Using the scRNA-seq data, we identified seven non-proliferative (MKI67−) goblet cell clusters (C0–C6) representing regional diversity and differentiation state (Fig. 2h, Extended Data Fig. 5k and Supplementary Table 3). Colonic goblet cells (C1) were enriched in intracellular vesicle transport, protein glycosylation and aerobic respiration, suggesting a higher secretion machinery consistent with thickness measurements (Extended Data Fig. 5l and Supplementary Table 4).

According to recent reports, next, we benchmarked the expression of membrane-bound mucins, key glycocalyx components that fortify the epithelium but remain difficult to recapitulate in vitro22. We observed a strong cell-type and region-specific gene expression comparable with the reference tissue (Fig. 2i). MUC6 and MUC5AC, which encode stomach mucins that are often expressed under pathological and metaplastic conditions23,24, were nearly absent. MUC12 and MUC17 staining in the engineered epithelium and tissue counterparts confirmed the specificity and maturation of the glycocalyx, revealing in vivo-like levels by day 12 of culture (Fig. 2j,k and Extended Data Fig. 5m). Finally, we functionally assessed the mucus upon colonization with the commensals Enterococcus faecium or Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus, which proliferated without compromising epithelial integrity (Fig. 2l and Extended Data Fig. 5n). Together, these results indicate that the platform can accumulate a complex mucus layer with in vivo-like and region-specific properties, opening newly introduced avenues for the study of human mucus and host–microbe interactions.

It has been revealed that unlike commensal microbiota, the foodborne pathogen S.Tm exploits motility and adhesion mechanisms to penetrate the mucus25, triggering an invasion-dependent inflammatory response that facilitates pathogen colonization26. Although extensive research has characterized the fundamental mechanisms underlying S.Tm infection, the exact epithelial responses and the resulting epithelial–immune signalling remain unresolved at the human level and at single-cell resolution.

Industry observers note that motivated by the higher mucus level and its potential role against pathogenic bacteria, we infected colonic epithelium with S.Tm 14028 in conditions with varying densities of mucus. At 18 h post-start of the infection (hpi), S.Tm triggered strong damage in conditions with less mucus (Mucuslo), whereas the epithelium remained largely unaffected in the presence of dense mucus (Mucushi; Fig. 3a–d and Extended Data Fig. 6a–d). Furthermore, the denser mucus led to a decrease in microbial burden, cell invasion and cytokine release, while preserving barrier integrity (Extended Data Fig. 6e–g). These protective effects were coupled with cell shedding, which predominantly localized at crypt openings, presumably impeding bacterial colonization (Extended Data Fig. 6h).

Recent findings suggest that next, we used single-cell transcriptome and accessible chromatin sequencing (scMultiome) to characterize the Mucushi colonic epithelium response at 24 hpi and epithelial breach (Extended Data Fig. 6i). We detected canonical cell types in control and S.Tm conditions with increased proportion of mature colonocytes upon infection, a shift reported in mouse tissue27 (Fig. 3e,f and Extended Data Fig. 6j–l). Of note, ‘colonocyte subtype 1’ (RNA clusters C7-1 and C7-2) and ‘subtype 2’ (RNA cluster C8) were nearly exclusive to the infection condition (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 6k). Overall, all cell types exhibited a pronounced response to infection with 3,056 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and 34,337 differentially accessible open chromatin regions (DARs) between conditions (Extended Data Fig. 6m–p and Supplementary Table 3). Pathway enrichment analysis highlighted hypoxia, NF-κB and barrier or cytoskeletal signatures, including upregulation of antimicrobials (LCN2 and PIGR), reactive oxygen species (DUOX2 and DUOXA2) and inflammatory cytokines (CCL20, IL18 and IL32; Extended Data Fig. 6q–s). Stem cells strongly upregulated LCN2, chemokines (CXCL1–3) and immunomodulators (TNF and LTB). Together, these results identify a complex innate epithelium response involving sensing, barrier maintenance and mucosal signalling.

We used the chromatin accessibility data to infer a gene regulatory network underlying the epithelial response (Fig. 3g). This network revealed transcription factor nodes and target genes that orchestrate a broad-spectrum response, along with clusters that specifically coordinate infection-specific states. We identified BHLHE40, ZNF292 and RBPJ as the top differentially expressed transcription factors in the colonocyte subtype 1, which exhibited a hypoxic signature that appears conserved under infections and inflammatory-related diseases28. STAT3 emerged as a central node of the colonocyte subtype 2. Phosphorylation of STAT3 (pSTAT3) has been linked to intracellular S.Tm infection29 via the virulence factor SteE30,31, leading to an anti-inflammatory transcriptional program that supports the bacterial niche. Co-staining of pSTAT3 and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) revealed a strong colocalization both in colonic and small intestinal samples, with no pSTAT3 detection in non-infected conditions (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 7a–c). These results, in addition to the expression of the STAT3 negative-feedback regulator SOCS3, suggest that this population is S.Tm specific and contains cells with intracellular bacteria.

Industry observers note that finally, we classified DEGs into co-expression gene modules based on expression differences across cell types between conditions (Supplementary Table 3). We found that the colonocyte subtype 2-specific gene module exhibited increased reactive oxygen species, endoplasmic reticulum stress, unfolded protein response and ferroptosis (Extended Data Fig. 7d and Supplementary Table 4). Furthermore, we observed a possible antagonistic interaction between host cell and pathogen, with non-cannonical inflammasome signalling (CASP4, CASP5 and IL18)32 and genes with anti-inflammatory roles (SBNO2 and TNIP3; Extended Data Fig. 7e,f). BACH1, a key oxidative stress and ferroptosis regulator competing with NRF2 (NFE2L2)33,34, was also among the top upregulated transcription factors (Extended Data Fig. 7g). Binding motifs of STAT3 and BACH1 were over-represented in S.Tm DARs, indicating that both might be regulators of this population (Supplementary Table 6). Finally, we identified putative gene regulatory regions with increased accessibility upon infection, including intronic and distal regions of IL18 and SLC7A11 in the presumably invaded cells (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 7h). Collectively, these findings identify a complex multipartite human epithelial gene regulatory response to S.Tm infection, confirm STAT3 activation in S.Tm-invaded cells, and demonstrate how engineered intestines can be used to illuminate human infection responses.

Central to S.Tm pathogenesis resides a specialized virulence machinery including two needle-like type III secretion systems (T3SS-1/2) that mediate invasion and intracellular survival26,35 (Fig. 3j). To study how virulence factors influence the host response to luminal and intracellular S.Tm, we performed short, high-load infections (approximately 3 h, multiplicity of infection of approximately 1:60, −mucus) using wild-type (WT) and mutant strains. Subsequent gentamicin treatment removed the luminal stimulus while maintaining intracellular S.Tm populations for several days (Extended Data Fig. 8a).

We observed that flagellum-driven motility (ΔfliC–ΔfljB (ΔFg)) contributed more to invasion than SiiE-dependent adhesion (ΔsiiF; Extended Data Fig. 8b). Consistent with our previous results (Extended Data Fig. 7a–c), internalized S.Tm predominantly localized basolaterally beneath the nucleus, presumably within Salmonella-containing vacuoles (SCV)35 (Extended Data Fig. 8c). Intracellular replication led to either cell extrusion events with luminal release or rupture of SCV-like structures that released S.Tm basally (Extended Data Fig. 8d and Supplementary Videos 2 and 3). The levels of IL-18 increased over 96 hpi and was a hallmark with WT but not avirulent ΔinvG–ΔssaV (ΔSPI-1/2) S.Tm, distinguishing this invasion signature from the broader luminal cytokine response (Fig. 3k and Extended Data Fig. 8e,f). In addition, the system demonstrated virulence sensitivity, as S.Tm SL1344 (ref. 36) elicited an exacerbated invasion-driven response marked by increased internalization, cell shedding and IL-18 secretion compared with S.Tm 14028 (Extended Data Fig. 8g).

Industry observers note that to resolve host transcriptional responses induced by luminal or intracellular S.Tm, we performed scRNA-seq on GFP+ (invaded (In)) and GFP− (non-invaded (Out)) cells infected with WTGFP, ΔSPI-1/2GFP, ΔssaVGFP (ΔSPI-2) or ΔsteEGFP strains at 24 hpi (Fig. 3j,l and Extended Data Fig. 8h,i). Invasion occurred across all cell types but was lowest in stem cells, probably given their crypt-base localization (Extended Data Fig. 8j). The luminal response of non-invaded (GFP−) colonocytes was comparable between WT and ΔSPI-1/2, involving hypoxia, barrier and cytokine genes (Fig. 3m). A low-abundant colonocyte state appeared independent of invasion and was marked by IFN signalling (MX1 and ISG15), probably reflecting extracellular bacterial recognition37 (Fig. 3m, ‘depleted non-infected’, Extended Data Fig. 8i and Supplementary Table 4). The intracellular response of invaded (GFP+) colonocytes, which matched the colonocyte subtype 2 state from the multiomic analysis, triggered a profound shift (approximately 4,000 DEGs) characterized by pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory, bacterial recognition, cytoskeleton and oxidative stress genes with variable patterns along differentiation (Fig. 3m, Extended Data Fig. 8k,l and Supplementary Table 2). Although effector contributions may differ functionally, the attenuated gene signature observed in ΔSPI-2, and especially in ΔsteE-invaded cells, positions SteE as a key driver of the intracellular transcriptional landscape (‘enriched in GFP+’; Fig. 3m and Extended Data Fig. 8i,l,m).

Among transcription factors, STAT3 (STAT3, SOCS3 and pSTAT3) was attenuated in ΔSPI-2 and absent in ΔsteE-invaded cells, confirming its SteE-mediated activation31 (Fig. 3m and Extended Data Fig. 8l,n). Invasion by WT and mutants elicited coordinated upregulation of the antagonistic BACH1–NRF2 transcription factor pair33 that coincided with reduced expression of iron homeostasis regulators (GPX4, FTH1, HMOX1 and FTL), suggesting predominant BACH1 activity34 (Fig. 3m and Extended Data Fig. 8l,o). SLC7A11 was a notable exception to this repression, possibly through non-canonical BACH1 activation34, STAT3 regulation38 or an alternative mechanism. Although the exact BACH1–NRF2 interplay and roles remain to be fully elucidated, these transcription factors appeared functionally coupled to intracellular S.Tm, as observed upon small-molecule inhibitor treatments (Extended Data Fig. 8p).

It has been revealed that finally, we classified S.TmWT-invaded cells by bacterial burden using imaging flow cytometry, identifying single-colony to high-load groups at 24 hpi (Extended Data Fig. 8q). To link intracellular replication levels to host response, we performed single-cell total RNA sequencing (VASA-seq) on index-sorted cells from GFPlo, GFPint and GFPhi levels (Extended Data Fig. 8r). GFPhi cells, with up to 35 colony-forming units (CFU) per cell, most strongly correlated with our previously defined intracellular gene module, linking the host response to S.Tm activity and replication rather than invasion alone (Extended Data Fig. 8s,t). Uniquely, VASA-seq recovered not only non-protein coding host transcripts but also bacterial genes involved in metabolism (mgtB, gltA and feoB) and SPI-2 machinery, highlighting the intracellular adaptation of the pathogen (Extended Data Fig. 8u,v and Supplementary Table 3). Collectively, these data provide a high-resolution, multi-modal atlas that uncovers how virulence factors and intracellular burden shape the invaded epithelial response.

Sources indicate that our transcriptomic analysis identified epithelial signals triggered by S.Tm infection and confirmed the epithelium as a sensor of pathogen presence. Elucidating the functional impact of these signals requires the presence of their target populations. Given that S.Tm infection was associated with induction of lymphocyte-targeting cytokines (IL-18 and TNF) and chemokines (CXCL10 and CCL20), we focused on T cells as putative responders and introduced them into the intestinal engineered tissues. In the human intestine, TRM cells reside within the mucosa to safeguard barrier integrity39. We have previously revealed that TRM cells integrate into ISC-derived organoids and respond to synthetic T cell receptor (TCR) engagement40. Building on this approach, we established immunosurveilled barriers by incorporating autologous tissue-resident immune cells into the ECM scaffold of our engineered tissues (Fig. 4a–c and Extended Data Fig. 9a–c). These cells were isolated primarily from the small intestine due to higher proximal mucosal immune cell density5. We first assessed immune cell interactions with the epithelium, in the absence of a pathogenic threat. As expected from their tissue-resident phenotype facilitating epithelial interaction (Extended Data Fig. 9d–h), intraepithelial lymphocytes infiltrated the epithelium at physiological rates and patrolling speeds comparable with the organ of origin41 without compromising barrier integrity (Fig. 4d–i, Extended Data Fig. 9i,j and Supplementary Videos 4–6). By contrast, blood-derived T cells barely integrated into the epithelium (Fig. 4f).

To resolve the cellular diversity and epithelium–immune crosstalk, we performed scRNA-seq after 1 week of co-culture. The immune compartment exhibited striking heterogeneity, comprising CD8 T (CD8 TRM) cells, CD4 T helper (CD4 TRM) cells, regulatory T cells, T helper 17 (TH17 TRM) cells, γδ T cells, natural killer cells, innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) and memory B cells (Fig. 4j), demonstrating maintenance of immune lineage fidelity (Extended Data Fig. 9k). TRM populations constituted the majority of the immune cell pool, remaining non-proliferative, consistent with their long-lived quiescent state in vivo42 (Fig. 4j and Extended Data Fig. 9d–g,k). Given their dominant representation, we refer to the entire immune compartment as ‘TRM cells’ henceforth. Although overall epithelial cell-type composition was unaffected (Fig. 4k and Extended Data Fig. 9l,m), immune cell presence induced epithelial antigen processing and presentation programs, marked by upregulation of MHC class I (MHC-I) components (HLA-B and B2M) and the MHC-II chaperone CD74 (Fig. 4l, Extended Data Fig. 9n–p and Supplementary Table 4). Transcription factor expression analysis in the enterocyte cluster linked gene expression changes to STAT1, IRF1 and IRF9, canonical hallmarks of IFNγ signalling (Fig. 4l), suggesting that immune-derived IFNγ facilitates this baseline immune priming43 (Fig. 4m). We confirmed IFNγ within culture supernatants at the protein level (Extended Data Fig. 9q).

Industry observers note that next, we found that engineered tissues recapitulate key epithelial–immune interactions, including IFNGR1/2–IFNG, IL15RA–IL15 (ref. 44) and TNFRSF14–CD160 (ref. 45) (Fig. 4m and Supplementary Table 7). Furthermore, introduction of resident immune cells drove upregulation of the butyrophilin-like (BTNL) molecules BTNL3 and BTNL8 within the epithelium, probably in a HNF4G-dependent manner46 (Fig. 4l). These epithelial BTNL molecules signal back to the immune compartment, facilitating maturation of Vγ4+ γδ T cells and establishing a protective mucosal circuit, whose disruption is linked to intestinal pathology47.

Together, these data suggest that engineered intestinal tissues preserve physiological immune cell behaviours and foster in vivo-like epithelial–immune interactions.

Having incorporated TRM cells into the engineered tissues, we next asked how they interpret epithelial-derived signals to orchestrate mucosal defence upon S.Tm infection. We challenged immunocompetent barriers with high-load S.Tm for 3 h following gentamicin treatment (Fig. 5a). Histological analysis confirmed bacteria within close proximity of intraepithelial lymphocytes (Fig. 5b). The presence of resident immune cells accelerated mucosal damage compared with epithelium-only controls, leading to increased epithelial shedding and loss of barrier integrity (Fig. 5c and Extended Data Fig. 10a–c). Attributing elevated epithelial damage to TRM cell activation, we analysed the basal compartment for inflammatory mediators observed in patients with gastroenteric Salmonella infection48,49. We identified two temporally distinct regimes of immune and epithelial responses. A rapid (10 hpi) first wave of IL-2 and IFNγ secretion, indicating a canonical CD4+ TH1 response, occurred concurrently with epithelial secretion of IL-18 (Fig. 5d). This initial response was followed by release of cytotoxic and antimicrobial effectors, including GzmB, IL-6 and TH17-associated cytokines (IL17A and IL-22). TNF, IL-13 and IL-1β were modestly induced (Fig. 5d and Extended Data Fig. 10d,e). Although facilitating pathogen clearance (Extended Data Fig. 10f), this TH1–TH17-driven TRM cell response was associated with mucosal injury.

In a recent development, to determine whether TRM cell activation requires epithelial invasion or only luminal exposure to the pathogen, we leveraged the S.Tm mutants introduced previously (ΔFg, ΔSPI-2 and ΔSPI-1/2; Fig. 3). We found that the extent of mucosal injury and the magnitude of TRM cell response correlated with S.Tm invasive capacity and epithelial IL-18 secretion (Fig. 5e,f and Extended Data Fig. 10g). Furthermore, in line with the stronger epithelial response described earlier (Extended Data Fig. 8g), S.Tm SL1344 induced a more rapid and severe immunopathology than S.Tm 14028 (Extended Data Fig. 10h). Together, these data link TRM cell responses to pathogen virulence, invasive capacity and subsequent epithelial cytokine secretion. Although TRM cell responses are classically defined by antigen-specific TCRs, their capacity for innate-like bystander responses is a critical yet poorly understood feature of human mucosal immunity. We sought to understand whether S.Tm-mediated TRM cell activation is driven by secreted epithelial signals rather than direct TCR binding to epithelial MHC. Inhibition of PI3K and p38 MAPK, essential for innate-like IFNγ induction50, significantly quelled the response, whereas TCR-dependent LCK inhibition51 highlighted no effect (Fig. 5g). Likewise, surface TCR expression remained stable during S.Tm infection, contrasting the expected downregulation triggered by synthetic TCR engagement via an EpCAM–CD3 bispecific52 (Fig. 5h). Conditioned media from infected epithelium-only barriers were sufficient to activate TRM cells, whereas direct stimulation with bacterial pathogen-associated molecular patterns (LPS and flagellin) failed to trigger degranulation (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 10i). We note that this non-cognate response appeared to be a hallmark of tissue residency, as allogeneic and autologous blood-derived T cells remained unresponsive to infection, despite exhibiting substantial CD45RO+ populations (Extended Data Fig. 9d), high viability and IL-2 induction capacity (Fig. 5i and Extended Data Fig. 10j,k). Together, these results establish S.Tm-induced TRM cell activation in this system as a TCR-independent bystander response that requires inflammatory signals relayed by the epithelium. The induction of IL-18 upon S.Tm invasion closely coincided with the kinetics of the T cell response (Fig. 5d), implicating this cytokine as a key epithelial orchestrator of T cell activation. This was supported by high expression of IL-18Rα on CD4+ TRM cells, which conferred pronounced responsiveness to exogenous IL-18 and S.Tm infection (Fig. 5j and Extended Data Fig. 10l,m). To assess its role as an epithelial messenger, we generated IL18 knockouts in intestinal organoids using CRISPR–Cas9, resulting in ablation of IL-18 expression at baseline and upon challenge (Fig. 5k and Extended Data Fig. 10n). Indeed, IL-18 levels in WT S.Tm-infected mutant barriers were comparable with those of the avirulent ΔSPI-1/2 infection and non-infected control (Fig. 5l). When assessing the TRM cell response, IL-18 deficiency significantly dampened the inflammatory response (Fig. 5l,m), attenuating intracellular IFNγ levels in the cytotoxic IL-18Rα+CD4+ responder population (Extended Data Fig. 10o). Critically, the loss of IL-18 protected the barrier from pathological shedding and thinning (Fig. 5n and Extended Data Fig. 10p) despite functional T cell responder potential, linking IL-18-driven T cell activation to immunopathology.

Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the epithelium orchestrates antibacterial mucosal defence by secreting IL-18 to trigger non-cognate, innate-like responses of the TRM compartment.

Recent findings suggest that we have reported bioengineered, luminally accessible human intestinal tissues comprising epithelia with periodically repeating crypts that maintain LGR5+ stem cells, in vivo-like cell composition and patterning, and retain transcriptomic signatures across multiple donors. Identical medium and biophysical culture conditions yield region-specific signatures due to stem cell origin. Cell-type maturation and a reduction in total apical volume enable the formation of a region-specific mucus layer with mature glycocalyx. In addition, autologous TRM cells patrol the barrier and engage in bidirectional crosstalk with the epithelium, conferring an immune-responsive state within epithelial cells via IFNγ signalling.

The modularity of the system enabled fresh inquiry into S.Tm infection in a human context, contributing to collective efforts to refine physiologically relevant enteric infection models53. Basolateral S.Tm localization within polarized cells presumably facilitates dissemination into the lamina propria, a phenomenon that has been reported in vivo54,55. In addition, the phenotypic divergence observed between SL1344 and 14028 strains could expand to clinical isolates and human-restricted pathogens (for example, Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhi, Shigella flexneri and Vibrio cholerae), including the study of host factors influencing bacterial gene expression and antibiotic susceptibility. We mapped the gene regulatory networks underlying luminal and intracellular S.Tm at single-cell resolution. The epithelium orchestrated inflammatory, metabolic and structural responses that accompany S.Tm colonization26 and demonstrate an innate-sensing capacity that coordinates multi-lineage immune recruitment in vivo. S.Tm invasion reshaped the host transcriptome through a SteE-dependent STAT3 gene regulatory hub that extends results in macrophages and immortalized lines29,31. The reduced SPI-2 contribution may stem from non-transcriptional effector roles or delayed activation resulting from the SPI-1-inducing pre-culture protocol56. In addition, changes in oxidative stress and iron homeostasis suggest a host–pathogen interplay associated with other intracellular infections57, warranting further study. Overall, these responses were highly influenced by the intracellular burden of the pathogen.

Industry observers note that advancing our previous work40 to an apically accessible immunocompetent system, we demonstrated that epithelial IL-18 upon S.Tm invasion is sufficient to drive TRM cell activation and cytokine release, reflecting clinical gastroenteric salmonellosis48,49. The system allowed us to elucidate the functional effects of this bystander T cell activation, aligning with previous reports of innate-like polyfunctional capabilities of TRM cells58,59,60. TRM cells intensified infection-mediated epithelial shedding, which probably contributes to pathogen clearance61 and is consistent with the rapid onset of diarrhoea during S.Tm infection. Although mouse studies have established the necessity of IL-18 for CD4+ T cell defence upon S.Tm infection62, it has been shown that enteric neurons, rather than the epithelium, serve as the critical source of IL-18 for intestinal protection63. We demonstrated that the human intestinal epithelium can potently activate TRM cells via IL-18 to drive defence responses, at least in an in vitro setting. Of note, S.Tm infection64 and IL-18 (ref. 65) have been linked to the onset of inflammatory bowel disease. Our data raise the possibility that this association may be underpinned by the appearance of a cytotoxic IL-18Rα+CD4+ T cell population58,62.

Although our platform provides a unique window into human intestinal in vitro modelling, several limitations remain. The engineered tissues lack villous structures, specialized Paneth or M cells, and myeloid immune lineages, crucial mediators of immunity against infection. The lack of fluid exchange might affect biophysical characteristics of a mucus layer accumulated by apical media reduction. Furthermore, S.Tm invasion rates probably exceed physiological levels due to mucus protection. Future studies may circumvent these limitations through bioengineering approaches9, mucus secretagogues, cytokine supplementation or the inclusion of additional commensal and immune lineages.

Sources indicate that beyond host–pathogen interaction, the engineered tissues and analytical framework expand what can be addressed ex vivo. The mature, patterned epithelium opens research directions in region-specific drugs and nutrient absorption, mucus biology and epithelial–TRM cell interactions implicated in inflammatory bowel disease pathogenesis. Overall, the platform brings the field closer to capturing complex, organ-level processes in a human setting that is controllable and tractable.

During the work on this project, a large number of microdevice prototype versions were fabricated using a range of microfabrication techniques, including cleanroom soft lithography, 3D printing, two-photon polymerization (2PP) lithography, computer numerical control (CNC) milling and plastic injection molding. The final chip is designed in a slide format (75 × 25 mm) containing three independent chips per slide. Each chip contained a central hydrogel chamber flanked by two side medium reservoirs and one top medium reservoir. The hydrogel precursor was injected through a loading port leading to the central gel chamber. A cylindrical stamp with a microtopography (for example, an array of biomimetic micropillars) on its base was placed onto a stamp-holding edge of the top reservoir before gel injection. After gel polymerization (see details in a separate section), the stamp was removed, leaving an inverse microtopography (for example, an array of microwells) on the hydrogel surface. The top and side reservoirs were then filled with PBS or cell culture medium. The top reservoir was used for cell seeding and subsequently served as the apical medium reservoir after epithelial coverage of the hydrogel and barrier formation. Medium from the side reservoirs passively diffused through the gel, supplying the epithelial tissue with nutrients from the basal side. Early prototypes were fabricated using conventional soft lithography and polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) molding workflows established at the Center of Micronanotechnology (EPFL). The 3D chip design was split into two photomasks that were sequentially aligned to enable the creation of pseudo-3D features and different heights for phase-guiding micro-pillars. Chip layouts were patterned onto chrome-coated fused silica substrates via laser lithography (VPG200, Heidelberg Instruments). Three layers of SU8 GM1075 (Gerlteltec) were sequentially spin coated onto dehydrated silicon wafers to achieve a total mold thickness of 750 μm. The first two 250-μm layers were soft baked, exposed to UV through the first photomask (MA6/BA6, Süss MicroTec) and post-baked. Then, the third SU8 layer was spin coated, soft baked and the second photomask was aligned to the existing pattern using dedicated alignment marks. After a final post-exposure bake and development with propylene glycol monomethyl ether acetate (PGMEA; Sigma), the molds were hard baked at 135 °C for 4 h and silanized overnight using vapour-phase trichloro(1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyl) silane (Sigma-Aldrich). PDMS (Sylgard 184, Dow Corning) was mixed at a 10:1 base-to-curing agent ratio, poured onto the molds, degassed under vacuum and cured at 80 °C for 24 h. PDMS replicas were cut, punched and plasma bonded to glass-bottom dishes. The strength of the soft lithography pipeline is in fabrication of high-resolution microfeatures and with relatively optimal throughput, as 10–20 chips can be produced from a single wafer. However, fabrication of the models taller than 500 μm is challenging and only step-like, pseudo-3D features from a single side of the PDMS layer can be fabricated. To overcome these limitations, we explored several other complementary fabrication strategies. Commercial 3D-printing techniques such as fused deposition modelling and stereolithography were used for the production of larger models (Formlabs Form 4). However, these methods lacked the resolution and surface finish required for high-quality PDMS molding and were suitable only for some early-stage proof-of-concept prototypes. Instead, here we used 2PP lithography using the UpNano NanoOne printer to fabricate detailed 3D features of the chip. In brief, 3D models of the microchip were created in Autodesk Fusion (latest version), exported as STL files and processed using UpNano Think3D software. The models were printed on glass coverslips using UpPhoto resin (UpNano). NanoOne stands out as the most developed printer for mesoscale manufacturing, enabling printing of large structures (10–20 mm in xy and up to 40 mm in height) due to several advanced technologies: a submerged printing mode in a large resin reservoir, high-power 1,000 W, 780-nm laser for fast printing with 5 × 0.25 numerical aperture (NA) objective and adaptive resolution technology that significantly reduces print times (up to 450 mm3 h−1). After printing, the coverslips were washed in isopropanol and silanized overnight using vapour-phase trichloro(1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyl) silane (Sigma-Aldrich). PDMS was cast, degassed, cured at 80 °C and then replicas were cut and plasma bonded to glass-bottom dishes. This method allowed us to fabricate high-quality prototypes for validation of the 3D microstructural design elements. However, the main limitation is the upscaling technology for fabrication of the large number of chips. More importantly, process flow is still resulting in the 3D topography features only from one side of the PDMS replica. To overcome the latter problem, commonly some laboratories fabricate multi-layered PDMS chips. In this approach, individual PDMS layers are fabricated separately, aligned and plasma bonded together. This direction was explored early on for fabrication of a few prototypes; however, the alignment process is tedious and unsuitable for large-scale chip manufacturing with the acceptable quality. To address this, inspired by industrial injection molding technology, we developed a cassette mold for PDMS curing. Molds were manufactured by CNC milling of acrylic, aluminum or steel, depending on the desired feature size and quality. Each cassette consisted of two mold parts bearing microtopographies of the bottom and top surfaces of the chip. When assembled, the parts fit precisely, enabling accurate alignment of both sides of the device. PDMS was injected into centre space of the mold, degassed in a vacuum chamber and cured in an 80 °C oven. After curing, the mold was opened and the PDMS sheets were cut and bonded to glass-bottom dishes. This process overcomes many of the limitations of previously described techniques and enables scalable production of hundreds of high-quality chips in a single batch. The main drawback is the need to adapt design features for CNC milling: some of the smallest features must be enlarged and sharp corners rounded. However, we did not consider this as a drawback as concurrently we began exploring industrial plastic molding technologies to eliminate the last remaining problem: the PDMS material itself. Although PDMS is ideal for prototyping, its high absorption of small molecules makes it unsuitable for translational applications and drug testing. Many of the learnings and design optimizations from the PDMS cassette-molding process were directly translated into the design of the final injection-molded plastic chip. Currently, the chip body is fabricated from cyclic olefin copolymer (COC) due to its low shrinkage, chemical resistance and optical transmission. The main body was fabricated as a single piece, followed by bonding of a 170-μm COC film to the bottom surface. A matching lid converting the slide was later designed and produced separately also via a COC injection molding process. After assembly, chips were packaged and sterilized using ethylene oxide gas. Large-scale chip production was outsourced to an external manufacturing facility.

In a recent development, stamps featuring crypt-mimicking microtopography were fabricated from PDMS via replica molding of 2PP-printed models. First, arrays of colon crypt-mimicking micropillars were designed in Autodesk Fusion (latest version). Several topographies were tested and optimized, the final microtopography design consisted of the slightly conical pillars, ranging from 70 to 120 μm in diameter (top to bottom) and 700 μm in height. The 3D model was printed using a NanoOne (UpNano) 2PP printer on glass coverslips with UpPhoto resin and a 10 × 0.4 NA objective. To generate a master mold with inverted topography, the printed structures were plasma activated and silanized overnight using vapour-phase trichloro(1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyl) silane (Sigma-Aldrich). PDMS (Sylgard 184, Dow Corning; 10:1 base-to-curing agent ratio) was poured over the master, degassed under vacuum and cured at 80 °C for 12 h. The resulting PDMS replica was cut, plasma activated and silanized overnight as above. This PDMS negative was then used repeatedly as a mold for casting final PDMS stamps using the same procedure (Sylgard 184, 10:1 ratio, cured at 80 °C for 12 h).

Recent findings suggest that to generate the ECM for the chip bovine TeloCol-6 type I collagen solution (5225-50 ml, Advanced Biomatrix) was neutralized following the manufacturer’s instructions and then mixed with Matrigel (356231, Corning) in 87.5:12.5 (v/v) ratio. A PDMS stamp with crypt-mimmicking array of pillar topography was placed in the central top reservoir. After the gel injection through the gel-loading port, the hydrogel was polymerized on a 37 °C hotplate for 10 min. After ECM polymerization, all chip reservoirs were topped up with PBS or cell culture medium. Prepared chips with hydrogels can be stored for multiple weeks at 37 °C at 5% CO2 (hereafter referred to as ‘incubator’) or in the +4 °C fridge before use. Hydrogel stiffness was measured using an MCR 702e MultiDrive oscillatory shear rheometer (Anton Paar) in a parallel plate configuration with a PP25/P3 measuring plate. The Young’s modulus (E) was estimated from the storage modulus (G′), assuming the hydrogel is elastic and nearly incompressible, using the relation E = 2 G(1 + ν) ≈ 3 G′, where Poisson’s ratio (ν) is approximately 0.5. Across multiple batches and replicates, the hydrogels yielded a Young’s modulus of 3,000 ± 500 Pa.

Industry observers note that in brief, intestinal tissue was processed by removal of the underlying muscularis, serosa and fat from the basal side of the intestinal tissue using forceps and scissors. The remaining mucosal tissue was thoroughly washed with DPBS (10010-015, Gibco), supplemented with penicillin–streptomycin (1,500 U ml−1; 15140122, Gibco), gentamicin (500 µg ml−1; 15750060, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and primocin (50 µg ml−1; ant-pm1, Invivogen) before using a glass coverslip to remove excess mucus from the luminal side and blood vessels from the basal side.

To circumvent the poor viability and phenotypic alterations associated with traditional enzymatic disassociations66,67, we adapted and optimized a scaffold-based egression method68 that we have previously shown maximizes tissue-resident immune cell recovery and maintains phenotypic integrity40. As previously reported40, our characterization via scRNA-seq and flow cytometry analysis indicated that the vast majority of the isolated cells are TRM cells. Therefore, we used the term TRM cells to describe the total immune cell fraction isolated from intestinal tissue. By flow cytometry, we characterized them as TRM cells based on the assessment of one or multiple of the following markers CD45RO+, CD69+, CD103+, CD45RA− and CCR7−.

Cleaned tissue was cut into square pieces (approximately 5 × 5 mm3) with a scalpel. Next, each fragment was loaded onto a 9 × 9 × 1.5 mm3 tantalum-coated, carbon-based scaffold (MSPP23281-1-REV-A, Ultramet) and cultured in 24-well plates (CC7682-7524, CytoOne) containing 2 ml of cytokine-free immune medium (Supplementary Table 1). Twenty-four hours later, scaffolds with tissue on were removed, and egressed cells were harvested from the bottom of the wells by thorough pipetting. Cells were then counted and biobanked in CryoStor (C2874, Sigma-Aldrich) before further use.

For isolation of donor-matched crypts for organoid establishment, an adjacent clean tissue piece (approximately 3 cm2) was used. Intestinal villi were removed from the tissue by using a glass coverslip. The tissue was then incubated on ice in DPBS + 10 mM EDTA (15575020, Thermo Fisher Scientific) on a shaker for 30 min. Next, a coverslip was used to scrape off the crypts of the tissue. Crypts were collected in organoid medium (Supplementary Table 1). Crypts were centrifuged and resuspended in GFR Matrigel (356231, Corning). After polymerization for 15 min at 37 °C, organoid medium was added with 10 µm Y-27632 (72305, Stemcell Technologies). Following organoid formation, organoids were passaged every 7 days (up to a maximum of 25 passages). After three passages, organoid mycoplasma tests (LT07-710, Lonza) were performed. All lines used in this study were verified as negative for mycoplasma. Organoid banking was performed using CELLBANKER 1 (11888, Nippon Zenyaku Kogyo). Passaging was performed as previously described52. In brief, organoid medium was removed and wells were washed with DPBS. Next, 500 µl of Gentle Cell Dissociation reagent (07174, Stemcell Technologies) was added and incubated for 2 min at room temperature before collecting the domes in a Falcon tube. After a further 15 min of incubation at room temperature, the suspension was centrifuged at 350g at 4 °C for 5 min. After removal of liquid, the pellet was harshly resuspended with organoid wash medium (Supplementary Table 1) to break the organoids. Broken organoids were centrifuged at 500g and the supernatant discarded before pellet resuspension in GFR Matrigel.

To generate LGR5, CDH1 and H2BC4 reporter lines, targeting vectors were designed as previously described69. Human intestinal organoids were incubated with 1.25% DMSO (v/v) and 10 µM Y-27632 (72305, Stemcell Technologies) 24 h before electroporation. Organoids (amounting to approximately 1 million cells per condition) were harvested, dissociated to clumps of 3–5 cells with TrypLE (12604-013, Gibco), washed twice with Optimem (31985070, Gibco) and then resuspended in High Performance Electroporation Solution (45-0805, BTXpress) containing up to 10 µg of targeting vector and 10 µg of Cas9 and guide RNA-expressing vector. Cells were electroporated using the NEPA21 Super Electroporator (Nepagene) with settings as previously described70. Y-27632 was kept for 48 h post-single-cell seeding in growth factor-reduced Matrigel (356231, Corning). Reporter-positive organoids were either picked manually or enriched via FACS.

To generate IL-18 gene knockouts, cells were transfected with 20 µg Cas9–GFP and guide RNA expression constructs at a 1:8 ratio and incubated overnight in culture medium containing 5% Matrigel. Transfected cells were FACS enriched and allowed to grow for 10–14 days. Up to eight clones were manually picked and genotyped by Sanger sequencing of the targeted locus.

S.Tm NCTC 12023 (identical to ATCC14028) and SL1344 WT and isogenic mutant strains were used as listed in Supplementary Table 1. If required for detection of Salmonella by GFP expression, plasmid pFPV25.1 was introduced by electroporation and maintained by selection with 50 µg ml−1 carbenicillin (Roth).

Sources indicate that mutant strains with deletion in invG or steE were generated by λ-Red recombination as previously described71 using pKD13 as template for amplification with Del13 primer sets (synthesized by IDT) listed in Supplementary Table 1, and pWRG730 for expression for λ-Red recombinase functions72. Proper insertion of the aph resistance cassette in target genes was confirmed by colony PCR using DelCheck for primers and K1 Red-Del. If required, the aph resistance cassette was removed by FLP recombination mediated by helper plasmid pE-FLP73. Resulting clones were checked for loss of kanamycin resistance and pE-FLP, and FLP-mediated deletion was confirmed by colony PCR using DelCheck For/Rev primer sets.

Recent findings suggest that strain MvP3487 was generated by P22 transduction of the ΔssaV::aph allele into MvP1764 according to standard procedures. Resulting mutant strains were checked for the absence of lysogens.

Industry observers note that for seeding of the chips—hereafter referred to as ‘engineered intestines’ once intestinal epithelial cells are included—approximately 4-day-old human intestinal organoids from different regions of the gastrointestinal tract (duodenum, jejunum, ileum and colon) between passages 5 and 25 were collected in base medium (Supplementary Table 1) and transferred to a 15-ml Falcon tube. Following centrifugation at 300g at 4 °C for 4 min, the base medium was aspirated and the pellet was thoroughly resuspended in base medium. After repeating the centrifugation step, organoids were singularized with TrypLE express solution (12604-013, Gibco) containing 250 U ml−1 DNase I (4536282001, Roche) and 10 µm Y-27632 (72305, Stemcell Technologies) for 8 min at 37 °C before harsh resuspension. This step was performed twice before swiftly blocking the dissociation by adding base medium with 10% FBS. Next, cells were passed through a 40-µm strainer (43-50040-51, PluriSelect) before centrifugation at 500g at 4 °C for 4 min. Afterwards, the cells were resuspended in chip medium (Supplementary Table 1) containing 10 µm Y-27632. Approximately 1.5 × 105 cells were seeded in a volume of 3 µl onto each micropatterned hydrogel. Approximately 150 µl chip medium with 10 µm Y-27632 was immediately added to each side reservoir of the engineered intestines, whereas the mid-chamber remained empty to allow the cells to attach to the ECM. After 30 min in the incubator, 100 µl chip medium (+10 µm Y-27632 + 5% FBS) was carefully added to the mid-chamber to avoid cell detachment. Culture medium was exchanged every second day. Approximately 5% of FBS supplementation was removed after the second day (details in Supplementary Table 1).

On the day of hydrogel seeding, TRM cells or peripheral blood mononuclear cells were thawed following our previously described protocol52. T cells were isolated from peripheral blood mononuclear cells using the EasySep Human T Cell Isolation kit (17951, Stemcell Technologies) and EasySep Magnet (18000, Stemcell Technologies) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Viability and number of immune cells were assessed with Trypan Blue (216040, Invitrogen) on a Countess II (Invitrogen). If the viability of the thawed TRM cells crawl-out was less than 75% (due to remaining tissue debris), Dead Cell Removal Kit (130-090-101, Miltenyi Biotec) was applied with MS columns (130-042-201, Miltenyi Biotec) on the OctoMACS separator (130-042-109, Miltenyi Biotec) following the manufacturer’s instructions (typically improved to more than 85% viability). Afterwards, immune cells were placed in the incubator until further processing. Chips were prepared as described above until hydrogel loading. Then, approximately 1 × 105 immune cells were mixed with 6 µl of ECM per chip. Next, 26 µl of ECM was dispensed through the loading port per chip into the mid-reservoir. Immediately after, 6 µl of the ECM-immune suspension was carefully dispensed onto a flipped PDMS stamp, with the micropattern facing upwards, and transferred using forceps onto the previously dispensed ECM in the mid-reservoir of the engineered intestine. Next, immune-hydrogel suspensions were polymerized at 37 °C for 15 min. After polymerization of the ECM, the immune chip slide was topped up with immune chip medium (Supplementary Table 1) to ease microstamp removal. After organoid dissociation and epithelial cell seeding as described above, 150 µl immune chip medium containing 500 pg ml−1 IL-15 (570306, BioLegend) and 10 µm Y-27632 was immediately added to each side reservoir of the engineered intestine, whereas the mid-chamber remained empty to allow for cells to attach to the ECM of the engineered intestine. After 30 min in the incubator, 100 µl immune chip medium (+500 pg ml−1 IL-15 + 10 µm Y-27632) was carefully added to the mid-chamber. Immune chip medium (+500 pg ml−1 IL-15) was exchanged every second day.

To assess the effects of bacterial components on TRM cells in suspension, LPS (100 ng ml−1; L3024-5MG, Sigma-Aldrich) and flagellin (50 ng ml−1; tlrl-epstfla-5, InvivoGen) were supplemented in immune medium and cultured for 48 h. Similarly, IL-15 (500 pg ml−1) and IL-18 (10 ng ml−1; 592106, BioLegend) were added in immune medium for TRM cell suspension cultures, either individually or in combination, for 48 h. For the assessment of T cell activation in response to the epithelial secretome, conditioned medium was harvested from the basal reservoirs of epithelium-only chips 48 hpi with S.Tm. This medium was collected, transferred to plates and maintained at −80 °C until the day of the experiment. Upon thawing, condition medium was mixed 1:1 (v/v) with fresh immune medium supplemented with 1,000 pg ml−1 of IL-15, resulting in a final concentration of 500 pg ml−1 of IL-15. TRM cells were subsequently cultured in this mixture for 48 h in suspension. Following these culture periods, cells were subjected to analysis by flow cytometry.

Recent findings suggest that for baseline phenotyping, immune cells were recovered from intestinal resections, filtered through a 40-µm strainer and processed directly. For assessment of luminal content, cells were recovered from the accessible luminal reservoir of the chips. For chip-harvested samples and suspension-cultured TRM cells intended for intracellular cytokine assessment, samples were treated with a protein transport inhibitor cocktail (00-4975-93, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 4 h before harvest.
