After further excluding ERCC transcripts and features with Ensembl-style identifiers beginning with ENSB, 3,137 genes were left as input for the differentially expressed test. We used nominal P < 0.05 as the cut-off to get marginally significant bacterial DEG.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Industry observers note that a-c) Representative mIF cross-section of engineered duodenal, ileal and colonic epithelia in direct comparison to the donor-matched primary tissue (ileum not matched), highlighting the stem-niche specific SOX9+ (cyan) and transit-amplifying Ki67+ cells (pink), matching abundance of MUC2+ goblet cells (green) and high expression of the region-enriched absorptive lineage marker (orange) in the E-Cadherin+ epithelium (grey). Nelson Dida believes that Ruben Amorim is showing he is a ‘great’ coach, and he gave his take on the Endrick to AC Milan rumours.

If anyone knows about the pressure of playing for Milan, it is Dida. Having been at the club from 2000 to 2010, he made over 300 official appearances for the Rossoneri and was part of an era that brought in eight major trophies under Carlo Ancelotti.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

He is widely regarded as one of the finest goalkeepers of his generation and was decisive in the 2003 Champions League final penalty shootout against Juventus. He also returned briefly as a goalkeeping coach, working for a year with Maignan.

Dida spoke to reporters who were present at the Galbiati Trophy and he answered a few questions regarding his former team, with his words relayed by MilanNews.

How do you think Amorim is doing?

In a recent development, “Amorim is proving to be a great coach. He took over Milan and is having a fantastic season. I think the attention is right because at Milan you can never make mistakes, but he has the ability to keep the team together to do well in the league.”.

If Maignan is hurt, would you come back and put the gloves on?

In a recent development, “We already have a goalkeeper at AC Milan: Lorenzo Torriani, a guy who’s doing well. I like him. Last year, too, he did well when he had opportunities. I think he’s a focused guy, if he gets more opportunities, he can continue to grow.”.

Are Milan growing towards something?

According to recent reports, “Milan are slowly growing. They’re doing well in the league, I think we can still do more, while in Europe we’re still missing something.”.

Would Endrick be a good signing?

“Endrick is a great player for me. When I see him play, he looks a bit like Romario, who is a bit small, but when he’s in the penalty area, he’s decisive. When he’s had the opportunity to play, he’s also scored goals.

Sources indicate that “I think he can really do well for Real Madrid and the national team, but I don’t know if he’s available to join Milan. I hope a Brazilian returns to play in the Italian league soon and wears the Milan shirt.”.

Breaking: Gary Neville debuts surprise defence of Diogo Dalot and names the THREE defenders Mauricio Pochettino should sell before Man United boo boy

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 10:42 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 12:38 EST, 17 November 2026.
  • Gary Neville has stood up for under-fire Manchester United man Diogo Dalot – and named three of his defensive team-mates he would rather see leave the club before him.
  • The Portugal international's limp performances have come under heavy scrutiny this season with the decline of Michael Carrick's side as autumn has worn on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By TAMARA PRENN, SENIOR SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 10:42 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 12:38 EST, 17 November 2026.

Gary Neville has stood up for under-fire Manchester United man Diogo Dalot – and named three of his defensive team-mates he would rather see leave the club before him.

The Portugal international's limp performances have come under heavy scrutiny this season with the decline of Michael Carrick's side as autumn has worn on.

But as Mauricio Pochettino prepares to take over at Old Trafford, Neville urged the latest manager not to immediately expel the defender, despite his drop-off in form.

According to recent reports, 'I think if he was in a decent back four he'd be alright,' Neville told Stick to United co-host Mark Goldbridge on Tuesday. 'But he's got a shocking back four alongside him.

'Positionally he's not great. He could be better on the ball. He could be better at everything he does. Of course he could. I just think he's such an easy target, Dalot. I honestly do.'.

Neville admitted that sometimes he listens to his fellow Man United-supporting friends deriding Dalot and wonders 'are they watching something that I don't see?'.

Gary Neville has defended Man United star Diogo Dalot - arguing that he has team-mates who are far weaker.

The Portugal international has come in for heavy criticism from supporters this season.

But in his opinion, there are three defenders that he would let go in the 'first wave' of changes in Manchester.

'I'd be getting (Noussair) Mazraoui well gone before him,' he continued. 'I'd be getting (Lisandro) Martinez gone well before him. I'll be getting (Matthijs) De Ligt gone well before him.

In a recent development, '(De Ligt has) got one big problem. He doesn’t play football. If a player is injury prone and doesn't play football, just because he hasn't played doesn't mean to say that he should go above a player who's played every single week and he's throwing his hand up. You want someone who's actually reliable and play. De Ligt has to go. De Ligt, Martinez, Mazraoui.'.

Another stalwart in the team that Neville was keen to have a second chance under Pochettino was Luke Shaw.

Sources indicate that 'He will keep Shaw because he knows him and he'll probably get the best out of him. The problem with Luke is injuries,' he added. 'So he'll have to manage him. So he'll have to bring a left back in. But let's just say who he'll keep.

'He'll keep Shaw. He'll keep (Harry) Maguire because he'll trust him and he'll think that he's basically a soldier and someone who can do a job for him.

'He'll keep (Leny) Yoro because I think he'll think "I've got something there that I can work with". (But) I think he's a little bit gangly, all over the place right now. And he looks like he's going to slip every time. He's got that sort of Bambi-on-ice (look).

In a recent development, 'Physically what will happen is with Yoro, he'll go one way or the other. I like the fact he's been brought into the French team. It tells me sometimes you just have got to connect the dots and think, "okay, well, if they think he's good, then we must be missing something here because we're not seeing it yet, are we?".'.

Neville went on to suggest that Yoro was lacking the connection within his body that Premier League rivals such as Jeremy Jacquet are already able to harness – something Sir Alex Ferguson had identified in Rio Ferdinand when he was at West Ham.

Like Ferdinand, Neville backed Yoro to flourish as he taps into that connection and improves his strength and stability.

According to recent reports, 'So Yoro he will keep: Yoro, Maguire and Shaw I think he'll keep and I think he'll keep Dalot. To start with,' Neville stated. 'He'll have to bring in three defenders to go above them. Let's be clear. He'll have to bring in three defenders.

'Mazraoui I would lose, De Ligt I would lose because he's injury prone. Martinez 100 per cent. 100 per cent. 100 per cent.'.

As well as struggling for form this season, Martinez has been a challenging presence in the Man United squad this term, boldly calling out the Man United hierarchy during a firebrand interview last month.

Neville was more interested in newly introduced head coach Mauricio Pochettino despatching Noussair Mazraoui and Matthijs de Ligt.

Lisandro Martinez has been an unsettled presence in the side this season and hit out at the club's recruiting last month.

The Argentina star implied that he was disappointed with the club's recruitment strategy over the summer, and was forced to hold clear-the-air talks to smooth his return to the side.

Neville added that he would send Ayden Heaven on loan to get experience in the lower divisions to 'build' his ability up, as it was borderline 'unfair' to be 'putting him in' the side at present.

But not all of the changes can come quickly for Pochettino, who has little time before taking charge of Man United against Liverpool at Anfield this weekend.

'First wave, end of the season,' Neville clarified of what he believes Pochettino's plan for change will be. 'No, he can't get rid of (them all) in January.

'He has to bring one or two defenders in January if he can. But he can't get rid of all those in his first wave. He's only got one month till January.'.

The drawn-out process of sacking Carrick began last week when Jason Wilcox and Omar Berrada flew to Monaco for talks with co-owners Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazer ownership group.

While his future was on the chopping block, Carrick held training sessions at Carrington before the axe finally swung last Thursday.

Pochettino was appointed days later and gave a tearful farewell press conference ahead of his penultimate game with the United States national team on Saturday.

Recent findings suggest that ‘I haven't prepared a speech, I'm talking with my heart,’ he told the press. ‘It's difficult for me to talk now because I am a very emotional guy.

‘When these moments arrive, it is always tough. Normally it is the opposite – you have been sacked! You cry because you want to stay. I think it was one of the most difficult decisions of our career, but you have to move forward.

‘Not too many opportunities can happen in your career with a side like Manchester United. That is difficult to turn down when it arrives.

‘In some part it’s a very sad decision, in another part we are professional and we are trying to make our dreams come true. We are excited for that step forward.'.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Matt Law | 19 Nov 2026 19:38, Last updated: 19 Nov 2026 19:39.

Mauricio Pochettino has explained the importance of 'creating the culture' at Manchester United, as the Argentine looks to build a positive environment following his arrival as head coach.

The 54-year-old will take charge of his first Man United match on Sunday afternoon, when the 20-time English champions tackle Liverpool at Anfield.

Pochettino officially started work as Red Devils head coach on Wednesday, having flown straight to England after managing his final USA game against Haiti.

The South American has taken charge of a team that right now sit down in 18th spot in the Premier League table, picking up just eight points from their first 10 games of the season.

“It's a mistake to see the [current] situation. We need to see the potential of this club. Of course, the circumstances are the circumstances, and we need to be responsible for the circumstances. But at the same time, we need to understand that it's a game and, to connect with the game, we need to feel free," Pochettino told Man United's official website.

“The players need to express their talent. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is the most important thing and that is our priority now – it’s to work with them and try to take the pressure.

In a recent development, “Pressure needs to bring energy, responsibility needs to bring energy. Because if not, it's too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back.

"When you connect with the game, you connect through your talent and when you feel freedom, when you feel happy, when you want to play for your teammates, when you want to play for your family, when you want to play for your club, your fans.

Sources indicate that “That is what we need to create all together and I think we have an amazing staff - we were talking a lot today. Then [we need to] settle all the principles and the ideas and to create our own philosophy and start from zero. I think with the power of this club and the fans supporting us, I think we will get in the place that we deserve to be.

Industry observers note that “To create the culture is the most crucial [thing]. Create the habits, the principles, and I think that is what we want to create. We need to [be] looking forward and to find a way to create the best habits and the culture that makes us close to winning every single game.

“The best squad that we can have are the players that we have and we need to love the players that we have. We need to support the players.

Sources indicate that "We need to provide all the tools for them to perform. It's only an act of responsibility now to start to work and provide them the facility to translate all their talent on the field.”.

Pochettino's training session on Thursday included both Harry Maguire and Patrick Dorgu, with the defensive duo both in line to be available against Liverpool.

The Red Devils are expected to bring a centre-back to Old Trafford in the January transfer window due to their problems in that area of the field.

Man United are planning to overhaul their defensive unit next summer, as Lisandro Martinez, Harry Maguire and Luke Shaw are all out of contract, while there is speculation surrounding the futures of Matthijs de Ligt, Noussair Mazraoui and Diogo Dalot.

However, due to the team's severe defensive problems this term, it is likely that a upcoming centre-back will be targeted when the winter window opens for business.

Man United have conceded 19 times in their 10 Premier League matches this season, which is the joint-third worst record in the division.

The Red Devils have actually not kept a single clean sheet in the Premier League this term, while they have also conceded eight times in their four Champions League matches.

Bassey has allegedly been identified by Man United as a leading target, with the 26-year-old's contract due to expire at the end of the campaign.

Fulham do have the option to activate another year on the Nigeria international's deal, but the club are looking to sign him to a long-term contract.

According to The Athletic, Fulham are currently pushing to extend his deal, with the London team having no intention of letting him leave in the winter market.

Bassey has captained Fulham this season, making 12 appearances in 2026-27, while he has represented the club on 113 occasions in all competitions.

The defender has also played for Rangers and Ajax during his professional career.

Bassey gained Champions League experience during his time at Ajax, while he has now played 104 times in the Premier League for Fulham, scoring three goals and registering one assist.

Fresh Man United head coach Mauricio Pochettino is expected to be backed with funds during the January transfer window.

Latest Update: The curious case of Sebastien Pocognoli looks certain to have a grisly ending... the SFA have hired a dud

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.
  • Published: 14:13 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 14:26 EST, 17 November 2026.
  • Of all the many stories written by F Scott Fitzgerald, one of the finest authors and wordsmiths of his time, The Great Gatsby will forever remain his masterpiece.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 14:13 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 14:26 EST, 17 November 2026.

Of all the many stories written by F Scott Fitzgerald, one of the finest authors and wordsmiths of his time, The Great Gatsby will forever remain his masterpiece.

In some of his other work written as he travelled across Europe, Fitzgerald also had a line about Switzerland, describing it as a ‘country where very few things begin, but many things end.’.

It is a curious quote and, like much of Fitzgerald’s work, is open to interpretation. As the man who also wrote The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, curiosity was a common theme.

As for the Curious Case of Sebastien Pocognoli, Switzerland may, indeed, be the country where everything came to an end.

It has been revealed that what unfolded in St Gallen on Monday evening was a horror show. Scotland were battered 4-0 by Switzerland’s B team. There is no way to sugar-coat a result like that, no way to dress it up as anything other than an embarrassment. They played OK for half an hour and then fell apart.

Pocognoli claimed afterwards that there were positives to be taken and how some of Scotland’s football was the best they have produced across his six matches in charge.

Sebastien Pocognoli is facing serious questions after a miserable Nations League campaign.

Utter nonsense. That was a manager clutching at straws at the end of a Nations League campaign which has been an unmitigated disaster pretty much from start to finish.

Let’s go back to the very start here. After Steve Clarke had pushed the Scottish Football Association (SFA) into awarding him a fresh four-year contract, only to then walk away after the World Cup, it was a chance for a fresh start.

On the day when Pocognoli was unveiled as the newly introduced head coach in August, Ian Maxwell and Craig Mulholland, the SFA’s chief executive and chief football officer, were beaming with positivity.

They told us all how data and AI had been used in the recruitment process, and how several clubs across Europe had been chasing Pocognoli.

They clearly viewed it as a coup to have landed the 39-year-old Belgian, who had won a league title in his homeland with Union Saint-Gilloise before a short stint with Monaco.

What would the data say now? Six games played, two wins, a draw and three defeats, five goals scored and ten conceded, seven points and a lousy third-placed finish in Group B1.

Both of those wins came against a North Macedonian side who lost all six of their games. They were a pub team – and Scotland still struggled to beat them at Hampden last Friday night.

Pocognoli was unable to inspire any resistance as his side succumbed to defeat in St Gallen.

Industry observers note that scotland lost 7-0 on aggregate to Switzerland over the two games. Against Slovenia, a 0-0 draw on the opening day in Ljubljana was then followed with a woeful 2-1 defeat at Hampden.

All of which begs a very simple question. Where, exactly, are the grounds for optimism here? How is this getting any better?

When Pocognoli arrived, he spoke about trying to change the style of play, get Scotland playing a more exciting brand of football, whilst bringing through a upcoming generation of players.

Sources indicate that it was not a rebuild. He inherited a group of players who were accustomed to success under Clarke and who qualified for three tournaments out of a possible four.

His remit was to help Scotland take the next step in major tournaments. With a more dynamic style of play, the job was to help the nation take the next step.

There has been no revolution thus far. No evidence whatsoever that this coach is capable of delivering results nor a better style of play.

According to recent reports, there is no satisfaction to be taken in any of this. When Pocognoli was appointed, it was, in the eyes of this observer, an interesting and progressive move.

SFA chiefs Craig Mulholland and Ian Maxwell proudly unveil upcoming boss Pocognoli at Hampden.

Over the past 48 hours or so, there has been a lot of revisionism from some folk about Clarke. ‘Aye, the grass isn’t always greener...’.

That’s garbage. Clarke’s time was up with Scotland. He should never have been handed a fresh four-year deal in the first place. At least he did the right thing in resigning after the World Cup.

It has been revealed that the whole thing was finished. The problem is that the SFA look like they have appointed a total dud as his successor. Both of those things can be true at the same time.

It is also worth remembering that the only reason we arrived at Pocognoli is because Clarke walked away. The SFA did not instigate any change.

The hiring of a fresh head coach was not a proactive change of direction, but a reactive move from an executive body who became accepting of Clarke’s limitations and allowed him to position them over a barrel.

In a recent development, listen, there is nothing inherently wrong with using data and metrics in football. It’s the modern way. Using data to inform decisions and recruitment processes is smart business.

Industry observers note that but the data in itself is no guarantee of success. There are some intangibles in football, things which are harder to quantify. Like a manager who blindly sticks to a system which is patently ill-suited to the players at his disposal.

Recent findings suggest that things like leadership and communication skills. We can cut Pocognoli some slack in that English is not his first language. He comes across as a thoroughly decent and likeable chap. He’s doing his best. He wants to embrace the culture and makes an effort to sing the National Anthem.

Scotland's defeat arose from individual mistakes, a common theme during the Belgian's reign.

Industry observers note that all of that is undoubtedly to be welcomed. Good on him. But would anyone describe him as an inspirational figure?

When you listen to him speak, have you ever felt slightly confused in terms of the message he’s actually trying to get across?

Sources indicate that how must that sound in the dressing room? When Andy Robertson spoke post-match on Monday night, there was frustration in his voice.

The captain insisted there is simply no time or patience with these things. Scotland need to deliver results now.

To be fair, there actually would be a degree of patience shown by the Tartan Army towards Pocognoli if there was something to actually believe in.

There was a lot of goodwill towards him at the start. If there were signs across these last six games that he could deliver a more exciting team to watch, they would show patience.

Industry observers note that but on the basis of what we’ve seen so far, there’s been absolutely nothing to suggest he can move this team forward. Ask yourself a very simple question – do Scotland pass the eye test?

Are we seeing a team who are playing on the front foot and creating chances? The answer, obviously, is no.

Recent findings suggest that steve Clarke celebrates Scotland's win over Denmark a year ago... how fans miss such highs.

Many Scotland fans are now confronting the possibility that we might not even qualify for Euro 2028, a tournament which we are co-hosting.

By finishing third in the Nations League, we will now be in pot three for the Euro qualifiers and will face a more difficult group.

Beyond that, we would be relying on the back-door method of one of the best-placed home nations not to qualify directly.

Industry observers note that those Euro qualifiers will start in March of next year. Does Pocognoli even make it that far? Or should the SFA hold their hands up, admit they’ve made a mistake, and rectify it?

That feels unlikely. But on the basis of what we have seen over these first six games, it’s hard to see how this gets any better.

In a recent development, we are worse now than we were at the end under Clarke. Much, much worse. This is not teething problems. It’s a team who have regressed massively under a head coach who was supposed to move the whole thing forward.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Naim Beneddra | 19 Nov 2026 20:47.

Manchester City could lose an experienced midfielder on a free transfer at the end of the season, with fresh reports suggesting that the player has already identified the European leagues in which he would prefer to continue his career.

Mateo Kovacic is expected to leave the Etihad Stadium when his contract expires in June 2027, according to transfer journalist Matteo Moretto, who has also provided an patch on the Croatia international's preferred destinations.

Speaking to Marca, Moretto claimed that the 32-year-old would welcome a return to Spain or Italy, where he previously represented Real Madrid and Inter Milan respectively.

"He will leave City at the end of the season," Moretto noted, before explaining that Kovacic "would like to return to Spain or Italy", although his salary expectations could influence his options.

The update comes as Kovacic struggles to secure regular playing time under Enzo Maresca, having fallen down the midfield pecking order since the Italian replaced Pep Guardiola.

While City have not officially revealed his departure, the midfielder is approaching the final seven months of his contract without a reported agreement over an extension.

Kovacic joined Manchester City from Chelsea in June 2023, signing a four-year contract in a deal worth an initial £25m, with a further £5m potentially payable in add-ons.

The Croatia international was recruited to provide experience, technical quality and composure in midfield, having previously enjoyed considerable success with both Real Madrid and Chelsea.

However, injuries have increasingly disrupted his time in Manchester.

The midfielder was restricted to just nine appearances during the 2025-26 campaign after undergoing surgery to address a troublesome heel problem.

Although he has returned to action this season, his opportunities have remained limited under Maresca.

Kovacic has made eight appearances across all competitions, contributing one goal and one assist, but only one of those outings has been a Premier League start.

He has also been used sparingly in the Champions League, with the manager preferring other midfield options for the majority of City's European fixtures.

His two full appearances in the EFL Cup underline the change in his status, although he was entrusted with the captain's armband in one of those matches.

The situation represents a considerable shift for a player who has won four Champions League titles and previously played an vital role in some of Europe's most successful teams.

Reports linking Kovacic with an exit have circulated for several months.

In September, the Croatian was reportedly considering a January departure after becoming frustrated with his lack of opportunities.

Moretto's latest information, however, points towards a summer move when Kovacic would become available without a transfer fee.

From January, the midfielder will be eligible to negotiate a pre-contract agreement with clubs outside England, potentially allowing him to arrange his next destination before the end of the campaign.

Kovacic's reported preference for Spain or Italy would represent a return to familiar surroundings rather than an entirely new challenge.

The midfielder spent two seasons with Inter Milan before joining Real Madrid in 2015, where he won three consecutive Champions League titles between 2016 and 2018.

He subsequently moved to Chelsea, initially on loan, and spent five seasons at Stamford Bridge before completing his switch to City.

His experience in Serie A has already attracted attention from Italian clubs.

Juventus were linked with a move for Kovacic in September, when reports suggested that the Turin giants had identified him as one of several potential free-agent signings for the summer of 2027.

The Bianconeri were also mentioned to be monitoring Fikayo Tomori and David Raum as part of their efforts to strengthen the squad without paying substantial transfer fees.

AC Milan have separately been mentioned among Kovacic's possible suitors, although there is no indication that either Italian club has reached an agreement with the player.

The possibility of returning to La Liga also remains open, but Moretto's comments did not identify a Spanish club presently negotiating for his signature.

His wages could prove the biggest obstacle to a move.

Despite the prospect of securing an accomplished international without paying City a transfer fee, interested clubs would still need to reach an agreement over a salary package acceptable to Kovacic.

For City, the latest revision raises the prospect of losing another member of Guardiola's former midfield without receiving a transfer fee.

Maresca's current selection decisions suggest that Kovacic is no longer regarded as an automatic starter, although the Croatian remains part of the squad and has not publicly confirmed any prepares to leave.

With his contract due to expire next June, the coming months could determine whether he completes his final season in Manchester or attracts an offer to bring forward his departure.

#15052. Global patterns and drivers of bee richness and endemism on islands

Global patterns and drivers of bee richness and endemism on islands

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 73 min read (14516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~73 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Islands account for a disproportionate share of global biodiversity1, yet insects, including invaluable pollinators such as bees2, remain underrepresented in island biogeography research3.
  • According to recent reports, islands are fundamental for studying patterns of biodiversity in time and space1,7.
  • Insects, the most diverse of all animal groups, remain underrepresented in global biogeographic studies and conservation assessments3.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Islands account for a disproportionate share of global biodiversity1, yet insects, including invaluable pollinators such as bees2, remain underrepresented in island biogeography research3. Here we present a global checklist of island bees, recording 4,147 species across 305 islands. Although islands comprise only about 6% of the Earth’s land area, they support around 20% of known global bee diversity, and 42% of insular species are endemic, making up around 8% of all known bee species. Island bee species richness peaks at mid-latitudes (at least in the Northern Hemisphere), mirroring continental trends4. Native richness increases with island area and declines with isolation, consistent with patterns in other taxa5. The strength of island species–area relationships varies among biomes and is steepest in Mediterranean-type systems, which also support disproportionately high bee richness relative to flowering plant diversity. The number of endemic species is highest on large tropical islands, reflecting extensive in situ diversification. Major centres of bee endemism include Madagascar, Malesia (the Greater Sundas and New Guinea) and the Hawaiian islands, where a single large radiation of Hylaeus (Nesoprosopis) dominates6. Among islands that are capable of supporting endemic species, endemism scales strongly with total richness. These findings highlight the need to integrate island bee diversity into global conservation planning and position bees as a model for understanding insect evolution and conservation on islands.

According to recent reports, islands are fundamental for studying patterns of biodiversity in time and space1,7. The isolation and limited opportunities for colonization of remote islands have fostered evolutionarily distinct and highly endemic flora and fauna5,8,9. Consequently, islands have long been central to fundamental questions in macroecology, evolution, community ecology and species conservation10. Yet, despite their ecological and evolutionary importance, major gaps remain in our understanding of island colonization, evolution and diversification across animal taxa, especially arthropods.

Insects, the most diverse of all animal groups, remain underrepresented in global biogeographic studies and conservation assessments3. This gap largely reflects logistical and taxonomic challenges of assembling standardized, high-resolution data for insects across geographically and politically fragmented islands, which results in inadequate understanding of species’ distributions11. Consequently, tests of island biogeography theory have disproportionately focused on vertebrates (especially birds) and land vascular plants, and systematic studies across multiple archipelagos remain scarce both for insects and other invertebrates12,13,14 (but see Proios et al.15 for land snails).

Notable global efforts targeting other insect groups do exist, such as the Global Ant Biodiversity Informatics (GABI) database16, as well as efforts motivated by pest and pathogen spread, such as a global checklist of mosquito distributions17, and of patterns of island invasion by beetles18. Comparable progress has been made for Lepidoptera at regional scales, including recent large-scale analyses of butterfly biogeography across tropical Asian islands19. Nevertheless, comprehensive global syntheses—such as those available for plants20—of insect diversity and endemism across island systems are virtually absent.

There are approximately 21,000 described species of bees worldwide21. They have an important role in global ecosystems, pollinating many wild flowering plants22 and crops23. On continents, bees exhibit a bimodal latitudinal diversity distribution, with peak richness in seasonally xeric mid-latitude regions that support ecosystems with a Mediterranean climate (hereafter referred to as Mediterranean-type ecosystems), as well as in adjacent desert and montane habitats2,4,24. This pattern deviates from the latitudinal diversity gradients of most other groups of plants and animals, which usually peak in the tropics25. Although the continental-scale biogeographical and ecological patterns of bees are becoming better understood, how they translate to island systems remains underexplored.

Sources indicate that generalizations about island bee biogeography have hitherto been rather qualitative in nature. For example, Michener2 noted that whereas very small bees might be carried over long distances by winds, wood-nesting bees may have dispersed across oceans via driftwood: a rafting hypothesis supported by quantitative evidence that wood-nesting bees are overrepresented in island faunas26, Michener also suggested Polynesian transport by seafarers for certain wood-nesting bee taxa that reached some of the most remote oceanic archipelagos, such as the Hawaiian islands. Consequently, bees detected by the even the first European voyages of discovery cannot be assumed to be native.

Recent phylogenetic evidence indicates that several bee lineages colonized upcoming biogeographic regions during the Neogene Period (around 23–2.6 million years ago) via island-hopping, showing how stepping-stone dispersal may have shaped bee composition. For example, the families Apidae, Megachilidae and Halictidae probably colonized Australia via movements from mainland Asia across the Indomalayan Archipelago27. Similar processes have been proposed to explain disjunct distributions in modern day Central America, where ancient archipelago chains acted as stepping stones between North and South America before the continents joined2.

It has been revealed that conversely, disjunct distribution patterns in other bee groups appear to reflect their more limited capacity to disperse and subsequently colonize islands. For example, following the breakup of Gondwana, stingless bees (Apidae, tribe Meliponini) appear to have been unable to cross the substantial marine barriers that appeared, and their present distribution in Indomalaya probably reflects episodes of sea level fluctuation and transient land-bridges, rather than long-distance overwater dispersal28.

These examples indicate the importance of accurately documenting insular bee diversity to achieve a more complete and fine-grained understanding of global bee biogeography and conservation. Yet, despite this need, comprehensive data remain sparse. Only 542 bee species have been assessed for the global International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List, including just 240 species recorded from islands and 68 island endemics. Of these assessed species, 26 are considered threatened, and for many of these, distributional data are not publicly accessible29. The limited representation of island taxa on global conservation lists does not reflect the well-established vulnerability of island biotas: for example, the majority of US federally listed endangered bee species are native Hawaiian endemics30.

In a recent development, here we present a global assessment of native bee diversity on islands. Specifically, we investigate: (1) global patterns of native bee richness and endemism; (2) the influence of island characteristics (area and isolation), topography (elevation) and climate variables on both native bee richness and endemism; (3) how endemism scales with richness; and (4) the relationship between insular bee diversity and angiosperm richness. We expect the patterns of insular bee richness and endemism to be shaped by area and isolation, as predicted by island biogeography theory7, but also by biotic and climate constraints and associations, including mutualistic relationships with flowering plants22.

By addressing these questions, our analyses fill knowledge gaps, providing a global baseline for investigating the evolutionary and biogeographic history, ecology and vulnerability of island bees, while highlighting priority regions for future research and conservation at both archipelago and single-island scales. More broadly, this baseline enables rigorous tests of major hypotheses in island biogeography and (meta)community assembly1 using this taxonomically diverse, and ecologically and economically important group.

Industry observers note that our final dataset consists of 11,065 unique island-native bee species combinations, representing 4,128 native species across 305 islands (see Methods for details of this classification) (Fig. 1a). Consequently, of the approximately 21,000 bee species described worldwide, our data indicate that 20% occur on islands. Of these, 42% (1,742 species) are restricted exclusively to islands, accounting for around 8% of all described bee species. Although this proportion is lower than that reported for vascular plants, for which 21% of the global flora are island endemic, with 14.5% single-island endemic species (SIEs)9, as well as terrestrial mammals (about 12% single-island endemics31) and rodents specifically (about 17% endemics to islands32), it nevertheless represents a slightly higher contribution of islands to global bee diversity relative to the approximately 5–6% of global landmass represented by islands globally1. Although we focus here on native bee richness, we also recorded introduced species to distinguish genuine native diversity from non-native species accumulation. We identified at least 54 species as introduced on 143 islands, with the western honey bee (Apis mellifera) being by far the most widespread, introduced to 127 islands in our dataset (Extended Data Table 1). Invasion due to anthropogenic drivers is a major threat to insular diversity33, and evidence, at least for A. mellifera, suggests negative effects of invasive bees on native biodiversity on islands (see, for example, ref. 34).

a, Map of global bee diversity on islands (n = 305 islands). Each circle represents an island for which there are recorded native bee species. The colour gradient is log-scaled and indicates the total number of native bee species recorded for each island; the size of the point or circle is proportional to the total number of endemic species found on each island. Endemism is measured as the total number of island (or island group; Methods) endemic species. Left, histogram showing the total number of endemic bee species by latitude. Bee species richness peaks in the Western Palaearctic Realm, whereas endemism (species only found on islands within these realms) is highest on Indomalayan (466 species) and Australasian (443 species) islands (Fig. 1b). Clear differences in island bee richness are also apparent among biomes (Fig. 2), however this pattern is influenced by variation in island area. Species richness was highest in Mediterranean-type biomes: Sicily (approximately 25,000 km2, 636 species), is the island with the highest species richness worldwide and Cyprus (approximately 9,300 km2, 384 species) has the highest species richness of the oceanic islands. The East Aegean islands (approximately 5,000 km2, 589 species) also support large bee faunas, dominated by widespread continental species, reflecting their limited degree of isolation. In contrast to the high richness, endemism on these islands is low, with only Crete (14 species) and Cyprus (23 species) showing comparatively high levels of island endemism. Despite its proximity to the Levant region and its complex origins in tectonic uplift, Cyprus is treated here as an oceanic island owing to its lack of historical land bridge connections to the mainland. The most species-rich Mediterranean-type oceanic island of strictly volcanic origin is Tenerife (2,000 km2, 57 species).

Industry observers note that tropical islands, by contrast, account for moderate overall native species richness compared with Mediterranean-type islands but markedly higher levels of endemism. Fresh Guinea supports 284 species, of which 210 (73%) are endemic, making it by far the richest island in the Australasian realm. The nearby Maluku Islands archipelago (34,000 km2) hosts 102 species, including 62 endemics (61%), and includes Seram (18,000 km2), the most species-rich tropical, oceanic island for bees (87 species).

It has been revealed that in the Neotropics, Hispaniola represents the most species-rich oceanic island, with 66 species. In the Nearctic, the predominantly oceanic California Channel Islands (approximately 910 km2) have a high overall richness (154 species) but low levels of endemism (5%). In the Afrotropics, Madagascar stands out with 226 species, of which 201 (89%) are endemic. Within Oceania, which consists only of oceanic islands, the Hawaiian islands (17,000 km2) are a major hotspot, with all 65 native species of wild bees belonging to a single lineage of Hylaeus (Nesoprosopis), and endemic to the archipelago6. Among other oceanic systems, the Mediterranean-climate Canary Islands (approximately 5,400 km2) host a similarly high number of endemic species (57 out of 128 species), although at a lower proportional level of archipelago endemism (AE) (45%).

Globally, bee richness on islands peaks in the Northern Hemisphere at mid-latitudes (Fig. 1a), mirroring the mid-latitude peak of bee richness observed on mainlands4. This pattern contrasts with the latitudinal diversity gradient seen in other diverse insect groups, such as ants, whose global richness peaks predominantly in the tropics35. The lack of an island-specific bimodal diversity pattern comparable to that found for the mainlands2,4 is probably a consequence of the limited number of Mediterranean-type islands in the Southern Hemisphere. This asymmetry reflects the true distribution of islands globally36, and not simply sampling bias; our global dataset confirms data availability and sufficient coverage across these regions (Fig. 3). This pattern occurs both on continental and oceanic islands, although many of the larger islands within the Mediterranean-type biome were continental or complex in origin. Such environments favour diverse wild bee assemblages through a combination of evolutionary history and ecological conditions. Bees are thought to have originated in the arid environments of Western Gondwana2,27, with limited but predictable rainfall that generates short yet intense blooming periods and a high flowering plant diversity in open habitats2,4,37. These conditions promote temporal synchrony between bee flight periods and floral resources, fostering increased specialization and resource partitioning that reduces competition. This synchrony promotes local speciation and therefore increases richness, allowing these regions to defy the traditional latitudinal diversity gradient2. Our global results support these conclusions but trait-based research focusing on the biome-specific patterns of habitat and dietary specialization of bees on islands are needed to directly test these claims.

Circle colour indicates sampling completeness measured as the sample-size-adjusted sample coverage (ranging from 0% (yellow) to 100% (purple)). The index combines Chao–Jost sample coverage64 with a weighted-by-sampling effort, based on the total number of occurrence records. Islands with dark purple colouring and large point sizes represent well-sampled regions with high confidence in richness estimates. Yellow and orange points represent under-sampled islands where true diversity is likely to be underestimated. Coverage was calculated using a species/island abundance (count of all occurrences per species per island) matrix of all records to estimate the proportion of the total individuals per island that belong to the observed species, using a non-parametric estimator that accounts for the frequency of rare species (singletons and doubletons). According to recent reports, to test fundamental aspects of MacArthur and Wilson’s theory of island biogeography7 for bee diversity, we used a mixed-effects model with archipelago identity as the random effect. The final best model was selected based on Akaike information criterion corrected for sample sizes (AICc) and included log10-transformed island area in km2 and its interaction with biome, as well as isolation (log10-transformed distance to continental mainland in km) as fixed effects. This model explains 66% of the variance in species richness through fixed effects (area, isolation, island type and biome), and 75% variance when including archipelago identity (conditional R2). This moderate difference in R2 values indicates that native richness is strongly governed by broad biogeographic variables, with some unexplained regional structure.

Industry observers note that island area shows a consistent positive effect on native bee richness but the island species–area relationship (ISAR) slopes differ significantly among biomes (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Table 1). Mediterranean-type biomes indicated the strongest species–area response (β = 0.50), which is significantly steeper than that of all other biomes (Supplementary Table 2). Tropical islands exhibit an intermediate effect, (β = 0.28), which is indistinguishable from temperate islands (β = 0.18). By contrast, desert (β = 0.02) and boreal (β = 0.02) islands display flatter slopes, indicating that island size is not a major constraint on bee diversity in these biomes. The impact of biome on species area slopes is observed more clearly on oceanic islands (Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 3), specifically, the ISAR slope for Mediterranean-type islands is significantly greater than for the others. This is not the case for continental islands, where these ISAR slope differences are far less pronounced (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 3).

Richness decreases with island isolation (β = −0.13, P < 0.003) (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Table 1), corresponding to a reduction of roughly 15% in species richness for each tenfold increase in distance from the mainland. This isolation effect is uniform across all biomes, supporting the fundamental principle that remote islands receive fewer colonists and consequently maintain lower richness as a function of their area7. We also observe a clear influence of island type on richness. Oceanic islands support substantially fewer species than continental (β = −0.19, P = 0.01) and fragment islands (β = −0.27, P = 0.01; Supplementary Table 2), consistent with their lack of past land connections to the mainland, more limited historical species pools and generally younger geological ages, whereas a high proportion of continental shelf islands were connected to the mainland only a few thousand years ago, leading to more ‘harmonic’ biotas1. Alternative models (ΔAICc < 2) additionally include positive relationships with temperature seasonality and annual precipitation. Neither climate variable has a statistically significant effect (Supplementary Table 4).

Our results support the conclusion that ISARs can vary considerably as a function of island geo-environmental properties12,38. Specifically, bees may benefit from biome-specific increases in ecological complexity in Mediterranean-type biomes owing to temporal differences in habitat availability, which can permit increased richness even at small scales, resulting in area having a stronger effect on richness than in tropical or temperate biomes2,4. The finding that Mediterranean-type islands in our models have the steepest ISAR slopes and highest richness values align with the high seasonality of the climate and flowering plant diversity characteristic of Mediterranean climates39, providing diverse nesting sites and floral resources throughout the year.

Industry observers note that although biomes explain considerable variation in richness on islands, they represent broad proxies for climate and habitat diversity. The steep ISAR slope for Mediterranean-type systems suggests that explicitly measuring finer-scale variables, such as resource availability and microhabitat diversity, may provide deeper insights into the mechanisms underlying island bee biogeography. Habitat diversity and environmental heterogeneity, and the potentially associated diversity of mutualist partners, can constitute vital predictors of species richness40. In our global models, these factors are likely to be implicitly incorporated when comparing between islands by combining area and biome. However, a single biome classification masks within-island variation as for many large islands with a high elevational range, such as Madagascar, Tenerife, Latest Guinea or Hawai’i (Big Island), representing the island as a single biome inevitably underestimates its pronounced environmental heterogeneity, which is recognized as a driver of high species diversity and endemism40. Additionally, regional geographic context is an important consideration, as shown by the islands of Lesvos and Cyprus, which show comparatively high species richness values for their area (positive residuals from the Mediterranean-type ISAR; top 5% among Mediterranean-type islands). These islands sit at the border between the European bee fauna and the exceptionally rich western Asian fauna, and the resulting high comparative species richness for their area may be due to this dual species pool from which bees can colonize41.

Sampling effort is uneven across regions, as expected for a global dataset (Fig. 3), with parts of Oceania, Indomalaya and Australasia being comparatively under-sampled. To account for this heterogeneity, we included sampling completeness, measured as the proportion of individuals belonging to observed species and weighted by sample size, as a fixed effect in the native richness model (Supplementary Table 1). Completeness has a positive effect on native bee richness (β = 0.21, P < 0.001; Extended Data Fig. 3). Islands with a greater sampling completeness tend to have higher estimated richness. However, controlling for sampling completeness does not weaken the central results above. The island–biome–area effects remained strong after adjusting for sampling completeness confirming that these patterns were not a result of uneven sampling effort. This indicates that the relationships between area, isolation and richness, and in particular the contrast between mid-latitude richness and high tropical endemism, reflects true ecological differences (Fig. 3). Future efforts to digitize and provide open access to museum collections42,43, conduct targeted expeditions to historically difficult-to-sample islands2,44 and harness citizen science platforms such as iNaturalist45 will be critical to resolving knowledge gaps in island bee diversity, an notable task given the projected gaps in global bee diversity46.

Recent findings suggest that to identify the biogeographic and climatic predictors of endemism and assess whether richness can explain endemism patterns, we tested the same linear mixed-effects models as for native richness (Fig. 4a,b). Across islands capable of supporting SIEs (SIE ≥ 1, n = 113), area is associated with increased SIE richness (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Table 5) and this relationship varies significantly with biome, as observed for richness. However, unlike richness, biome-specific area slopes for SIE differs significantly between tropical and temperate islands, with a steeper relationship in tropical islands (Δ = 0.27, P = 0.01), whereas the difference between tropical and Mediterranean-type islands was marginal (Δ = 0.28, P = 0.06; Fig. 4a and Supplementary Table 6). Isolation (log10-transformed distance to nearest landmass larger than 1,000 km2) has only a weak, non-significant positive influence (β = 0.09, P = 0.11; Fig. 4a,b). Temperature seasonality had a significant positive effect on SIE (β = 0.28, P = 0.018), and sampling completeness and elevation range each appeared as significant positive predictors in alternative models within ΔAICc < 2 (Supplementary Table 7). We note that sampling completeness could bias endemism estimates in both directions, overestimating endemism on well-studied islands where the same species have not yet been recorded elsewhere, and underestimating it where undiscovered endemics remain.

Industry observers note that the observed patterns are consistent across data subsets but without the interaction of area and biome. On oceanic islands with endemics (n = 69), area remains the strongest predictor (β = 0.32, P < 0.001, R2 = 0.38; Extended Data Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 5). Among islands rich in SIE (>5% of native richness; n = 96), SIE richness increases with area (β = 0.36, P < 0.001, R2 = 0.66) and increases marginally with sampling completeness (β = 0.16, P = 0.02) (Extended Data Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 5). These results parallel global patterns of vascular plant endemism on islands47. The mid-latitudinal peak in bee species richness2, seen on islands predominantly in the Northern Hemisphere, does not translate into increased bee endemism. Rather, bee endemism is greatest in the tropics (Extended Data Fig. 5). Patterns for AE are broadly similar. Across islands hosting AEs (n = 217) area was again the main predictor and interacted with biome (Supplementary Table 5). However, AE–area slopes were consistent across tropical, temperate, and Mediterranean-type biomes, with only desert islands showing a significantly lower rate than tropical islands (Δ = 0.35, P = 0.01; Supplementary Table 6). Isolation (distance from mainland) is non-significant (β = −0.04, P = 0.48) and sampling completeness is also included as a significant effect, suggesting that islands with high numbers of AEs are also the best studied (β = 0.14, P = 0.01). Additionally, there is a significant positive effect of elevation (β = 0.18, P = 0.01) suggesting that topographically complex islands support a greater diversity of endemics at the archipelago scale (Extended Data Fig. 6).

A model predicting SIE from overall native richness alone reveals a clear correlation (R2 = 0.44) and improved significantly with the inclusion of biome (ΔR2 = 0.15, χ2 = 33.1, P < 0.001; Supplementary Table 8). Although adding the interaction term yields a significant model improvement (ΔR2 = 0.02, χ2 = 8.15, P = 0.04), post hoc pairwise comparisons reveal no significant differences in slopes between biomes after correcting for multiple testing (Supplementary Table 8). This indicates a practically uniform global rate of increasing SIE with richness but with distinct baseline shifts; specifically, Mediterranean-type islands support significantly fewer baseline SIEs than all other biomes (Extended Data Fig. 7). Conversely, for AEs (R2 = 0.55), the full interaction model results in the best fit (ΔR2 = 0.14, χ2 = 72.54, P < 0.001; Extended Data Fig. 7 and Supplementary Table 8), demonstrating that the rate endemic species accumulate with increasing richness is biome-dependent. Pairwise comparisons indicate that the slope for Mediterranean-type biomes (0.42 ± 0.10) is significantly flatter than in desert (0.83 ± 0.12, P = 0.02), tropical (0.96 ± 0.03, P < 0.001) and temperate (0.75 ± 0.06, P = 0.01) biomes, indicating a partial decoupling between richness and AE (Supplementary Table 9). Although Mediterranean-type islands generally support fewer AEs than expected across the richness gradient, the Canary Islands stand out as an exception, showing high AE richness consistent with their high overall richness, although probably enhanced by their relative isolation from the primary Mediterranean source pool (Extended Data Fig. 6). This divergence also highlights that the AE model probably captures more ancient diversification compared with the SIE model48,49. This partial decoupling contrasts with vascular plants, for which the richest islands also tend to host the highest numbers of endemic species, particularly in the case of large tropical islands9. Our results are consistent with previous macroecological studies50, suggesting that the relationship between richness and endemism is not simple and varies among taxa.

According to recent reports, together, these findings reveal that bee endemism is concentrated on large tropical islands and certain oceanic archipelagos rather than in areas of peak species richness globally. New Guinea and Madagascar stand out for supporting both high numbers and high proportions of endemic species. By contrast, certain other island systems, including the Caribbean, the Philippines and the Hawaiian islands, are characterized by only a high proportion of endemics. This apparent divergence between patterns of richness and endemism suggests a distinction between the factors structuring island assembly attributable to colonization and evolutionary diversification in bees. Wet, humid tropical conditions, combined with greater isolation of many oceanic tropical islands, present environmental barriers to bee colonization2. Therefore, successful colonizers are presented with greater ecological opportunity, and this can lead to high in situ diversification1. These patterns suggest distinct evolutionary histories: high endemism in Madagascar probably reflects multiple independent radiations51, whereas in other systems single radiations account for high proportions of endemism, such as Palaeorhiza in New Guinea52, Hylaeus (Nesoprosopis) in the Hawaiian archipelago6 and Lasioglossum (Homalictus) across Pacific islands such as Samoa and Fiji53,54. Conversely, the factors that support high richness in Mediterranean-type islands are likely to include: (1) the adaptation to arid environments; but also (2) frequent arrivals from nearby continental source pools, providing sufficient gene flow to inhibit in situ diversification and thus result in lower endemism55. Globally, bees provide evidence that endemism, and by extension extinction risk, is not inextricably linked to overall species richness, often diverging into regions of high endemism but low richness or high richness with low endemism56.

Building on these findings, we additionally examine how plant diversity, as a potential biotic driver, covaries with bee richness, given that bees depend strongly on flowering plants for food and nesting resources22,24. Across the 175 islands for which we have both angiosperm richness data and native bee richness, we observe a positive correlation: angiosperm richness alone explains 49% of variation in bee richness across islands (R2 = 0.49), a relationship that persists after accounting for island area and isolation (β = 0.64, P < 0.001; Fig. 5a and Supplementary Table 10). The slope of the relationship between angiosperm and bee richness is largely consistent across biomes (likelihood ratio test: χ2 = 7.02, P = 0.06). However, temperate islands show a slightly steeper relationship compared with the tropical baseline (β = 0.55, P = 0.015; Fig. 5a and Supplementary Table 10). Additionally, we observe differences from the baseline in total supported bee richness in Mediterranean-type islands: they support 5.6 times more bee species than tropical islands at equivalent plant richness, area and isolation (P < 0.001; Fig. 5b and Supplementary Table 11).

Native angiosperm richness was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation for degrees of freedom (β = 0.60, 95% confidence interval [0.36, 0.84], t(126) = 5.00, P = 1.89 × 10−6). b, Bee species richness for each island (n = 175 islands) adjusted to the global mean angiosperm richness, area and isolation.
