Latest Update: An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 107 min read (21399 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~107 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars1,2.
  • It has been revealed that in April 2025, a previous study12 reported the unusual and gradual brightening of an AGB star (named WNTR23bzdiq/WTP19aalzlk) in the Andromeda Galaxy.
  • Ultraviolet to mid-IR light curve, constructed using POSS-2, PS1, CFHT, PTF, ZTF, GIT, WINTER, NEOWISE, SPHEREx, P60 and Swift data, with symbols and colours denoting different telescopes and filters (see legend and section ‘Follow-up observations’).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars1,2. This is theorized to happen through common envelope evolution (CEE)3, when the stars orbit in a loosely bound, shared convective envelope, triggering an inspiral due to frictional drag4,5. However, this inspiral in such a system has never been observed directly. Here we present observations of AT 2025abao, a transient eruption in the Andromeda Galaxy, which originates from the CEE of an approximately 7M⊙ asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star with its companion. Extensive pre- and post-eruption spectroscopy is best explained as an approximately 0.7M⊙ companion inspiralling within the convective AGB envelope that powers a seven-year period of gradual brighteningone of the first direct observations of frictional drag energy dissipation induced by CEE. This phase is radiatively efficient, consistent with predictions for convective transport in CEE5,6,7,8. The subsequent merger of the companion with the primary core powers the ejection of the outermost 10% of the stellar envelope at speeds about 10× the primary escape speed, and empirically constrains the fraction of dissipated orbital energy available to unbind the convective common envelope4,9,10,11, 0.01 ≲ α ≲ 0.4. This end-to-end characterization using multi-survey observations demonstrates a path towards mapping the landscape of CEE outcomes with upcoming surveys.

It has been revealed that in April 2025, a previous study12 reported the unusual and gradual brightening of an AGB star (named WNTR23bzdiq/WTP19aalzlk) in the Andromeda Galaxy. Multiwavelength observations of this source indicated that this brightening may be powered by energy deposition of a companion spiralling through the outer convective envelope of the star12—marking the onset of common-envelope evolution (CEE)3,4,13,14, or possibly a brief brightening caused by nuclear energy input from thermal pulses in late-stage stellar evolution12. The quiescent progenitor star reveals no signs of variability between 1989 and the start of its brightening in 2018 (Fig. 1). Modelling the spectral energy distribution (SED) of the quiescent progenitor12, we find that the source is consistent with an approximately 7M⊙ star in its early-AGB phase—exhibiting a photospheric temperature of Teff ≈ 3,650 K, radius of Reff ≈ 350R⊙, and total luminosity L ≈ 1.8 × 104L⊙ (see section ‘Modelling the progenitor SED’). The large infrared (IR) excess in the SED indicates a wind mass loss rate of \(\dot{M}\approx 1{0}^{-5}{M}_{\odot }\,{\mathrm{yr}}^{-1}\)—substantially higher than the expectations for isolated early AGB stars15—and supports a state of prolonged enhanced mass loss.

Ultraviolet to mid-IR light curve, constructed using POSS-2, PS1, CFHT, PTF, ZTF, GIT, WINTER, NEOWISE, SPHEREx, P60 and Swift data, with symbols and colours denoting different telescopes and filters (see legend and section ‘Follow-up observations’). a–c, The three panels are continuous in time, but use different x-axis scales to illustrate the quiescent progenitor phase (2005–2015, a), the precursor phase (2015 to early 2025, b) and the eruption (late 2025 to early 2026, c). Panel a also indicates fluxes from 1989 POSS R and I-band images (dotted red and orange lines, 1σ uncertainties as shaded regions). SPHEREx spectrophotometry was converted to W1 and W2-band photometry (brown, magenta diamonds) by synthetic photometry over the spectrum using the respective transmission profiles.

From 2018 to early 2025, the star brightened gradually, exhibiting two distinct episodes, during which its optical (0.4–0.8 μm) flux increased by a factor of 2−3 over a period of about 1,000−1,500 days. The source subsequently faded rapidly by a factor of about 2 in optical flux for approximately 300 days, even as its IR (1–5 μm) emission continued to brighten by a factor ≳5. Modelling the multicolour evolution, we find that the brightening phases sustained a near-constant photospheric temperature of about 3,800 K, before cooling to around 3,500 K during the rapid optical fading (see section ‘Modelling the multiband SED during the slow precursor brightening’).

In a recent development, in July 2025, the source was serendipitously observed during its rapid optical fading by the first sky survey of the SPHEREx mission16, providing a precise glimpse of the stellar photosphere during this phase. Modelling the SPHEREx SED (see section ‘SPHEREx pre-outburst SED modelling’) using models of dusty stellar atmospheres, we find that the stellar radius and luminosity have increased to R ≈ 860R⊙ and L ≈ 105L⊙, respectively, whereas the corresponding photospheric temperature has dropped to T ≈ 3,460 K. The SPHEREx data indicate a substantial increase in the circumstellar dust mass and mass loss rate relative to the progenitor star, corresponding to the ejection of about 0.1M⊙ of gas (for typical dust-to-gas ratios) and an increased mass loss rate of approximately 10−2M⊙ yr−1 at this epoch.

Industry observers note that in October 2025, the star underwent a dramatic eruption17,18 immediately following the rapid optical fading—brightening by a factor of about 100 in r-band over 25 days and exhibiting a sudden increase in its photospheric temperature to about 8,000 K. Over the next 80 days, the luminosity plateaued, whereas the effective temperature steadily cooled to about 3,000 K (Fig. 2; see section ‘Photometric evolution of the LRN eruption’). The peak bolometric luminosity during the eruption reached about 1.5 × 106L⊙ and was accompanied by a steady photospheric expansion speed of around 330 km s−1. Spectra obtained at early times during the eruption17 show a blue continuum with narrow hydrogen emission lines (vFWHM ≈ 900 km s−1), gradually transitioning to exhibit redder continua over the eruption duration—exhibiting narrower hydrogen and metallic lines, such as Fe and Ca, before eventually developing broad absorption features due to TiO and VO molecules at late phases(>50 days since g-band peak; Fig. 3 and section ‘Spectroscopic evolution of the LRN eruption’).

It has been revealed that a, Evolution of photospheric temperature (bottom), photospheric radius (middle) and bolometric luminosity (top). The purple lines and shaded regions mark values and 1σ uncertainties from fitting stellar models to precursor SEDs; the purple dots (right) show those from blackbody fits to eruption SEDs. The two panels in a are contiguous in time but use different x-axis scales. Corresponding values of V838Mon (red)21 and M31-LRN-2015 (black)49,50 are shown for comparison. The yellow-dashed line (radius panel) indicates a photosphere expanding at 330 km s−1. b, Quiescent progenitor SED (black points), precursor SPHEREx spectrum (red) and post-eruption SED from SPHEREx, JWST and ground-based data (purple), labelled by phase relative to the g-band peak. Best-fit models are plotted as lines, and relevant inferred properties with 1σ uncertainties are indicated.

From October 2025 to February 2026, we obtained a series of optical spectra of the eruption that reveal clear signs of shock interactions between the ejecta and circumstellar material (see section ‘Spectroscopic evolution of the LRN eruption’). The Hα line in a spectrum obtained 4 days after the g-band peak demonstrates an emission component and a narrow absorption feature whose minimum is blueshifted by about 15 km s−1 (Fig. 3). During the next 80 days, the emission component gradually narrows and becomes stronger, indicating that the fast ejecta decelerate as they crash into the neutral ejecta and shock them (Fig. 3). The evolution of the velocity of the emission component matches the expectation for momentum-conserving interactions between fast-moving ejecta and circumstellar material with a density profile ρ(r) ∝ r−2 (Fig. 3). The line profile at late times is asymmetric, with a stronger blueshifted emission component from shocked ejecta along the line of sight. These profiles have been observed in type IIn supernovae and attributed to circumstellar material in disk geometries viewed along the equatorial plane19.

On 24 December 2025, 47 days after the g-band peak, we obtained James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations of the eruption that coincided with the second sky survey of SPHEREx (Fig. 2). Modelling the combined SPHEREx and JWST SEDs (see section ‘Post-outburst JWST and SPHEREx SED modelling’), we find a warmer stellar photosphere compared with the precursor—surrounded by an optically thin dust shell located at a distance of about 5 × 104R⊙. The inferred radius of the dust shell lies beyond both the maximum distance reachable by material ejected during the eruption or the seven-year precursor phase, and the maximum radius out to which dust could be sublimated by the 2025 eruption (see section ‘Enhanced mass loss around the quiescent progenitor system’). We therefore conclude that the JWST observations probe remnants of dust around the progenitor that were formed during its prolonged phase of enhanced mass loss. Combining the properties of the dust shell inferred from the progenitor SED with its radial extent inferred from JWST yields a total dust mass of about 6 × 10−5M⊙ surrounding the quiescent progenitor, about 10 years before eruption (see section ‘Enhanced mass loss around the quiescent progenitor system’).

Recent findings suggest that the 2025 eruption of AT 2025abao shows the defining hallmarks of luminous red novae20,21,22,23 (LRNe; Figs. 2 and 3), a class of transients established to arise from impulsive energy injection into a common envelope during the merger of a star with its companion20,22. However, AT 2025abao is set apart from all previously known LRNe by its progenitor primary, which is unambiguously an evolved AGB star with an extended convective envelope. This progenitor system resembles those considered in the classical CEE formalism for compact binary formation3,5,6,11, in which a loosely bound convective common envelope can theoretically be ejected by an inspiralling companion24. By contrast, all known LRN progenitors have primary stars on the main sequence or in the Hertzsprung gap22,23,25, where the more tightly bound radiative envelopes are expected to inevitably drive the system towards merger25. Thus, AT 2025abao provides the first view of a classical CEE progenitor system continuously monitored from its onset through its culmination.

It has been revealed that a, Continuum-normalized Hα spectral profiles coloured by spectrograph and labelled by phase relative to the g-band peak. Each spectrum is offset by a constant (dotted horizontal lines). The dashed vertical line marks zero expansion velocity. b, Representative optical spectra of the AT 2025abao eruption from 285 days before to 91 days after the g-band peak, compared with LRNe AT2019zhd (ref. 51), M31-LRN-2015 (ref. 34) and AT2021biy (ref. 52) at similar phases. c, Evolution of FWHM velocities (and 1σ uncertainties) of the Hα emission inferred using Gaussian fits, compared with the theoretical velocity deceleration expected from momentum-conserving interactions between fast-moving ejecta and CBM40 (blue).

We leverage our multiwavelength dataset to draw the first direct constraints on the CEE phase, starting with the nature of the companion star. As the companion approaches the primary star, unstable mass transfer from the primary star over the centuries preceding CEE is expected to drive outflows of unbound material that enhance the mass loss rate of the quiescent system26,27,28,29. Comparing the dust mass measured around the quiescent system to theoretical estimates (see section ‘Comparisons to theoretical predictions of enhanced mass loss’) from detailed simulations30,31 and analytical prescriptions32,33 of unstable mass transfer constrains the mass ratio (q = Msecondary/Mprimary) of the progenitor binary to q ≈ 0.1, indicating that the companion is a low-mass star of about 0.7M⊙ (Fig. 4).

a, Peak precursor luminosity compared with primary escape speed for AT 2025abao, V1309Sco (ref. 20) and M31-LRN-2015 (ref. 34), coloured by precursor duration in orbital periods at the surface of the primary. The lines show the kinetic luminosity of outflows at various mass-loss rates (dashed grey, equation (5)) and drag luminosity from an inspiralling companion (red, equation (7)) for the mass ratios in the legend. b, Theoretical estimates of dust mass around the quiescent progenitor (black line, analytical; squares, MESA simulations) compared with that ejected during the precursor (see section ‘The precursor’), coloured by binary mass ratio. The shaded region spans the progenitor dust range by varying the analytical-model parameters (see section ‘Comparisons to theoretical predictions of enhanced mass loss’). The red star shows measured values with 1σ uncertainties. c, Envelope binding energy compared with radius (black) from the MESA model of the 7M⊙, 340R⊙ AGB primary star, inferred orbital energy dissipated by the companion (red), observed ejecta kinetic energy (blue) and observed radiated energy during the precursor (green). The solid lines are median values; shaded regions mark 1σ uncertainties. d, CE efficiency α compared with binary mass ratio. The inferred mass ratio and its 1σ uncertainty is marked with the purple solid line and shaded region. The black-shaded regions are ruled out by a core merger in this system and its observed ejected mass. Black points show α measurements from post-CE binary systems53 (see section ‘The energetics of common-envelope evolution’).

It has been revealed that observations of previously known LRNe show gradual brightening by several magnitudes over tens to hundreds of orbits before the eruption20,34, attributed to outflows from the outer L2 Lagrangian point as the companion approaches the primary35,36. These outflows form an expanding photosphere around the binary, preventing a direct view of the inspiral phase. However, the precursor phase of AT 2025abao is challenging to explain in its entirety by the same mechanism—the low escape speed of the AGB primary of AT 2025abao makes such L2 outflows energetically insufficient to power the observed luminosity (about 1038 erg s−1), even if all of the kinetic energy were radiated away (Fig. 4). The long orbital period around the AGB primary also implies that the approximately 7-year precursor phase spans fewer than 10 orbits at the surface, substantially shorter than the other LRNe and that expected for dynamical outflows.

Instead, the precursor can be explained by energy deposition from a companion spiralling through the outer envelope of the primary (Fig. 4), signalling the onset of CEE. Adopting the Bondi–Hoyle formalism37 (see section ‘The precursor’), the energy dissipation rate due to frictional drag on an approximately 0.7M⊙ companion orbiting near the photosphere of the AT 2025abao primary is Ldrag ≈ 3 × 1038 erg s−1, consistent with the observed precursor excess luminosity. The corresponding timescale, |Eorb|/Ldrag ≈ 1,000 days, or a few orbits, is also broadly consistent with the observed duration of the precursor. The near-constant photospheric temperature and steadily increasing radius during the precursor phase (Fig. 2) indicate frictional drag induces a quasi-static expansion of the AGB star—probably mediated by efficient transport of excess energy to the stellar surface by convection5,6. The total radiated energy during this phase is about 1046 erg.

According to recent reports, the dust mass measured from the first SPHEREx observation constrains the mass outflow rate during this phase to around 10−2M⊙ yr−1. Assuming this mass is ejected at the escape speed of the primary (about 85 km s−1), the low outflow kinetic power (about 1037 erg s−1) compared with the observed luminosity (around 1038 erg s−1) indicates that most of the dissipated orbital energy is radiated during this outer inspiral. We can independently estimate the mass of the companion by comparing the measured mass to theoretical expectations of mass loss due to an inspiralling companion (see section ‘The precursor’), which yields a mass ratio q ≈ 0.1, consistent with that inferred from dust around the quiescent progenitor. As the energy dissipation rate increases rapidly with decreasing orbital separation, the final 300 days of the precursor phase marked by a temperature drop probably mark the breakdown of quasi-static expansion and the onset of a rapid inspiral from the outer layers to the core. This period corresponds to about 10 dynamical timescales of the envelope of the primary star, in line with theoretical predictions of the inspiral duration in these systems4,38.

In a recent development, the energetics of the 2025 LRN eruption constrain the mass of the ejecta and the circumbinary material (CBM; see section ‘The LRN eruption’), as well as the fate of the companion star at the end of CEE. As the rise time of the eruption is governed by photon diffusion through the ejecta39, our observations imply Mej ≈ 0.1–0.2M⊙ ejected during the merger. The fast continuum photospheric expansion coincident with spectral line deceleration indicates that these ejecta expand freely in the polar direction but are obstructed by CBM in the equatorial plane40,41. The observed velocity deceleration from about 900 km s−1 to 150 km s−1 (Fig. 3) indicates that the ejecta sweep up about five times their mass. Assuming the CBM covers approximately 20% of the merger ejecta32 gives a total CBM mass of about 0.1–0.2M⊙, broadly consistent with the CBM mass estimated from the SPHEREx SED. The kinetic energy dissipated by these interactions is about 3 × 1047 erg, while the energy radiated during the plateau phase is about 4 × 1046 erg, indicating that shock interactions release sufficient energy to power the observed light curve of the AT 2025abao eruption, as previously theorized40,42.

The ejecta properties can be used to infer the fate of the binary (see section ‘Constraining the outcome of CEE in AT 2025abao’). Assuming that the dissipated orbital energy is the primary energy reservoir, the observed kinetic energy of about 1048 erg requires the companion to have inspiralled to a radius of approximately 3R⊙—coincident with the He core of the primary, suggesting that the companion merged with the core. A merger is further supported by the low unbound mass of 0.2−0.4M⊙ that corresponds to only about 10% of the envelope of the primary. This indicates that the envelope is still intact, rather than being entirely ejected, as expected for a surviving binary. Finally, the AT 2025abao eruption—indicative of impulsive energy injection—is extremely similar to other LRNe that are known stellar mergers. We therefore suggest that AT 2025abao represents a CEE event that culminated in the merger of the binary components, which can be directly tested with future observations (see section ‘Constraining the outcome of CEE in AT 2025abao’).

During the rapid plunge to the primary core, the companion dissipated approximately 1048 erg, of which only about 1% was radiated away (around 1046 erg) and a similarly small amount (about 1046 erg) was expended to unbind the observed ejecta (see section ‘The energetics of common-envelope evolution’, Fig. 4). Instead, almost all orbital energy was expended to accelerate the ejecta to high kinetic energy (about 1048 erg). This is in contrast to the slow inspiral that powered the precursor phase, when most of the dissipated energy was radiated away. Our observations thus indicate a transition from a radiatively efficient slow inspiral to a kinetically efficient plunge, consistent with theoretical expectations of CEE inside a convective envelope5,6.

We examine AT 2025abao in the context of the widely used energy formalism9,10,11 (see section ‘The energetics of common-envelope evolution’), which predicts the outcome of CEE in binary systems using an efficiency parameter α that relates the fraction of the dissipated orbital energy (ΔEorb) to the envelope binding energy (Ebind). For AT 2025abao, an inspiral of the low-mass companion (\(q\approx {0.1}_{-0.05}^{+0.10}\)) down to the He core of the 7M⊙ primary releases ΔEorb ≈ 8 × 1047 erg, whereas the binding energy of the primary envelope is about 1.6 × 1047 erg. A merger that fails to eject the envelope therefore implies \(\alpha \lesssim {0.2}_{-0.1}^{+0.2}\). The partial unbinding of the outer envelope requiring approximately 1046 erg further implies α ≳ 0.01, bounding the efficiency as 0.01 ≲ α ≲ 0.4. This constraint is consistent with that inferred from post-CE binaries, which suggest low values of α ≈ 0.1–0.3 (refs. 43,44). However, this formalism assumes that transferred orbital energy is primarily expended in gravitationally unbinding the envelope, whereas our observations show that the dominant energy sink was instead the acceleration of a small fraction of the envelope to speeds well exceeding the local escape speed. The formalism thus provides a useful parametric prescription for predicting CEE outcomes, but fails to capture all the underlying physics.

The inferred bipolar morphology of ejecta in AT 2025abao—expanding freely in the polar directions but confined by equatorial material—confirms the long-standing hypothesis that bipolar planetary nebulae can be shaped by CEE in binary stars45,46,47. CEE in giant stars, similar to that probed here, is also a key step in forming close white dwarf binary systems11 (see section ‘The energetics of common-envelope evolution’), including gravitational wave sources detectable by the future Laser Interferometer Space Antenna. Finally, the multi-decade observations of AT 2025abao demonstrate the way forward to use long-baseline, multiwavelength surveys to connect pre-CEE progenitors to their outcomes. Upcoming surveyors such as the Vera Rubin Observatory48 and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope should routinely find these systems in approximately 100 Milky Way-like galaxies within about 15 Mpc—charting the landscape of binaries undergoing CEE.

Recent findings suggest that the slow brightening of the star WNTR23bzdiq at J2000 coordinates α = 00:38:48.60, δ = +40:46:08.21, detected by the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER)54 survey was first reported in early 2025 (ref. 12). This source was independently identified in a dedicated search for transients using data from the NEOWISE55,56 survey (survey name WTP19aalzlk), and was also detected in the optical by the Zwicky Transient Facility57,58,59,60 (survey name ZTF21abcvhyx). Its rapid brightening in late 2025 was first noted on 2025 October 17 UT by K. Itagaki and independently by R. Fidrich on 18 October 2025 (http://www.cbat.eps.harvard.edu/unconf/followups/J00384865+4046079.html). It was first reported to the Transient Name Server and assigned the name AT 2025abao by ref. 61 on 20 October 2025.

According to recent reports, on 2 November 2025, a previous study17 noted its spectroscopic transition to hot temperatures and the emergence of hydrogen emission lines, resembling early-time properties of the class of eruptions called LRNe22. Over the next 2 months, the spectrum transitioned back to colder temperatures with molecular absorption features (see section ‘Spectroscopic evolution of the LRN eruption’)—the hallmark observational signatures of LRNe22. This robustly establishes AT 2025abao as an LRN, and rules out other low-luminosity eruptions such as Intermediate Luminosity Red Transients62. Reference 18 published optical-IR observations of this source and an independent analysis of the LRN.

Industry observers note that in our analysis, we assume a distance to M31 of 0.77 Mpc (ref. 63), and correct for a Galactic line-of-sight extinction of E(B − V) = 0.09 mag (ref. 64). Following ref. 12, we do not assume additional reddening from M31, as this source is located at the outskirts of the galaxy.

Sources indicate that before proceeding, we briefly clarify the terminology regarding LRNe and CEE adopted in this paper. As the late-2025 eruption AT 2025abao is a bona fide member of the phenomenological LRN class, we refer to it as such throughout the article. LRNe have been established to originate from stellar mergers in binary systems22. AT 2025abao is the first known LRN in which the progenitor primary star is an evolved AGB star with a convective envelope. This makes it a unique probe of classical CEE, which we explore in this paper.

Sources indicate that reference 12 presented optical-IR photometric observations from 2005 to April 2025, compiled using data from the Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope (CFHT), the Palomar Transient Factory (PTF)65, the intermediate Palomar Transient Factory (iPTF)66, the Pan-STARRS (PS1)67,68,69, ZTF, WINTER and NEOWISE surveys. We now describe additional observations of this source.

In the optical, ZTF continued observing AT 2025abao as part of its routine survey operations in the g, r and i bands from April 2025 to February 2026. The ZTF photometry was retrieved using the SkyPortal/Fritz alert brokering system70,71. Moreover, we observed it with the Spectral Energy Distribution Machine (SEDM)72 camera on the 60-inch telescope at Palomar Observatory in the ugri filters on several epochs between November 2025 and February 2026, and reduced the data using FPIPE73. We also monitored it with the GROWTH-India Telescope (GIT)74 in the SDSS g′, r′, i′ and z′ filters at approximately daily cadence and reduced the data with the GIT data processing pipeline74. Finally, we downloaded archival red (RG610) and IR (I) band images from the second Palomar Optical Sky Survey75 (POSS-2) taken on 1 October 1989 and 23 September 1993, in which the progenitor source of AT 2025abao is clearly detected. We calibrated the images relative to the PS1 catalogue and performed aperture photometry to determine the archival brightness of the source.

In the near-IR, the source was observed as part of the routine survey of WINTER from May 2025 to September 2025 during its precursor phase. After the rapid brightening, we obtained Y, J and Hs band observations with WINTER, at a cadence of about 3 days until February 2026. These data were processed using the WINTER data reduction pipeline implemented using mirar76,77. Furthermore, we observed the source with the Wide-Field InfraRed Camera78 on the 200-inch Hale Telescope at Palomar Observatory in the J, H and Ks bands on 26 December 2025; these observations were processed using Python routines for reduction and calibration.

Recent findings suggest that we observed AT 2025abao with the prototype Cerberus high-speed imager mounted at the prime focus of the 200-inch Hale Telescope at Palomar Observatory (G.M. manuscript in preparation), to search for any evidence of rapid variability. The observations were performed on 25 November 2025, lasting 14.7 min in the SDSS-r band at 1 s cadence. AT 2025abao was clearly detected with a signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) of >300 in individual exposures.

Sources indicate that we triggered target-of-opportunity observations (principal investigator V.K.) with the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory79 to obtain ultraviolet (UV) and X-ray imaging on 3 November 2025. The source was detected in all UV bands (u, UVW1, UVM2 and UVW2) by the UltraViolet/Optical Telescope (UVOT)80, but no X-rays were detected in the X-ray telescope81 observations. We continued monitoring the source with Swift/UVOT from 8 November 2025 to 15 November 2025 with a cadence of approximately 2 days.

Sources indicate that the UVOT observations were downloaded and reduced using uvotredux (https://github.com/robertdstein/uvotredux)82, a Dockerized open-source Python package for automated UVOT data reduction using swifttools (https://github.com/Swift-SOT/swifttools) and HEASoft (https://heasarc.gsfc.nasa.gov/docs/software/lheasoft/). Photometry was extracted assuming a 5″ aperture centred on the position of the transient, and background was estimated using an offset 10″ aperture. The X-ray telescope observations were reduced using the online tool83.

According to recent reports, the field of AT 2025abao was first observed by the SPHEREx space mission from 0.7 μm to 5 μm as part of its survey when the source was in its precursor phase, between 9 July 2025 to 15 August 2025, with 95% of the observations conducted before 22 July 2025. The field was observed again between 18 December 2025 and 1 January 2026, during its eruption phase. We used the public SPHEREx spectrophotometry tool to obtain the 0.7–5 μm spectrum of this source at both epochs. The data were examined for quality cuts similar to the metrics described in ref. 84.

Sources indicate that reference 12 presented optical and near-IR spectra of the precursor phase obtained between October 2023 and January 2025. Here, we describe further spectroscopic observations.

Sources indicate that on the night of 8 September 2025, when the source was still in its precursor phase, we obtained a medium-resolution (R ≈ 2,700) near-IR spectrum with the SpeX spectrograph on the NASA Infrared Telescope Facility (IRTF) as part of program 2025B061 (principal investigator D.F.). The spectrum was reduced using the idl package spextool85 and corrected for telluric absorption using the package xtellcor86.

During the 2025 eruption, we obtained a series of R ≈ 8800 optical spectra with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) on the 8-m Gemini North telescope on several nights from 11 November 2025 to 6 February 2026. These observations were obtained as part of Director’s Discretionary Time Program GN-2025B-DD-111 (principal investigator V.K.), and comprised six spectra using the R831 grating (R ≈ 8,800) and six with the B1200 grating (R ≈ 7,400), all using the 0.25 arcsec slit. Data were processed using Data Reduction for Astronomy from Gemini Observatory North and South (DRAGONS)87 software.

We obtained a series of five R ≈ 6,000 optical spectra with the Next Generation Palomar Spectrograph (NGPS) on the 200-inch Hale Telescope at Palomar Observatory, from 11 November 2025 to 26 January 2026 (principal investigator M.K.). These spectra used the 0.4 arcsec slicer, providing the highest spectroscopic resolution. The data were reduced using standard procedures for long-slit spectroscopic data reduction and flux calibration using a custom pipeline developed for NGPS.

According to recent reports, we obtained an R ≈ 4,000 optical spectrum with the Binospec spectrograph88 on the 6.5-m MMT telescope on 13 November 2025 (principal investigator N.R.). The 600 lines per mm grating was used in 3 × 120 s exposures centred at 6,500 Å and 5 × 120 s exposures centred at 8,500 Å. The data are reduced with standard procedures implemented in PypeIt89, and the resulting one-dimensional (1D) spectra are trimmed to remove areas of the spectrum that are contaminated by light from the second order of the grating.

We obtained an R ≈ 25,000 optical spectrum with the Fibre-fed Echelle Spectrograph (FIES)90 mounted on the Nordic Optical Telescope on 23 November 2025 through Fast-Track proposal 72-405 (principal investigator S.d.W.). Observations consisted of 2 × 1,800 s exposures in low-resolution mode and were reduced using the standard FIEStool (https://www.not.iac.es/instruments/fies/fiestool/) pipeline.

Recent findings suggest that we obtained two R ≈ 2,500 optical spectra with the OSIRIS+ spectrograph on the 10.4-m Gran Telescopio Canarias on the nights of 25 December 2025 and 20 January 2026 under program 24-GTC20-A/25B (principal investigator D.J.). On both occasions, three spectra each of 60 s exposure time were obtained using the R2500V and R2500R gratings, in combination with a 0.6-arcsec long slit. Data were reduced and coadded using PypeIt89.

We obtained a series of R ≈ 650 spectra from 24 October 2025 to 30 January 2026 with the Hanle Faint Object Spectrograph (HFOSC) on the 2.4 m Himalayan Chandra Telescope using gratings Gr7 and Gr8 (programs HCT-2025-C3-P27 and HCT-2026-C1-P13, principal investigator S.C.). The spectra were reduced using standard procedures in IRAF.

In a recent development, we obtained a spectrum with the Kast Double Spectrograph at the 3.05 m C. Donald Shane telescope at the Lick Observatory (principal investigator R.M.R.) on the night of 21 November 2025. On the red side detector, the 300/7,500 grating was used, which has a dispersion of 2.55 Å per pixel, and R ≈ 2,800. On the blue side, the 600/4,310 grism was used, which has a dispersion of 1.02 Å per pixel, with R ≈ 3,850. The spectra were reduced using the UCSC Spectral Pipeline (https://github.com/msiebert1/UCSC_spectral_pipeline)91, based on methods described in refs. 92,93.

Industry observers note that we obtained three R ≈ 100 spectra using the Integral-Field Unit spectrograph SEDM72,94 on the 60-inch telescope at Palomar Observatory on 4, 5 and 13 November 2025. These spectra were reduced using the pysedm software95.

In a recent development, we obtained two R ≈ 3,000 NIR spectra of the eruption with the Near-InfraRed Echelle Spectrograph on the Keck II telescope on 9 November 2025 and 12 December 2025 (principal investigator M.K.). We also obtained a spectrum with the Triplespec spectrograph on the 200-inch Hale Telescope at Palomar Observatory on 8 December 2025, and one with NASA/IRTF on 24 December 2025. These spectra were reduced using spextool and xtellcor, as described above.

Recent findings suggest that we obtained mid-IR observations with the JWST on 24 December 2025—under Director’s Discretionary Time Program 12487 (principal investigator V.K.). AT 2025abao was spectroscopically observed with the Medium Resolution Spectrograph on the Mid-InfraRed Instrument96,97, and imaged with Mid-InfraRed Instrument in the F1800W, F2100W and F2550W filters. We downloaded standard level 3 data products available on the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes. The source is detected with S/N ≥ 100 in all JWST observations. We also obtained a GMOS optical spectrum, SpeX NIR spectrum, and Wide-Field InfraRed Camera NIR photometry within a day of the JWST observations. The serendipitous SPHEREx observations were conducted within a week around the epoch of the JWST observations.

Industry observers note that reference 12 modelled the archival SED of the progenitor star and derived \({T}_{\mathrm{eff}}={\mathrm{3,500}}_{-200}^{+200}\,{\rm{K}}\), log(L/L⊙) = 4.2 ± 0.1, Rstar ≈ 350R⊙ consistent with a 7 ± 2M⊙ star in its early AGB phase. The properties of the dust shell depended on the method used: modelling with the PHOENIX model photospheres98 and the radiative transfer code DUSTY99 gave Tdust ≈ 1,450 K, and τV ≈ 2.7, whereas a comparison to pre-computed Grid of Red Supergiant and Asymptotic Giant Branch Models (GRAMS)100,101,102 suggested Tdust ≈ 1,000 K and τV ≈ 1.9. Reference 12 adopted dust opacities from ref. 103 for their DUSTY modelling. However, our JWST data indicate that the dust is comprised of warm oxygen-rich silicates (see section ‘Post-outburst JWST and SPHEREx SED modelling’). Using the updated opacities, we redo the DUSTY progenitor SED modelling using Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling implemented using the Python package emcee104 and the methods outlined in ref. 12. Briefly, we used the log_g=0.0 PHOENIX models as inputs to DUSTY to generate model SEDs for given values of stellar effective temperature (Tstar), dust shell temperature (Tdust) and dust optical depth (τV), which are free parameters in our modelling. Similar to ref. 12, we use a standard MRN distribution for the dust grain size and a dust radial density profile ρ(r) ∝ r−2 expected for wind-like mass loss. We also assume the dust outer-to-inner shell radius ratio (Y) of two for these models, but we note that the constraints on Tstar, Tdust and τV are not sensitive to the exact values of this parameter. We fit the models to the observed SED to derive posterior distributions of these parameters, which are shown in Extended Data Fig. 3.

From our updated modelling, we derive slightly higher stellar parameters of \({T}_{\mathrm{eff}}={\mathrm{3,650}}_{-50}^{+50}\,{\rm{K}}\), \(\log \,(L/{L}_{\odot })=4.2{5}_{-0.02}^{+0.02}\), \({R}_{\mathrm{star}}=330\pm 50{R}_{\odot }\) and dust parameters of \({T}_{\mathrm{dust}}={\mathrm{1,100}}_{-100}^{+100}\,{\rm{K}}\) and \({\tau }_{V}={1.9}_{-0.3}^{+0.3}\)—in good agreement with the GRAMS dust parameters. The inner radius of this dust shell is \({R}_{\mathrm{dust,in}}={\mathrm{4,100}}_{-1,000}^{+1,000}\,{R}_{\odot }\). Comparing to solar abundance stellar evolutionary tracks from MESA Isochrones and Stellar Tracks (MIST v.2.5)105,106,107 downloaded from https://waps.cfa.harvard.edu/MIST/) and the PAdova TRieste Stellar Evolution Code (PARSEC v.2.0)108,109,110,111, we find these values consistent with those expected for a \({7}_{-1}^{+1}\,{M}_{\odot }\) star in its early AGB phase, consistent with ref. 12.

Recent findings suggest that reference 12 revealed that the progenitor brightness did not vary substantially from 2005 to 2015. The even older POSS-2 measurements from 1989 presented here (Fig. 1) suggest that there were no substantial variations for at least a 26-year period. From early 2018 to October 2025, the source steadily brightened at all wavelengths. It first underwent an approximately 1 mag bump from 2020 to 2023. After this, the source rebrightened until December 2024 and then faded by 1 mag over the next 250 days in the g- and r-bands; however, it stayed constant in the i band and brightening in the IR (J, W1 and W2) bands. It then remained in its low optical state for about 50 days until October 2025, when it underwent its eruption.

We constructed multiwavelength SEDs by combining ZTF, NEOWISE and SPHEREx observations during this phase. We interpolated between the measurements using Gaussian process regression to fill in temporal gaps. The Gaussian process model, implemented with the Python package scikit-learn112, used a Radial Basis Function kernel with an added White Noise kernel to account for observational noise, similar to that in ref. 12. For epochs between 2018 and 2024, we fit the SEDs using PHOENIX photospheric models, DUSTY and emcee as described in section ‘Modelling the progenitor SED’. The resulting luminosities, stellar radii and temperatures are plotted as solid lines with the uncertainties marked with shaded regions in Fig. 2. We note that during this phase, the SEDs only have five points covering the 0.4 –4.5 μm wavelength range, of which several g-band measurements are low S/N. Consequently, the inferred values have larger uncertainties compared with the progenitor SED (for example, the uncertainty on stellar temperature ranges from about 100−200 K during this phase compared with the approximately 50 K uncertainty on the progenitor temperature). Despite this, we do not find any changes in the stellar temperature larger than about ±200 K during this phase. This is also consistent with the g–r and r–i colours during this phase that do not show any variations larger than around 0.5 mag (ref. 12). From early to mid-2025, we repeated the above modelling procedure, but for W1 and W2 fluxes we used the Gaussian-process-interpolated values between the last NEOWISE epoch from 2024 and the first SPHEREx epoch from mid-2025. For the last about 20 days of the precursor phase, we only have g- and r-band observations, and DUSTY modelling is infeasible with just two data points. Instead, we simply fit a blackbody model to the SED; however, blackbody fits to only optical data can underestimate the luminosities and radii at these temperatures at which the radiation is expected to peak in the IR region. Based on the 2019–2024 data, we find that using only gr data underestimates the luminosity by a factor of about 2.3 compared with modelling the full SED. For the final phase, we corrected for the luminosities and radii by this factor. These values are plotted as hollow circles in Fig. 2 and should be interpreted with caution.

According to recent reports, our modelling highlights that for most of the precursor phase except the final 300 days, the star stayed at roughly constant temperature \({T}_{{\rm{star}}}\approx {\mathrm{3,800}}_{-200}^{+200}\) K (possibly slightly warmer than the progenitor, as noted in ref. 12), as it steadily expanded and became more luminous. The luminosity and radius increase occur in two ‘ramp-up’ episodes (Fig. 2), corresponding to the two bumps in the optical light curve. Both bumps are accompanied by small increases in dust optical depth (from τV ≈ 1.9 to τV ≈ 2.8), evidenced by the IR brightness continuing to rise even after the optical fades. Moreover, the rapid optical decline at the end of the second bump is accompanied by a temperature drop to about 3,400 K and a rapid around 1.5× increase in luminosity and radius in 200 days—the fastest expansion rate during this phase. Towards the end of the precursor phase, our modelling shows that the star has brightened to about six times its initial luminosity, expanded by about 2.5 times its initial size, and cooled slightly compared with its initial temperature. The inner dust shell temperature and radii are poorly constrained because of the sparse IR SED coverage—the temperature \({T}_{\mathrm{dust}}\approx {\mathrm{1,000}}_{-300}^{+300}\,{\rm{K}}\), whereas the radius expands slowly by a factor of 3 compared with the progenitor.

In a recent development, the 0.7–5 μm SPHEREx spectrum taken about 120 days before the eruption g-band peak provides the best constraints on the pre-eruption state of the system. We combine this with contemporaneous gr measurements from ZTF and model the SED using the PHOENIX models, DUSTY and emcee as described in section ‘Modelling the progenitor SED’. We derive \({T}_{\mathrm{star}}=3,46{0}_{-60}^{+70}\,{\rm{K}}\), \({T}_{\mathrm{dust}}=87{0}_{-200}^{+200}\,{\rm{K}}\) and \({\tau }_{V}={2.6}_{-0.3}^{+0.7}\). The total integrated luminosity is \(L={9.7}_{-0.5}^{+1.1}\times 1{0}^{4}{L}_{\odot }\), corresponding to a dust shell inner radius \({r}_{\mathrm{dust},\mathrm{in}}={1.6}_{-0.7}^{+1.4}\times 1{0}^{4}{R}_{\odot }\) and a stellar effective radius \({R}_{\mathrm{star}}\,=\) \(86{0}_{-30}^{+50}\,{R}_{\odot }\). The best-fit model to the SPHEREx data is shown in Fig. 2, and the posterior distributions on the parameters are shown in Extended Data Fig. 4. We note that the SPHEREx spectrum exhibits NIR water vapour absorption bands stronger than those predicted by the best-fit photospheric model. The SED also exhibits a mixed-temperature behaviour, in which fitting only the NIR data (≥1 μm) yields a lower temperature (T ≈ 3,000 K) than the full optical + NIR data. Both these features can be attributed to increased molecular absorption from circumstellar material around the progenitor primary, as noted by ref. 12 based on other spectra obtained during the precursor phase.

According to recent reports, we note that ref. 18 compared the SPHEREx SED with dusty stellar models and found good agreement of the 1–2.5 μm region with Teff ≈ 3,100 K models—in line with our lower derived photospheric temperatures from the NIR portion described above. However, we also note that their comparisons use stellar models with log_g = 1.0, whereas the observed radius during the precursor and the quiescent phase indicates log_g ≈ 0.

According to recent reports, after the precursor phase ended in September 2025, the source began brightening rapidly. We constructed multiwavelength SEDs using broadband UV to NIR photometric data obtained during this phase. We fit blackbody functions to the SEDs to derive photospheric radii, temperatures and luminosities, which are plotted in Fig. 2. Based on its evolution, this eruption can be divided into three phases: an initial rise lasting about 25 days, a plateau phase lasting around 80 days, and a late decline lasting at least about 30 days.

The initial rise began when the ZTF g-band started brightening on 19 September 2025 (MJD 60937), whereas the r-band began brightening a bit later on 2 October 2025 (MJD 60950). In the next 25 days, the source brightened by 5 magnitudes in the g- and r-bands, while simultaneously becoming hotter. During this phase, the temperature increased rapidly to approximately 8,000 K compared with 3,500 K in the precursor, and the luminosity increased to about 2.5 × 1039 erg s−1—about 10 times that at the end of the precursor phase. The photospheric radius at the start of the initial rise is about three times smaller than in the precursor phase, indicating that the photosphere has moved inwards. During the rise, the photosphere expands rapidly with expansion speeds of about 330 km s−1, significantly higher than the slow expansion in the precursor phase.

It has been revealed that on 27 October 2025 (MJD 60975), the rapid brightening stopped, and the eruption transitioned to a ‘plateau’ phase. The luminosity increased steadily to about 6 × 1039 erg s−1 over the next around 80 days, during which the temperature dropped to approximately 3,000 K. The g-band brightness peaked on 7 November 2025 (MJD 60986), after which it gradually faded by about 1 mag in the next 80 days. During this plateau phase, the bluer bands (u, UVW1, UVM2, and UVW2) faded, with the bluest bands fading fastest, whereas the redder bands (r, i, J and Hs) brightened, with the reddest bands increasing fastest. The photospheric radius continued to expand with a speed of about 330 km s−1.

It has been revealed that the plateau phase ended on 13 January 2026, when the luminosity and photospheric radii started decreasing. As Fig. 1 shows, the redder bands started to fade before the bluer ones, suggesting that the photospheric temperature increased slightly. The source was still in this phase by mid-February 2026, when it went into solar conjunction.

Industry observers note that the peak luminosity of about a few 1039 erg s−1, rapid transition from hot to cold temperatures, and photospheric expansion speeds of 330 km s−1 are hallmark signatures of LRNe. Figure 2 compares these properties with M31-LRN-201541,49,50 and V838Mon21, which had similar peak luminosities to AT 2025abao. The main difference is that the duration of the plateau phase in AT 2025abao is longer than that in the other events. Other than this, AT 2025abao is similar to these events.

Extended Data Fig. 1 and Extended Data Fig. 2 show the optical and NIR spectroscopic evolution of AT 2025abao. Spectra presented by ref. 12 spanning 2023 to early 2025, during the precursor phase, resembled late M-type stars with oxygen-rich molecules12. We present an additional NIR spectrum from IRTF during this phase, obtained on 9 September 2025 (Fig. 2), which also exhibits these features.

During the initial rise in October 2025, the spectrum had transitioned to a hot blue continuum with strong hydrogen emission lines, with a Gaussian full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) of about 900 km s−1. Several narrow metallic absorption lines such as Na ID, Fe II are also visible. In the next 3 months through the plateau and late decline phase, the spectrum gradually cooled down and developed absorption features of oxygen-rich molecules, closely resembling a late-time spectrum of the LRN AT 2021biy (refs. 52,113). This spectral evolution is the hallmark of LRNe (for example, refs. 20,21,22,23,34,51,113,114,115,116; Fig. 3), cementing the classification of AT 2025abao.

Recent findings suggest that our spectroscopic coverage allows us to trace ejecta velocities in all phases of the eruption. Low-resolution spectra during the initial rise suggest that the FWHM velocities decreased from about 900 km s−1 to 600 km s−1 until the g-band peak. The subsequent higher-resolution spectra from NGPS, GMOS, FIES and Binospec show that this velocity decreased within 20 days to approximately 150 km s−1 and remained low for at least 80 days after the g-band peak (Fig. 3).

The Hα lines in these spectra exhibit a two-component profile, with a broader emission component and a narrower absorption component (Fig. 3). The centre of the absorption component in the earliest spectrum is about 20 km s−1 blueshifted relative to rest wavelength, confirming the presence of slow-moving, neutral CBM. With time, the absorption component weakens while the emission component strengthens, indicating that the CBM is being swept up by the shock. At late times, the line profile is asymmetric, with a stronger blueshifted emission, indicative of a recombination front moving towards us along the line of sight. These spectra unambiguously show the presence of shock interactions between fast-moving merger ejecta and slower-moving material. Similar asymmetric line profiles seen in interacting type IIn supernovae have been attributed to disk-like geometries for the circumstellar material19. This is in line with theoretical expectations for equatorially focused CBM geometry32,40. Moreover, it provides a natural explanation for the fast photospheric expansion speeds despite the decelerating spectral line velocities—the merger ejecta are mostly spherically symmetric and expand freely in the polar directions, setting the continuum radiation, while a small fraction are obstructed in the equatorial plane by CBM and decelerated by shock interaction. Our observations of the decelerating ejecta suggest that our view to AT 2025abao is close to edge-on, consistent with that suggested in ref. 18 from a similar analysis of hydrogen line spectral profiles. We note that this exact picture has been theoretically proposed for LRNe in ref. 40, and our observations provide an unambiguous confirmation of this model.

The NIR spectra during the plateau phase (Extended Data Fig. 2) exhibit a bluer continuum compared with the precursor phase spectra and show several metallic absorption lines as well as absorption bands due to CO. Weak CO bands are present even in the earliest post-eruption spectrum taken on 9 November 2025, when the optical spectra do not exhibit any molecular absorption, indicating that some of the pre-existing CO gas remained intact even after the LRN eruption destroyed a large fraction.

Our JWST observations taken 47 days after the g-band peak, together with serendipitous SPHEREx and contemporaneous ground-based optical-NIR observations, provide the earliest optical to mid-IR SED of a post-eruption LRN. Figure 2 shows the 0.5–25 μm SED of the source. These observations show that the SED peaks around approximately 1 μm and declines at longer wavelengths. The SPHEREx spectrum at this phase differs substantially from that in the precursor phase, exhibiting much weaker molecular absorption bands and a bluer continuum. The JWST Medium Resolution Spectrograph spectrum shows a clear, broad emission feature spanning 8–12 μm, attributed to optically thin silicate dust. This emission feature exhibits a peculiar morphology, with humps on the red and blue sides relative to the peak.

Sources indicate that we model the SED using DUSTY and emcee. For the DUSTY modelling, we assume the input radiation is a single blackbody that is surrounded by a dust shell comprising single-sized dust grains and a ρ ∝ r−2 density profile. We examined several dust compositions and find that the shape of the silicate emission feature can be best replicated using opacities for a combination of warm oxygen-rich silicates (Sil-OW) from117 and amorphous silicates of enstatite composition (enst) from118. Both these compositions have been commonly observed around evolved AGB and RSG stars (for example, refs. 119,120). The blackbody temperature (Tstar), dust shell temperature (Tdust), dust optical depth (τV), dust grain size (a), dust shell thickness (Y) and the fractional abundance of Sil-OW relative to enst (asilow) are free parameters. We fit the models to the SED using Markov Chain Monte Carlo implemented with emcee with broad, uniform priors and derive posterior distributions on the parameters, shown in Extended Data Fig. 5.

Industry observers note that from our modelling, we derive \({T}_{\mathrm{star}}={\mathrm{3,840}}_{-50}^{+50}\,{\rm{K}}\), \({T}_{\mathrm{dust}}=87{0}_{-120}^{+80}\,{\rm{K}}\), \({\tau }_{V}=0.1{0}_{-0.04}^{+0.03}\), \(a=0.1{1}_{-0.03}^{+0.03}\,{\rm{\mu }}{\rm{m}}\), \(Y=2{4}_{-12}^{+16}\), \({a}_{{\rm{silow}}}={0.6}_{-0.1}^{+0.1}\) (uncertainties represent 16th and 84th percentiles). The total integrated luminosity \(L={9.6}_{-0.4}^{+0.4}\times 1{0}^{5}{L}_{\odot }\), and the radius of the inner dust shell \({r}_{\text{dust,in}}\,=\)\({4.7}_{-0.8}^{+1.6}\times 1{0}^{4}{R}_{\odot }\).

We analyse the optical light curve of AT 2025abao using a Lomb Scargle (LS) periodogram121,122 to search for periodic signatures. No evidence of periodicity was found in the PTF/iPTF data from 2010 to 2015 (also noted in ref. 12). For the precursor phase, Gaussian process fits were used to detrend the smooth long-duration (≥500 days) variations out of the light curve12, and an LS analysis on the detrended data did not reveal any significant periodic signatures between 2018 and 2025. However, two consecutive about 87-day-long bumps were seen in the r-band light curve in 2023 (ref. 12). The r-band eruption light curve during the plateau phase exhibits low-amplitude (about a few 0.1 mag) flickering with timescales of a few days; however, we do not detect any significant periodicity in these data. The typical cadence of our observations rules out any periods longer than approximately 1 day during the plateau phase of the eruption.

Recent findings suggest that we also analyse the high (1 s)-cadenced observations taken during the eruption plateau using Cerberus, to search for short-timescale intrinsic variations. After correcting for common atmospheric variations using a collection of comparison stars, we find a normalized excess variance (refs. 123,124, NXV) of 3 × 10−5, with light curve scatter of about 0.7%. This is consistent with the NXVs of the comparison stars, indicating no significant intrinsic variability in AT 2025abao beyond the photometric noise. However, we cannot rule out variability on longer timescales or outside the observation window, especially given the limited (14.7 min) baseline of these observations.

Recent findings suggest that our archival photometric observations show no substantial variations from 1989 to 2018. The progenitor SED constructed using data from 2010 to 2012 thus represents the state of the system in the three decades before eruption.

Our DUSTY progenitor modelling can be used to derive the mass loss rate of the progenitor primary, using.

where ηgd is the gas-to-dust ratio, vwind is the terminal wind velocity, τV is the dust optical depth and κV ≈ 5 × 103 cm2 g−1 is the opacity in the V-band. Assuming a typical vwind ≈ 15−20 km s−1 and η ≈ 200, our DUSTY modelling suggests a mass loss rate \(\dot{M}\approx 1{0}^{-5}{M}_{\odot }\,{\mathrm{yr}}^{-1}\). This is substantially higher than what is expected for an isolated early-AGB star, for example, from the prescription in ref. 15, which suggests an expected \(\dot{M}\approx 1{0}^{-7}{M}_{\odot }\,{\mathrm{yr}}^{-1}\). This indicates that the primary star was in a phase of enhanced mass loss before the precursor brightening began.

In a recent development, enhanced AGB mass loss in the presence of a binary companion has been studied by several studies. Primary stars close to or past Roche-lobe overflow lose mass at rates of 10−4−10−3 M⊙ yr−1 (for example, refs. 33,125,126)—over two orders of magnitude larger than standard AGB winds. Even before Roche-lobe overflow, tidal interactions between the AGB star and the companion can increase the mass loss rate26. Binary systems with high eccentricity can undergo enhanced mass loss at periastron126,127. These eccentric binaries can also undergo grazing envelope evolution, in which the companion can launch jets because of enhanced accretion during periastron128,129. Another possibility is the wind Roche-lobe overflow scenario27,28,29,130, in which winds from the AGB star can be equatorially focused onto the secondary, resulting in accretion rates of about 100 times larger than standard wind mass accretion. Although a fraction of this mass is accreted onto the companion, the remainder can escape from the L2 Lagrangian point and produce equatorial, spiral outflows from the system131, consistent with the geometry of the CSM inferred from our spectroscopic observations (see section ‘Spectroscopic evolution of the LRN eruption’). Mass loss rates from unstable mass transfer in binary systems has been calculated in refs. 25,33. These outflows carry out angular momentum from the binary, shrinking the orbit and bringing the stars closer to the onset of CEE.

Our JWST observations probe the outer layers of dust formed during this enhanced mass loss phase. The inner radius of the dust shell in the JWST observations is rdust,in ≈ 3 × 1015 cm. This dust could not have condensed in material ejected in the LRN eruption, as this would imply ejecta speeds exceeding 6,000 km s−1, which are not observed. This dust could also not have condensed during the precursor eruption phase, as that would require precursor ejecta velocities ≥160 km s−1, substantially higher than the escape velocity at the surface of the progenitor (87 km s −1). This indicates that the dust existed even before the precursor, during the enhanced mass loss phase of the binary system. Comparing the dust optical depths and dust shell inner radii inferred from the JWST observations to the progenitor further highlights that both dust components are probably part of the same dust outflow. Assuming ρ ∝ r−2, the dust optical depth τ is inversely proportional to \({r}_{{\rm{dust,in}}}^{-1}\). Our inferred values show that \({\tau }_{\mathrm{progenitor}}/{\tau }_{\mathrm{JWST}}=1{8}_{-6}^{+18}\) is broadly consistent with \({r}_{\mathrm{JWST}}/{r}_{\mathrm{progenitor}}=1{2}_{-5}^{+7}\). We also find that the JWST dust lies just beyond the distance out to which pre-existing dust could be destroyed by the 2025 LRN eruption. The maximum distance within which dust can be destroyed by this eruption is given by132.

Sources indicate that where Lpeak is the peak luminosity of the eruption, Qr is the dust scattering efficiency in the r-band (taken from ref. 103), a is the grain size, and Ts is the dust sublimation temperature. This suggests that the AT 2025abao eruption destroyed dust only out to about 1015 cm, lower than the dust shell inner radius derived from the JWST observations (approximately 3 × 1015 cm). We therefore conclude that the dust probed by the JWST observations is remnants of the pre-existing dust from enhanced mass loss in the progenitor binary, which was not sublimated by the 2025 eruption.

Recent findings suggest that the dust mass surrounding the progenitor binary before merger can be used to constrain its mass ratio. Our inferred DUSTY parameters can be converted to the total dust mass using133.

Recent findings suggest that the most uncertain parameter in equation (3) is the shell thickness Y, as we cannot determine it uniquely for the progenitor or the JWST SED. As both the progenitor and JWST SEDs probe the same dust shell, Yprog = (rin,JWST/rin,prog)YJWST. Using the values inferred from our SED modelling, we derive a dust mass around the progenitor of \({M}_{\mathrm{dust,prog}}={6}_{-4}^{+5}\times 1{0}^{-5}\,{M}_{\odot }\) .

We now compare this dust mass estimate with theoretical expectations from Roche-lobe overflow from a binary system. First, we use the Python package RLOF33 that models mass loss from a binary system before the onset of common-envelope evolution using a semi-analytical formalism developed in refs. 32,33. We make several assumptions about the progenitor binary system— we assume a primary mass of 7M⊙ and the primary radius of 350R⊙, a structure coefficient of 4/3 and an adiabatic structure coefficient of 5/3, and no co-rotation of the binary system. Varying these parameters results in about 50% variations in the mass loss rates33,134. We compute the cumulative mass lost by integrating the mass loss rates output by RLOF for several mass ratios (q = Msecondary/Mprimary) ranging from 0.01 to 1, and convert them to dust masses assuming a dust-to-gas ratio Xdg = 5 × 10−3.

Second, we computed stellar and binary models with MESA, v.r12115, using a numerical setup closely following30, with modifications specific to the present system as described below. We adopted a solar metallicity of Z = 0.0142 (ref. 135). Convection was treated using the Ledoux criterion136, with a mixing-length parameter αMLT = 1.82, semiconvection with αsemi = 0.1 (ref. 137), and the same overshooting prescription used in the MIST calibration106. Wind mass loss was included through a Reimers prescription on the RGB with ηR = 0.1 (ref. 15) and a Blöcker prescription on the AGB with ηB = 0.2 (ref. 138). We used an extended nuclear network, constructed from pp_cno_extras_o18_ne22.net with add_co_burn, to follow consistently the H-, He-, and C/O-burning channels relevant for these donor models. The numerical mesh was refined relative to the default settings near convective boundaries and strong composition gradients.

Industry observers note that motivated by the inferred progenitor properties, we focused on a 7M⊙ donor sequence, which provides the closest match to the allowed progenitor region in the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram. Within this sequence, we selected donor models that filled their Roche lobe at Rd ≃ 340R⊙, corresponding to the observationally allowed progenitor region. For each such donor model, we considered accretor-to-donor mass ratios Ma/Md = {0.01, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5}, and thus different companion masses, setting the initial orbital separation in each case with the Eggleton approximation for the equivalent-volume Roche-lobe radius139. In all calculations, the initial orbit was assumed to be circular. Mass-transfer rates were computed with the Kolb prescription140. To bracket the uncertain role of mass and angular-momentum loss, we considered two limiting cases: fully conservative mass transfer and a fully non-conservative isotropic re-emission limit, in which all transferred material that is not retained is removed from the vicinity of the accretor with the specific orbital angular momentum of the accretor141,142. In all calculations, the accretor was treated as a point mass.

In a recent development, we do not include tides or donor rotation in our fiducial calculations. The reason is that, in the regime of interest here, the decisive phase of the interaction is the rapid mass-transfer runaway after the onset of Roche-lobe overflow. Once mass transfer begins, the transfer rate rises on a timescale of only decades, such that the resulting orbital evolution is controlled primarily by the unstable mass-transfer feedback rather than by the much slower tidal redistribution of angular momentum. In this sense, the omission of tides and rotation is a deliberate simplification aimed at isolating the dominant driver of the final approach to outer-lobe overflow.

Industry observers note that as a consistency check, we carried out a small set of additional MESA calculations, including donor rotation and convective-envelope tides, using the Hut_conv prescription, which is based on ref. 143. These exploratory models show that, although many systems formally enter the Darwin-unstable regime before contact, the donor is already strongly non-synchronous by that stage, indicating that tidal torques are too weak to maintain co-rotation during the rapid late-AGB expansion. As a result, the subsequent evolution from first Roche-lobe overflow to outer-lobe overflow is nearly unchanged relative to the non-rotating models. This supports our interpretation that, for the systems considered here, crossing the Darwin boundary signals the loss of a stable synchronized equilibrium, but does not by itself introduce a new fast inspiral timescale144.

Apart from ordinary Roche-lobe overflow, we tracked the outer-lobe radius of the donor using the fit in ref. 30, and terminated the one-dimensional binary calculations when the donor filled its outer lobe. Beyond the onset of outer-lobe overflow, the mass loss is expected to become strongly non-spherical and dynamically driven, such that the subsequent evolution is no longer robustly represented by hydrostatic one-dimensional calculations; this is the same motivation adopted in ref. 30 in delimiting the regime of validity of the MESA binary models. At that point, we stored the full stellar structure and used it to evaluate the binding energy of the remaining envelope. For a chosen mass coordinate m, we calculated.

where u is the specific internal energy.

Sources indicate that we compare the theoretically computed dust masses about 10 years before the orbital separation becomes equal to the primary radius to our inferred progenitor dust mass from above in Extended Data Fig. 6. Our measured dust mass suggests that the progenitor binary has a low mass ratio \(q=0.1{0}_{-0.05}^{+0.10}\), suggesting that the companion is a low mass 0.7M⊙ star.

Sources indicate that following the quiescent phase, the system started brightening slowly, starting in 2018. This precursor phase differs phenomenologically from other LRNe, in which it has been well-studied. First, the optical light curves of other LRNe such as V1309Sco (ref. 20), M31-LRN-2015 (refs. 34,49,50) and AT 2019zhd (refs. 51,52) show that they brightened by several magnitudes over their quiescent luminosities during their precursor phase, whereas AT 2025abao brightened only by about 1 mag (Extended Data Fig. 7). Second, the AT 2025abao precursor phase lasted about 7 years, corresponding to <10 orbital periods of the system (Porb ≈ 280 days for a low mass companion orbiting close to the surface of the primary, and larger for companions further away). This is substantially shorter than in other well-studied LRN precursors such as V1309Sco and M31-LRN-2015, in which the slow precursor brightening lasted for over a hundred orbits (Fig. 4).

Industry observers note that the precursor brightening seen in LRNe has generally been attributed to outflows from the binary system, for example, from L2 mass loss, that can produce a slow brightening of the binary over several hundred orbits34,35,36. However, these outflows cannot power the precursor brightening in AT 2025abao. The kinetic luminosity of the outflows is given by.

Industry observers note that where the radiative efficiency η ≪ 1 (ref. 35). This is significantly lower than the precursor luminosity increase of ⪆ 1038 erg s−1 observed for AT 2025abao, even for mass loss rates as high as 1M⊙ yr−1. Furthermore, this is also lower than the quiescent progenitor luminosity (about 7 × 1037 erg s−1), showing that outflows are not energetic enough to alter the brightness of the progenitor. As noted in ref. 35, slow brightening due to L2 mass loss, similar to that seen in V1309Sco, is expected only for short-period binaries (P ≤ 30 days), where the outflow kinetic energy is high relative to the binary luminosity. This condition is true for LRNe with main-sequence or Hertzsprung gap progenitors such as V1309Sco and M31-LRN-2015, and thus L2 mass loss is probably responsible for slow brightening by several magnitudes over around hundreds of orbital timescales that precede their main eruption. By contrast, for binaries such as AT 2025abao, L2 outflows pile up around the binary but are not energetic enough to increase the binary luminosity. This is shown in Fig. 4, which reveals the precursor luminosities and durations as functions of the escape velocity from the primary star. AT 2025abao has the lowest primary escape velocity and the shortest precursor duration (in orbital period units) and cannot be powered by L2 mass loss (grey dashed lines).

Instead, the AT 2025abao precursor is consistent with being powered by energy dissipation due to frictional drag on the companion, as it spirals through the outer envelope of the primary star. The rate of this energy dissipation has been calculated in the context of planetary engulfment by giant stars145,146,147,148,149,150, and can be calculated as.
