It has been revealed that where M1 is the mass of the primary and a is the orbital radius where the companion dissipates energy. Assuming ρ(r) ∝ r−3 in the outer envelope, and the density at the photospheric radius R1 is \({\rho }_{1}\approx 0.1\frac{3{M}_{1}}{4{\rm{\pi }}{R}_{1}^{3}}\) (ref. 148), the energy dissipation rate is given by.

for a companion spiralling at the photosphere of the primary, which is consistent with the median observed precursor luminosity. As noted in ref. 12, the characteristic timescale over which this energy is dissipated is |Eorb|/Ldecay ≈ 1,000 days, corresponding to about five orbits of the system, consistent with the observed durations of the precursor bumps.

In a recent development, our observations show that for most of the precursor phase, the star puffed up at constant photospheric temperature to approximately 2.5 times its initial size. This quasi-static phase is also radiatively efficient—as the drag luminosity Ldecay exceeds the energy required to unbind material and launch outflows (about \(\dot{M}{v}_{\mathrm{esc}}^{2}\))—most (≳90%) of the drag luminosity is radiated. As a reference for the orbital separations involved, attributing the observed excess precursor luminosity entirely to Ldecay suggests that the companion inspiralled from an orbital separation of about 1.5R1 at the start of the precursor to about 0.9R1 at the end of the quasi-static phase. The total excess energy radiated during this quasi-static phase is approximately 1046 erg, consistent with the orbital energy lost during this inspiral in the outer envelope of the primary.

It has been revealed that identifying the precursor variations with a companion inspiral provides an independent constraint of the binary mass ratio (q = M2/M1). A lower limit comes by requiring that a companion inspiralling at the photosphere dissipates energy comparable to the progenitor luminosity, that is, Ldecay(R1) > Lprogenitor, which gives q > 0.05. Similarly, assuming that most of the orbital energy is radiated away, the maximum luminosity of the precursor can be used to impose an upper limit on the companion mass, as \({L}_{\mathrm{decay}}({R}_{1}) < 2{L}_{\mathrm{precursor}}^{\max }\), which gives q < 0.2. These constraints agree well with those determined from the quiescent mass loss measurements above.

Our SPHEREx SED provides an estimate of the mass lost from the system during this inspiral. Our inferred dust parameters (see section ‘SPHEREx pre-outburst SED modelling’) and equation (3) correspond to a dust mass during the precursor phase \({M}_{\mathrm{dust,precursor}}={3}_{-2}^{+3}\times 1{0}^{-4}\,{M}_{\odot }\). For ηgd ≈ 200, this corresponds to a total mass \({M}_{\mathrm{precursor}}=0.0{6}_{-0.04}^{+0.06}\,{M}_{\odot }\). This estimate is broadly consistent with a CBM mass of about 0.1 M⊙ inferred from the spectroscopic properties of the LRN eruption in the section ‘The LRN eruption’. Theoretically, we estimate the mass loss rate during the precursor phase by assuming that it is proportional to the rate at which mass is gravitationally swept up by the companion146.

According to recent reports, where we define βml as a mass-loss efficiency. For βml ≈ 0.1 and a precursor phase duration of about 7 years, this suggests approximately 0.1M⊙ expelled during this phase, broadly consistent with the observed estimates.

According to recent reports, these observations of a quasi-static, radiatively efficient inspiral in the outer envelope of the primary closely match the expectations of theoretical CEE studies that include the effects of convection5,6. These studies show that, as the companion inspirals through the outer convective envelope, excess energy can be efficiently transported to the stellar surface by convection and radiated away. The outer inspiral is therefore expected to be radiatively efficient and not contribute significantly to launching outflows and unbinding the envelope5. Theoretical light curve models of the inspiral phase in these systems predict timescales and luminosities broadly consistent with those observed in the AT 2025abao precursor8.

It has been revealed that our observations of the final about 300 days of the precursor phase show a drop in the photospheric temperature. As Ldecay ∝ a−5/2, energy dissipation increases rapidly as the companion spirals further into the star, and eventually the companion can no longer respond quasi-statically. This phase therefore probably corresponds to a plunge of the companion deep within the envelope of the primary, eventually culminating in the LRN eruption. The duration of this phase corresponds to about 6 dynamical timescales of the envelope.

These observations agree well with CEE simulations involving AGB primaries, which predict a rapid plunge-in phase lasting a few hundred days38,151,152,153,154,155. A possibly relevant case is one in which the initial binary is eccentric151,152. In these cases, the orbital separation oscillates on timescales of about hundreds of days apart from decreasing rapidly (for example, fig. 7 in ref. 151) as the binary circularizes while undergoing CEE. It is reasonable to expect this behaviour to be imprinted on the precursor luminosity. As noted in ref. 12, the r-band precursor of AT 2025abao indicates modulations on three distinct timescales—a long bump lasting 1,500 days, followed by two small-amplitude bumps lasting about 87 days each, followed by the second long-duration bump of around 1,000 days. These timescales could be indicative of an eccentric orbit for the progenitor binary. Future detailed theoretical modelling of the precursor phase of AT 2025abao will help explore this possibility.

In summary, our modelling of the precursor phase highlights that it was powered by a low mass companion spiralling through the outer envelope that eventually underwent a dynamical plunge-in deep into the stellar envelope.

Industry observers note that following the precursor phase, the source rapidly brightened and transitioned to the LRN eruption with fast-moving ejecta, marking the culmination of CEE. The rise time to peak luminosity is governed by the photon diffusion timescale through this fast ejecta, and is given by39,41,156,157.

For tpk ≈ 20−25 days and vfast ≈ 800−900 km s−1 from our early time spectra, we get Mej ≈ 0.14−0.25M⊙. The expected peak luminosity from cooling of this expanding ejecta is about 2 × 1039 erg s−1 (ref. 157), consistent with the observed peak luminosity at the end of the initial rise. As outlined in refs. 40,41, this initially ejected material is probably spherically symmetric and expands freely in the polar direction, but it can be obstructed by pre-existing CBM in the equatorial plane.

Our spectra show clear signs of shock interactions of the fast-moving ejecta with CBM. The hydrogen emission line velocity decreases from about 900 km s−1 to 150 km s−1. This velocity deceleration matches the expectation for momentum-conserving collisions between fast-moving ejecta and CBM with a density profile ρ ∝ r−2 (ref. 40) (Fig. 3). The total CBM swept up is about five times the initial ejecta mass. Assuming that the CBM is distributed in a disk that covers 20% of the solid angle subtended by the initial spherically symmetric ejecta, the total mass of CBM swept up is approximately 0.1−0.2M⊙, comparable with the mass of the fast-moving ejecta. These estimates are also consistent with the mass lost during the precursor phase estimated in the section ‘The precursor’. The total kinetic energy dissipated is about 3 × 1047 erg, indicating that these shock interactions are energetic enough to power the observed plateau that radiated a total energy of about 4 × 1046 erg. This confirms theoretical studies of the role of shock interactions in powering LRN light curves40,42.

It has been revealed that the AGB progenitor primary of AT 2025abao differs from those of other LRNe, which have main sequence or Hertzsprung gap primaries22,23,113,114,115,158,159,160,161,162. Main sequence or Hertzsprung gap stars have tightly bound radiative envelopes, and companions that are engulfed in these envelopes are expected to merge with the core of the primary star24,25, whereas the loosely bound convective envelope of the AGB progenitor primary of AT 2025abao makes a successful envelope ejection possible. However, several pieces of evidence indicate that CEE in AT 2025abao culminated in a merger.

First, the kinetic energy of the fast-moving ejecta is about 1048 erg. Assuming orbital energy decay is the main energy reservoir, this requires the low-mass (q ≈ 0.1) companion to have inspiralled down to a radius of about 3R⊙ (Fig. 4), which coincides with the radius of the helium core of the primary. Second, the total unbound mass during the precursor and eruption phases is approximately 0.2−0.4M⊙, which is a small fraction (approximately 10%) of the primary envelope, suggesting that most of the primary envelope has remained intact after the event. Third, the main eruption of AT 2025abao is similar to other LRNe (Extended Data Fig. 9), which are known to result from stellar mergers. Finally, the transition from the slow variations during the inspiral to the rapid brightening of the main eruption to high luminosities (>1039 erg s−1) points to a sudden energy deposition episode within the common envelope, which would be expected in case of a violent merger of the companion with the primary core.

Although this evidence points towards a stellar merger, we discuss future observations that would conclusively rule out a tight surviving binary that is gradually inspiralling within and stripping away the remnant envelope through a self-regulated inspiral, as proposed by several theoretical studies163,164,165,166,167. First, sustained mass loss from a surviving binary would likely result in a slow or no evolution of the dust shell radius inferred from late-time IR observations168. By contrast, a merger would have a shell expanding at speeds comparable to those inferred from the eruption, as has been seen in other LRNe168. Second, using equation (7), the energy deposition rate of the companion inspiralling at an orbital separation of about 10R⊙ is Ldecay ≈ 1037 erg s−1. As this luminosity is comparable to that of the progenitor primary star—and LRN remnants remain overluminous relative to their progenitors even a decade after eruption168,169—observations conducted decades later could be sensitive to this energy dissipation. Third, additional energy deposition from a surviving binary would also provide mechanical power to the ejecta, affecting their kinematics. Extended Data Fig. 8 indicates the expected spectral velocity evolution, similar to section ‘Spectroscopic evolution of the LRN eruption’, but by including an additional mechanical power source of magnitude \(\dot{E}\). The observed velocity evolution from our spectra constrains the mechanical power deposited by such a binary to \(\dot{E} < 1{0}^{40}\,\mathrm{erg}\,{{\rm{s}}}^{-1}\). For context, the orbital energy of a binary comprising the primary core and the companion at a separation of about 10R⊙ is approximately −1047 erg. Assuming all dissipated orbital energy is converted to mechanical power, this limit implies that the orbital decay timescale of a surviving binary exceeds about 100 days. Spectral line profile monitoring over a longer temporal baseline will probe lower values of \(\dot{E}\), corresponding to longer decay timescales. Finally, dynamical instabilities can produce large-amplitude pulsations in the surviving envelope165, which should be detectable by future photometric monitoring of AT 2025abao.

Assuming that orbital energy decay constitutes the main energy reservoir, the energy budget of the CEE event in AT 2025abao can be expressed as.

Sources indicate that where ΔEorb is the total orbital energy lost by the inspiralling companion, Eunbind is the energy expended in unbinding part of the envelope, Erad is the energy radiated away, and KEej is the kinetic energy imparted to the ejecta. We plot these quantities inferred for AT 2025abao from our observations in Fig. 4. We find that during the rapid plunge, almost all ΔEorb (≈ 1048 erg) was transferred to the kinetic energy of a small amount of unbound material that requires Eunbind ≈ 1046 erg to unbind it. During this phase, only a small fraction of ΔEorb was radiated away (Erad ≈ 1046 erg). We note that this differs from the quasi-static slow inspiral phase, during which most of the energy dissipated due to frictional drag was radiated away (see section ‘The precursor’). Therefore, it seems that the initially radiatively efficient slow inspiral that powered the slow brightness variations rapidly transitioned to a kinetically efficient plunge that powered the rapid eruption.

We now examine AT 2025abao in the context of the energy formalism of CEE4,9,10,11 that is widely used in binary population synthesis models to predict the outcome of CEE in binary systems. In this formalism, a binary is considered to have survived the CEE by successfully ejecting the common envelope if.

It has been revealed that holds true for a value of af, the final orbital separation, exceeding the core radius of the primary. Ebind is the binding energy of the envelope exterior to af, ΔEorb(af) is the orbital energy lost in an inspiral to af, and α is an efficiency parameter representing the fraction of orbital energy that goes into unbinding the envelope. Observational constraints on α have primarily been derived by backward modelling of post-CE binary systems43,44,53,170,171,172,173,174,175. Although this method is limited by several uncertainties about binary evolution53, the indicative constraints obtained by modelling close double white dwarf (WD) systems and WD-M dwarf binaries suggest low values of α in the range of 0.1−0.3 (refs. 43,44).

Sources indicate that as seen in Fig. 4, the dissipated orbital energy exceeds the envelope binding energy for orbital separations lower than 20R⊙. Adopting values of α ≈ 1 would therefore suggest that the binary survived at this orbital separation, inconsistent with our observations that point to an even deeper inspiral (to about 3R⊙) resulting in a stellar merger. Building on this, we use the progenitor binary parameters inferred for AT 2025abao to constrain the values of α that would make equation (11) consistent with the observed merger outcome of its CEE.

Industry observers note that we determine the binding energy of the primary envelope as a function of radius from our MESA model (as defined in section ‘Comparisons to theoretical predictions of enhanced mass loss’ and plotted in Fig. 4). We note that our binding energy calculation includes the internal energy of the envelope (as in ref. 44). We compare this with the dissipated orbital energy of a low-mass object \(q={0.1}_{-0.05}^{+0.10}\) through this envelope. Our observations indicate the companion inspiralled to merge with the helium core (R ≈ 3R⊙), resulting in a dissipated orbital energy of about 8 × 1047 erg. The binding energy of the envelope outside this radius is about 1.6 × 1047 erg. A stellar merger implies equation (11) is never true for af > 3R⊙, which implies \(\alpha < {0.2}_{-0.1}^{+0.2}\). The uncertainty in this upper limit comes from the uncertainty on the companion mass (Fig. 4). Our upper limit of α ≲ 0.4 is broadly consistent with the values inferred from the post-CE binary systems described above. In a similar vein, an absolute lower limit on α can be inferred from our observations using the inferred ejecta mass. Our observations show that approximately 0.2−0.4M⊙ was unbound from the system. The energy required to unbind the outermost about 0.2−0.4M⊙ of the envelope is about 1046 erg. Comparing this to the dissipated orbital energy shows that α ≳ 0.01.

Industry observers note that we compare this direct constraint on α with that derived for modelling post-CE binary systems. We use the mass ratios and α values inferred for the progenitors of such systems in ref. 53 in Fig. 4. As the α values reported in ref. 53 do not include the contribution of internal energy, we multiply their reported values by 0.5 to include its dependence on the envelope-binding energy (section 4 of ref. 53). Although the uncertainties on the post-CE α measurements are high, the values are broadly consistent with our constraint.

The low values of α inferred for post-CE systems (about 0.01–0.3; refs. 43,53) are consistent with a picture in which a substantial fraction of the released orbital energy is ultimately not available to unbind the envelope. This effective reduction in the coupling of orbital energy to envelope ejection could arise for several reasons, including energy being transported outwards and radiated, energy going into other forms of envelope motion or expansion, or uncertainties in the envelope binding energy used in the standard energy formalism. Efficient convection in the extended AGB envelope provides a physically motivated mechanism for transporting deposited orbital energy to the surface, where it can be radiated away5,6,8. The observed transition from a prolonged radiatively efficient phase to a rapid plunge provides further evidence consistent with this latter interpretation.

Recent findings suggest that we note that although the energy formalism is a useful parametric prescription for predicting the outcomes of CEE, our observations demonstrate that it fails to fully capture the underlying physics of CEE. The α-prescription assumes that the transferred orbital energy is primarily expended towards unbinding the envelope and ejecting it at the escape velocity of the primary star. However, our observations show that only about 1% of the orbital energy was used to unbind a small fraction of the envelope, and a large fraction was expended to accelerate these ejecta to speeds much higher than the primary escape speeds. Future detailed simulations will shed light on the physics of CEE in AT 2025abao.

The progenitor binary system of AT 2025abao resembles the progenitors of post-CE binaries hosting massive white dwarfs176,177,178. Reference 179 modelled 2M07515777+1807352—a binary system comprising a 1.08M⊙ WD with a 0.66M⊙ main sequence companion—and found that it probably formed through a CEE episode when the massive primary (about 6–7M⊙) was in its early or thermally pulsing AGB phase. The inferred progenitor masses for this system are thus remarkably similar to those of AT 2025abao. If confirmed by future observations, our identification of a likely merger in AT 2025abao would suggest that the formation of these systems requires CEE to occur during the thermally pulsing AGB phase, when the envelope is even more extended than that of the early-AGB primary in AT 2025abao.

In a recent development, in summary, our observations of AT 2025abao present an end-to-end characterization of a system undergoing CEE. Extended Data Fig. 10 indicates a graphical representation of the different phases of AT 2025abao presented. Looking ahead, searches for CE transients that leverage synergies between optical and IR time-domain surveys, such as the Vera Rubin Observatory48 and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope are poised to uncover the diversity of CEE outcomes. These surveys have the sensitivity to characterize CE transients similar to AT 2025abao in about 100 Milky Way-like galaxies to a distance of around 15 Mpc (refs. 8,52,180).

Optical spectra of the AT 2025abao eruption. Its spectral evolution matches the characteristic evolution seen in LRNe — blue continuum with emission lines at early times that transitions to a red continuum with molecular absorption features at late times.

Near-infrared spectra of AT 2025abao, from its precursor phase (red) and the eruption (blue). The spectra during the precursor phase resemble late M-type stars, while those during the eruption reveals a transition to hotter temperatures. Notably, the CO absorption bands are seen in all spectra, indicating that some molecular gas remains intact even after the eruption.

See section ‘Modelling the progenitor SED’ for details.

See section ‘SPHEREx pre-outburst SED modelling’ for details.

See section ‘Post-outburst JWST and SPHEREx SED modelling’ for details.

It has been revealed that theoretically calculated dust mass around the quiescent progenitor system as a function of binary mass ratio using analytical prescriptions (black line) and detailed simulations (squares). The black shaded region marks the range expected by varying stellar parameters in the analytical model (section ‘Comparisons to theoretical predictions of enhanced mass loss’). The observed dust mass from the archival progenitor SED and the JWST observation is shown in purple, which constrains the system mass ratio to \(q=0.1{0}_{-0.08}^{+0.10}\).

Previously identified sources such as V1309Sco, M31-LRN-2015, AT 2019zhd (circles) exhibit a gradual brightening by several magnitudes prior to its eruption. AT 2025abao (stars) differs from these sources, as it only highlights a bumpy  ≈ 1 magnitude brightening before transitioning to its eruption.

It has been revealed that evolution of FWHM velocities inferred from our spectra (red), compared to theoretical expectations for momentum-conserving collisions with CBM following a ρ(r) ∝ r−2 density profile (blue solid line). The broken lines indicate the expectation by including an additional mechanical power source, such as a surviving binary, injecting momentum into the ejecta. Our observations constrain the magnitude of this power source \(\mathop{E}\limits^{.}\lesssim 1{0}^{40}\) erg s−1.

According to recent reports, LRNe for which progenitor primary stars have been identified are plotted as coloured points, colour-coded by the binding energy of the star. LRNe with no progenitor identifications are plotted as grey points. The eruption of AT 2025abao (star) is remarkably similar to other LRNe, despite having a progenitor with the lowest binding energy ever measured.

a, The quiescent binary system comprising a  ≈ 7 M⊙ AGB and a  ≈ 0.7 M⊙ star, surrounded by an extended dust shell from mass loss from the binary following Roche Lobe overflow of the primary. b, The precursor brightening phase that began in 2018, marking the onset of CEE, powered by frictional drag on the inspiraling companion lasting for  ≈ 7 years. The mass outflow rate during this phase is  ~10−2 M⊙ yr−1, producing  ~0.1 M⊙ of CBM in an equatorial disk around the binary (dark brown). c, The ballistic eruption in late 2025 from the merger of the inspiraling companion with the primary core, resulting in the ejection of  ≈ 0.1 − 0.2 M⊙ of the primary envelope, and sublimation of a large fraction of dust around the binary. d, The eventual lightcurve powered by shock-interactions between freely expanding merger ejecta (indicated by yellow arrows) and equatorially focused CBM. The surviving pre-existing dust is traced by our JWST observations. The black arrows between the panels indicate the progression of time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Omari Hutchinson has spoken about his preferred role, while praising the AC Milan fans and revealing his belief the Scudetto is a realistic target.

Hutchinson joined Milan on an initial loan deal from Nottingham Forest with an option to buy. He scored his first goal for the club in the away win over Udinese last month, and is getting more regular minutes on the right side.

In a recent development, read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

In fact, the head coach Ruben Amorim has even deployed him as a wing-back on occasion. Given the injuries to Alexis Saelemaekers and Samuel Chukwueze the Englishman’s role has become an even more important one than first imagined.

It has been revealed that hutchinson met with fans this afternoon at the Milan Store in San Babila in the city centre. While at the event, the winger gave an interview to the reporters who were present, with MilanNews relaying his words.

Industry observers note that how have these first few months at Milan been? Are you raising your game?

“It’s going well, the coach is happy, but I think there’s still a lot to do. I’m earning myself some space… From here on out, we have to keep winning.”.

We often see you on the wing. Do you prefer to play there or as a second striker?

It has been revealed that “Personally, I like to play anywhere, but preferably on the right flank. Then, wherever the coach puts me, I try to adapt, do my job, and perform to my best, following his tactical instructions. He knows what I can do with the ball. He simply tells me to create and give my all.”.

How is your relationship with Amorim?

“He talks to me about what to do with the ball and to do my best.”.

Why this difference in performance between Serie A and the Europa League?

According to recent reports, “It’s hard to say… There have been games where we haven’t performed well due to silly mistakes, but I think we need to push forward from now on and get back on track for the Europa League. We have the right team to do it. We need to win and be at our best in every game.”.

What has struck you most about the fans in Italy these past months?

According to recent reports, “Definitely the passion surrounding the club. At the stadium, everyone is behind the team. It’s fantastic, I’ve never experienced anything like it before.”.

Do you think Milan can win the Scudetto?

“We’ve got the players, we have a good squad, and even though we’re still missing some leaders at times, I think we’re building on that. I think the coaches and the coaching staff are guiding us very well. Once everything clicks together perfectly, we’ll do great things.”.

Do you still see yourself at Milan in the coming seasons?

“It’s my dream. After this season, I hope to be signed permanently. I see myself playing here for a long time to come.”.

What’s the feeling of playing in a historic stadium like San Siro?

“It’s crazy. The fans, even the away fans… It’s a unique feeling. It makes you want to give your all for the fans, create special moments, and win.”.

What are the differences between the Premier League and Serie A?

“They’re both tough. When other teams play against Milan, they always want to give their all. They’re always tough matches. Tactically, it’s more defensive here.

“In the Premier League, you probably have more space and the quality is probably a little higher, but Serie A is a tough league. There’s not that substantial a difference, there’s not that big a gap.”.

Is there any team-mate you’ve grown close to?

“No, I have a good relationship with everyone. They’ve all welcomed me very well, and obviously it’s easier with the guys who speak English.”.

Do you dream of making the national team?

It has been revealed that “I’m trying to focus on my club. I want to perform well for Milan and then we’ll see.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Seye Omidiora | 19 Nov 2026 21:32.

Tottenham Hotspur are sweating over the availability of James Maddison ahead of Saturday's Premier League encounter with Ipswich Town, with question marks remaining over whether the attacking midfielder will be fit enough to feature.

Roberto De Zerbi is contending with a lengthy list of injury doubts, as Mykhaylo Mudryk, Martin Dubravka, Savio, Mathys Tel, Lucas Bergvall and Tosin Adarabioyo all face late assessments for various ankle, knee, muscle and calf concerns, while Xavi Simons and Wilson Odobert remain sidelined with knee problems.

With Dubravka doubtful, Antonin Kinsky is poised to retain the gloves between the sticks behind a four-man rearguard featuring Pedro Porro, Micky van de Ven, Andy Robertson and Jan Paul van Hecke.

Remarkably, no Spurs player has scored more league goals than Van Hecke this term, a notable statistic for the two-goal centre-back as the hosts prepare to welcome the Tractor Boys.

In the engine room, Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes are expected to form a central midfield partnership to dictate the tempo of the contest.

Further forward, Archie Gray could be deployed in an advanced central role if Maddison is not risked from the off, flanked by Mohammed Kudus and Omar Marmoush in a dynamic creative trio.

Although Kudus has yet to score a league goal this season, the playmaker's three assists and ability to threaten from unlikely positions make him a potential match-winner for the home side.

Leading the line will be Dominic Solanke, who will look to capitalise on that creative service and spearhead the North Londoners to maximum points on Saturday afternoon.

Tottenham Hotspur possible starting lineup:.

Kinsky; Porro, Van Hecke, Van de Ven, Robertson; Tonali, Fernandes; Kudus, Gray, Marmoush; Solanke.

#15014. Man United head coach Mauricio Pochettino is "the right character" for the Red Devils but he has "a lot to prove"

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1033 w)

Man United head coach Mauricio Pochettino is "the right character" for the Red Devils but he has "a lot to prove"

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Matt Law | 19 Nov 2026 22:09, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 09:06.
  • Ahead of Manchester United's trip to Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday, Sports Mole's Football Editor Matt Law discusses what will be Mauricio Pochettino's first match in charge of the 20-time English champions.
  • According to recent reports, A nice easy start.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Matt Law | 19 Nov 2026 22:09, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 09:06.

Ahead of Manchester United's trip to Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday, Sports Mole's Football Editor Matt Law discusses what will be Mauricio Pochettino's first match in charge of the 20-time English champions.

According to recent reports, A nice easy start. United have only won one Premier League game this season, so there are no easy games at the moment.

Industry observers note that it is a quick turnaround for Pochettino. He had the second USA game against Haiti, finishing at midnight UK time on Tuesday, then flew straight to England and into Carrington to begin work, and was back in again today, Thursday, to prepare.

In a recent development, the preparations are far from ideal with players coming back from international duty, but they are what they are. I think what will be very interesting going forward is the shape Pochettino settles on. I still think it will be a 4-2-3-1 for the majority.

Recent findings suggest that we know Pochettino likes high pressing and fast attacking transitions. There are suggestions he likes Marcus Rashford a lot, though perhaps more the Rashford of a few years ago than the one who has been injured and is potentially coming back in.

According to recent reports, he likes his full-backs to attack. The counter-pressing. He likes his attacking midfielders to be creative, so expect Bruno Fernandes to be given fewer defensive duties and more of a free role in that number 10 position.

Recent findings suggest that pochettino spoke about mentality and togetherness, the culture, and he will want his team aligned. There are no suggestions the players threw Carrick under the bus.

Sources indicate that ultimately it was a mixture of Carrick not being tactically good enough and the players not responding in the end to the management style. The change had to happen.

He speaks on Friday afternoon and will give a team news revision at that point. Suggestions are that Harry Maguire had a slight injury in the Villa game but should be fine. Luke Shaw may or may not be fit. Marcus Rashford may or may not be fit. There will be no Sesko. There will be no Baleba. Lisandro Martinez is back from his suspension.

Sources indicate that patrick Dorgu is back too. He did not play for Denmark over the break but came off the bench to great effect against Villa last time out.

Suddenly there are a lot more options in the defensive areas of the pitch, which has been the major problem for Man United this season.

The midfield is going to be interesting for this game. Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo started against Villa. Andrey Santos is an option in that area of the field as well.

Industry observers note that mason Mount has played there, but I am not convinced by Mount in central midfield. Baleba being out is a major one, because I feel he could be a key player under Pochettino.

There are suggestions he will be out for a shorter period than initially thought after picking up that muscular injury against Roma in the Champions League.

It has been revealed that can Dorgu get himself back in the team? He could be a big player for them going forward. But for now, the key thing is getting the team together and working out how they are going to play.

There is no rest for the wicked either. They go to Portugal next week for the Sporting Lisbon game in the Champions League, then welcome Brentford, then Newcastle and Coventry, then back in Champions League action against Leipzig.

It has been revealed that this period is incredibly busy. The fact that Pochettino was appointed at the end of last week and then had to wait through that second USA game is not ideal, but we have had ideal preparations before and it has still gone wrong anyway.

I do like the Pochettino appointment. He has got a lot to prove. He seems like the right character, and you can tell he really wanted this job.

It is the job he has been linked with numerous times without it ever coming off. Now feels like the right time, and hopefully United can get something against Liverpool.

United's recent record against Liverpool is good. Three games unbeaten, winning both Premier League games last season, including that 2-1 win at Anfield with that late Harry Maguire header.

Recent findings suggest that united are down in 18th in the Premier League: one win, five draws, four defeats. Fourteen goals scored is not awful. Nineteen goals conceded is awful.

Gary Neville said recently that the back four that finished against Villa would get you relegated, and it is difficult to argue against that, but it should be strengthened for this match.

One Premier League win all season is diabolical. Ultimately it is why Carrick lost his job. But the recent performance against Villa, getting two late goals and avoiding defeat, was a major positive.

Going forward, the story is Pochettino, but it is also the players. Where is the professional pride? Can there be a bit more solidity at the back and an end to the defensive errors?

Senne Lammens has had a good start to his career but questions are now being asked. There are a few shots going in around him that he really should be doing better with, and what is happening in front of him is not helping in that regard.

It has been revealed that I would like to see a settled team in the Premier League. Changes have to happen for European games, but get a settled team, get the system playing, get Fernandes in his best position, and get the wingers sorted, whether that is Rashford. Amad Diallo has not scored in almost a year now, so he may have to come out of the team.

I think you are keeping Mbeumo through the middle. Cunha has been decent of late. He has got the players there. Looking forward to this one and we will see what Pochettino can come up with.
